On design cycles, Goodwin believes you can compress the gap between observation and volume realization, but not to shipping a new chip every few weeks, because fabs have three to five month cycle times and chips need a three to five year amortization window. His memorable line: "The equivalent of the frontier model for the chip space is if you can just find a way to structurally carve out a three to six months advantage, you will be winning all of those deployments." He also offered a heuristic for AI timelines: always question your logical assumption, then divide it by four.
https://www.youtube.com/@NoPriorsPodcast

## 🎙 PODCASTS
**Takeaway**: A chip startup is betting that the key to faster AI inference is not just raw compute, but a fundamental rethinking of memory bandwidth to handle the long contexts and massive models that power the next generation of agents.

On the **No Priors** podcast, host **Sarith** spoke with **Walter Goodwin**, founder and CEO of **Fractile**, a full-stack AI chip company building very fast inference chips for the world's largest models. Goodwin explained that while there is an "extraordinary zoo" of AI chips, many are "relatively identikit," relying on the same HBM memory and Tensor Cores. Fractile's bet is on speed, but they realized early on that an SRAM-based approach, while offering high bandwidth, wouldn't scale to the growing context lengths of modern models. This led them to a new architecture focused on achieving extremely high bandwidth to higher-capacity DRAM memories.

Goodwin argued that the real value of speed is not a "snappier chatbot" but in making long-running agents radically faster. He described a "tantalizing mismatch" today where fast inference chips have high bandwidth but low capacity, and are not running long context attention, forcing a flip back to a GPU. Fractile aims to solve this by uniting the scalability of DRAM with the speed advantages of SRAM-based chips. He believes that by compressing the chip design cycle, a company can have more shots on goal and maintain a rolling frontier of bets.

When asked about the timeline for AI to design a full chip from intent to a GDSII file, Goodwin suggested a heuristic of dividing conventional estimates by four. He noted that while final sign-off will remain with established players like **Cadence** and **Synopsys**, there is a huge opportunity for "fuzzy placement algorithms" and surrogate models to accelerate the iterative parts of chip design, much like how AI is now guiding AI model development but remains bottlenecked by compute time for experiments.

A memorable quote from Goodwin: "It's equivalent of the frontier model for the chip space is if you can just find a way to structurally carve out a three to six months advantage, you will be winning all of those deployments."

On No Priors, Walter Goodwin, founder and CEO of full-stack AI chip company **Fractile**, explained why he started the company in summer 2022 around a bet on speed for the world's largest models. He noted the physical constraints remain real: three to five month fab cycle times, three to five year amortization windows, and data center power limits, so the value is in shortening the latency between observation and volume ramp, not shipping a fundamentally new chip every few weeks.

On No Priors, host Sarith spoke with Walter Goodwin, founder and CEO of full stack AI chip company **Fractile**, about what it means to be full stack, the technical bets they're making, why he's so focused on memory bandwidth, and his predictions for frontier model architectures. **Garry Tan** of **Y Combinator** described **Capy** as a 24/7 standup for your agents, highlighting unexpected cross-session coordination where a collaborator's fix wave steered around his own work across multiple threads, all model agnostic. ## 📰 OFFICIAL BLOGS

**Claude for Small Business** now includes 43 workflows and 27 new integrations with tools small businesses already use, including **Shopify**, **Salesforce**, **TikTok**, **Atlassian**, **Zoom**, **Xero**, **Gusto**, **Square**, **Stripe**, and **Zapier**. ## 🎙 PODCASTS

**Takeaway**: Fractile is betting that the real bottleneck for frontier AI is not compute but memory bandwidth, and that a three to six month structural advantage in chip design wins every deployment.

On **No Priors**, **Walter Goodwin**, Founder and CEO of **Fractile**, explained why his company builds very fast inference chips for the world's largest models. He described the current chip landscape as an "extraordinary zoo" of relatively identikit chips, where hyperscalers like **Google** with **TPU**, **Meta** with **MTIA**, **Microsoft** with **Maya**, and **OpenAI** with **Jalapeno** all rely on a small number of ASIC houses, with **Broadcom** as the largest. Fractile's bet is different: after starting with an SRAM-based approach like **Groq** or **Cerebras**, they moved toward working closely with memory vendors to get extremely high bandwidth access to higher capacity **DRAM** memories. Goodwin argued that the snappier chatbot is the "faster horses" of fast inference, and the real prize is making long-running agents radically faster. He noted a tantalizing mismatch: fast inference chips have super high bandwidth but incredibly low capacity, so they cannot run long context attention and still flip back to a GPU. Fractile aims to unite the scalability of DRAM with the speed advantages of SRAM-based chips, with a platform ramping in the second half of next year. On the pace of chip design, he said he always questions logical assumptions and divides timelines by four, suggesting that intent-to-GDSII prototyping could arrive in a few years rather than ten. He also drew a parallel to RSI work: extreme intelligence can guide experiments, but then you are experiment bottlenecked, and the same applies to chip design where place and route tools still run for days.

**No Priors** hosted Walter Goodwin, Founder and CEO of **Fractile**, to discuss building full-stack AI chips for frontier labs. The key takeaway is that winning the AI chip race requires a full-stack approach to carve out a structural 3-6 month advantage over competitors.

Walter explained that **Fractile** is building very fast inference chips for the world's largest models. He noted that the current chip landscape is filled with "relatively identikit chips" from hyperscalers and ASIC houses like **Broadcom**, which all rely on similar technologies like **HBM** and **Tensor Cores**. **Fractile**'s bet is on a full-stack approach, owning everything from front-end design to physical design and advanced packaging, which allows for a more agile closed loop.

A key technical bet for **Fractile** was moving away from an **SRAM**-based chip design, which they worked on for the first two years. They became concerned about its scalability, particularly with growing context lengths. Their new focus is on working with memory vendors to achieve extremely high bandwidth access to higher-capacity **DRAM** memories. He also discussed the challenge of chip design cycles, noting that while AI can accelerate front-end design, physical constraints like fab cycle times (3-5 months) and the need for a 3-5 year amortization window remain. He believes the goal is not to ship new chips every few weeks, but to shorten the latency between an architectural observation and its realization in volume, allowing for more shots on goal.

## 🎙 PODCASTS
**Takeaway**: A full-stack chip startup is betting that raw inference speed, not just snappier chatbots, is the real capability unlock for long-running agents.

On No Priors, host Sarith spoke with Walter Goodwin, Founder and CEO of Fractile, a full-stack AI chip company building very fast inference chips for the world's largest models. Goodwin started the company in summer 2022 after seeing foundation models generalize across everything and wise voices arguing for pouring more compute into models at test time, the AlphaGo lesson brought to language modeling. Their mission: run huge models much faster than today's chips while scaling to models beyond the frontier and extraordinarily long contexts.

Goodwin described an "extraordinary zoo" of accelerators where many are relatively identikit, sharing HBM, Tensor Cores, and advanced packaging with TSMC, with a small number of ASIC houses like Broadcom delivering designs. Fractile instead goes all the way up and down the silicon stack, with front end designers, its own physical design team, back end implementation, and advanced packaging work, all at about 150 people. The bet on speed informed the architecture: after roughly two years on an SRAM-based chip like Grok or Cerebras, they grew worried about scalability as context length ballooned, and pivoted to working with memory vendors to get extremely high bandwidth access to higher capacity DRAM. The platform ramps in the second half of next year, uniting DRAM scalability with SRAM-like speed.

On where speed matters, Goodwin invoked Henry Ford: the snappier chatbot is the faster horse, while the real elevator on capability is making very long running agents radically faster. He flagged a tantalizing mismatch where fast inference chips have high bandwidth but low capacity, so long context attention still flips back to a GPU. He also argued the chip design cycle can compress, but not to shipping a new chip every few weeks, because fab cycle times run three to five months and chips need a three to five year amortization window. Asked about a top semi CEO's prediction of ten years to go from chief architect intent to a usable GDS two file, Goodwin said to divide by four and subtract a bit. His memorable line: "The equivalent of the frontier model for the chip space is if you can just find a way to structurally carve out a three to six months advantage, you will be winning all of those deployments."

He sees a dearth of efforts that go all the way up and down the silicon stack to build fundamentally new capabilities.

For the first two years, Fractile worked on an SRAM-based chip, drawn by the extremely high bandwidth between compute and weights or KV cache, which can drive thousands of tokens per second. But by late 2023 and 2024, growing context length made scalability a concern, pushing the company toward working closely with memory vendors to get extremely high bandwidth access to higher capacity DRAM. The platform ramping in the second half of next year aims to unite the scalability of DRAM with the speed advantages of SRAM-based chips. Goodwin calls the snappier chatbot "the faster horses of fast inference," and points to a tantalizing mismatch: fast inference chips have super high bandwidth but incredibly low capacity, so long context attention still flips back to a GPU.

On architecture churn, he notes models arrive about every two weeks, but sanity comes from finding what is common: LLMs always want orders of magnitude more memory bandwidth, and remain autoregressive and low batch. He is skeptical of shipping a fundamentally new chip every few weeks, citing fab cycle times of three to five months even in a hot lot scenario and the need for a three to five year amortization window. Asked about a top semi CEO's prediction of ten years until intent from a chief architect becomes a fully usable GDS2 file, Goodwin applies his heuristic: divide by four and subtract a bit. He expects end-to-end prototyping within a few years, but notes place and route still runs conventional algorithms for days, and final sign-off with Cadence and Synopsys will not change for quite some time.
https://www.youtube.com/@NoPriorsPodcast

## 🎙 PODCASTS

**Takeaway**: The chip race's real prize is not a faster chatbot but radically faster long-running agents, and whoever compresses the gap between an architectural insight and volume deployment wins the frontier.

On No Priors, Walter Goodwin, founder and CEO of full stack AI chip company **Fractile**, explains why he started in summer 2022 around two observations: foundation models generalizing across everything, and the need to pour more compute into models at test time, the way AlphaGo became superhuman when rolled out at scale. Fractile builds very fast inference chips for the world's largest models, aiming to run them far faster than today's chips while scaling to models beyond the frontier and to extraordinarily long contexts.

Goodwin describes an "extraordinary zoo" of accelerators where many are relatively identikit: HBM memory, Tensor Cores for matrix multiplication, advanced packaging at TSMC, with hyperscaler efforts like Google's TPU, Meta's MTIA, Microsoft's Maya, and OpenAI's Jalapeno largely delivered through a small number of ASIC houses, Broadcom being the largest. He argues there is a dearth of teams going all the way up and down the silicon stack, from architecture and front end design down to physical design and foundry interactions. Fractile is about 150 people, skinny in every sector but owning front end design, physical design, back end implementation, and advanced packaging in house, which lets it run a much more agile closed loop.

The technical journey is the most interesting part. For the first two years Fractile worked on an SRAM based chip, like Grok or Cerebras, exploiting SRAM's extreme bandwidth because it lives on the same silicon as the logic, driving thousands of tokens per second. Toward the end of 2023 and into 2024 they grew worried about scalability, not just model parameters but growing context length. That pushed them toward working closely with memory vendors and logic foundry partners on skunkworks projects to get much higher bandwidth to higher capacity DRAM, a platform ramping in the second half of next year that unites DRAM's scalability with SRAM-like speed. Goodwin calls the snappier chatbot the faster horses of fast inference; the real elevator on capability is making very long running agents radically faster. He notes the tantalizing mismatch today: fast inference chips have super high bandwidth but incredibly low capacity, so long context attention still flips back to a GPU.

On timelines, he questions the assumption that intent-to-GDS2 is ten years away, offering a heuristic of dividing such estimates by four. He sees prototyping end to end within a few years, but notes genuine bottlenecks: place and route tools running for days on NP hard problems, three to five month fab cycle times even on hot lots, and the need for a three to five year amortization window. His framing of the payoff is the sharpest moment of the episode: "It is the equivalent of the frontier model for the chip space: if you can just find a way to structurally carve out a three to six month advantage, you will be winning all of those deployments." The goal is a rolling frontier of bets, ready to trigger the ramp, with more shots on goal rather than a new chip every few weeks.

He expects end-to-end prototyping within a few years, with conventional place and route tools and DRC/LVS signoff remaining valuable bottlenecks for a long time. His closing image is the one that lingers: crack open an NVIDIA system and you find six to nine custom chips working together, so Fractile is trying to build the machine that gives it a rolling frontier of bets and a perennial three to six month wedge.

## 🎙 PODCASTS

**Takeaway**: A full-stack chip startup argues that the real prize in fast inference is not a snappier chatbot but radically faster long-running agents, and that winning means structurally carving out a three to six month advantage.

On No Priors, host Sarith spoke with Walter Goodwin, founder and CEO of full-stack AI chip company **Fractile**. Goodwin explained that Fractile builds very fast inference chips for the world's largest models, a bet on speed held since the company started in summer 2022. He described a landscape full of "relatively identikit chips," where hyperscaler efforts like Google's **TPU**, Meta's **MTIA**, Microsoft's **Maya**, and OpenAI's **Jalapeno** are largely delivered in partnership with a small number of ASIC houses, Broadcom being the largest. All of them lean on the same **HBM**, Tensor Cores, and TSMC advanced packaging, leaving a dearth of teams going all the way up and down the silicon stack. Fractile, about 150 people, keeps front end design, physical design, back end implementation, and advanced packaging in house for an agile closed loop.

The technical journey is the heart of it. For the first two years, Fractile worked on an **SRAM**-based chip, like Grok or Cerebras, betting on extremely high bandwidth between compute and weights or KV cache. But scalability worries, especially growing context length, pushed them toward working with memory vendors to get extremely high bandwidth access to higher capacity **DRAM**. The platform ramping in the second half of next year aims to unite the scalability of DRAM with the speed advantages of an SRAM chip. Goodwin framed the payoff sharply: "The snappier chatbot is kind of the faster horses of kind of fast inference." The real elevator on capability is taking multi-trillion parameter models and running them at many thousands of tokens per second for very long running agents.

He also offered a memorable line on the competitive stakes: "It is the equivalent of the frontier model for the chip space: if you can just find a way to structurally carve out a three to six months advantage, you will be winning all of those deployments." On timelines, he pushed back on a top semi CEO's estimate of ten years to go from chief architect intent to a fully usable GDS2 file, saying he would divide it by four and subtract a bit. He noted that chip design still contains loops with conventional solutions to NP hard problems, like place and route running for days, and that as intelligence accelerates, those trials become the bottleneck, making approximate or surrogate approaches increasingly valuable.

## 🎙 PODCASTS

**Takeaway**: Fractile is betting that the next chip war is won on memory bandwidth, not raw compute, and that a three to six month structural speed advantage is enough to win every frontier deployment.

On **No Priors**, host Sarith spoke with **Walter Goodwin**, Founder and CEO of **Fractile**, a full stack AI chip company building very fast inference chips for the world's largest models. Goodwin started the company in summer 2022, seeing both the arrival of foundation models and the need to pour more compute into models at test time, the way AlphaGo became superhuman when rolled out at scale. He argues the chip landscape is full of relatively identikit designs: HBM memory, Tensor Cores, advanced packaging at TSMC, with most hyperscaler efforts delivered in partnership with a small number of ASIC houses, Broadcom being the largest. Fractile instead owns the whole stack, roughly 150 people spanning workload understanding, front end design, physical design, back end implementation, and advanced packaging, which lets it run a much more agile closed loop. The company spent its first two years on an SRAM-based chip, like Grok or Cerebras, before worrying about scalability as context lengths grew. Goodwin is blunt that a snappier chatbot is the faster horses of fast inference; the real prize is making long-running agents radically faster. He notes the tantalizing mismatch today: fast inference chips have super high bandwidth but incredibly low capacity, so they cannot run long context attention and still flip back to a GPU. On timelines, he applies a heuristic of dividing conventional estimates by four, suggesting architect intent to a usable GDS two file could come in a few years rather than ten, though final signoff with Cadence and Synopsys will not change soon. He also draws a parallel to RSI work: extreme intelligence can guide experiments, but you still end up experiment and compute-time bottlenecked.

Thariq highlighted that "You should know" is a great way to stay on top of what's possible with **Claude**, calling it "a great example of the kind of things mods enable."

Guillermo Rauch praised a writeup on **Jev** and Python, and celebrated the team shipping fast.

Aditya Agarwal celebrated his second portfolio company IPO this week with **Moneyview**, reflecting on the founders' journey as "long, hard and tough as nails."

**Claude for Small Business** now includes 43 workflows and 27 new integrations with tools including **Shopify**, **Salesforce**, **TikTok**, **Atlassian**, **Zoom**, **Xero**, **Gusto**, **Square**, **Stripe**, and **Zapier**. The product has been installed more than 900,000 times since launching in May. New workflows extend Claude from back office operations to growing the business, with a fall schedule of free workshops in 10 US cities and over 750 workshops from 150+ Approved Claude SMB Trainers.

Pedro Rubio, Founder and CEO of Blackfyre GovCon, shared: "What used to take me 120 hours now takes five minutes." Cara Roellgen, Director of Strategy and Innovation at KBSO Consulting, called Claude "an equalizer for small businesses." Garrett French, Owner of Driller Design Co., described a daily briefing workflow: "At 6:00 am every morning, it goes and looks through our CRM, gets all of the to-do list items, prioritizes them, and sends out an email saying, here's what needs to be done today."

https://claude.com/blog/claude-for-small-business-launches-new-workflows-integrations-and-training-programs

## 🎙 PODCASTS

**Takeaway**: Fractile is betting that the future of AI inference belongs to chips that combine the speed of SRAM-based designs with the capacity of DRAM, targeting long-running agents rather than just snappier chatbots.

Walter Goodwin, Founder and CEO of Fractile, joined No Priors to discuss building full-stack AI inference chips. He explained that Fractile started in summer 2022 with a bet on speed, recognizing that foundation models would need more compute at test time. The company initially worked on SRAM-based chips like Grok and Cerebras, achieving thousands of tokens per second, but grew concerned about scalability as context lengths expanded.

"We started to worry about the scalability of this approach," Goodwin said. "There are two things that grow with AI today. One is obviously the parameters of the model. But the other was this growing context length."

This led Fractile to pivot toward working with memory vendors to achieve "extremely high bandwidth access to higher capacity memories." Goodwin described the current landscape as having "a tantalizing mismatch" where fast inference chips have "super high bandwidth memory but incredibly low capacity" and can't run long context attention without flipping back to a GPU.

The company's platform, ramping in the second half of next year, aims to unite "the scalability of these higher capacity, lower cost DRAM memories that you have on a GPU, on a TPU with all of the speed advantages that you get from a Grok chip or a Cerebras chip."

Goodwin sees the real value of speed in "taking these very long running agents and making them radically faster," not just creating snappier chatbots. He compared the latter to Henry Ford's famous observation about faster horses.

On the chip design cycle, Goodwin believes AI can compress timelines significantly. "A heuristic that has been successful over the past couple of years is to just always question your logical assumption and then divide it by four on time scale." He noted that while physical constraints like fab cycle times of three to five months remain, the ability to iterate faster means "more shots on goal."

The competitive landscape includes NVIDIA systems with "anywhere between six and nine custom chips all built by NVIDIA," creating a gap Fractile hopes to close. Goodwin's goal is to build "a rolling frontier of bets" that could give a three to six month advantage: "The equivalent of the frontier model for the chip space is if you can just find a way to structurally carve out a three to six months advantage, you will be winning all of those deployments."

https://www.youtube.com/@NoPriorsPodcast

**Takeaway**: Fractile is betting that the winning chip will not be the fastest chatbot accelerator but the one that can run multi-trillion parameter models at thousands of tokens per second with economical memory.

On No Priors, Walter Goodwin, Founder and CEO of Fractile, explains why he started a full stack AI chip company in summer 2022 around a single bet: speed. He argues the frontier model equivalent for the chip space is structurally carving out a three to six month advantage, which wins all the deployments. He describes the current landscape as an extraordinary zoo of relatively identikit chips, all leaning on HBM, Tensor Cores, and TSMC advanced packaging, with front end design handed off to ASIC houses like Broadcom. Fractile instead keeps the whole story in house, about 150 people spanning workload understanding, front end design, physical design, back end implementation, and advanced packaging, to run a more agile closed loop.

The technical journey is the most interesting part. For the first two years Fractile worked on an SRAM based chip, chasing extremely high bandwidth between compute and weights or KV cache. But growing context length made scalability a worry, pushing them toward working with memory vendors to get extremely high bandwidth access to higher capacity DRAM. Goodwin calls the snappier chatbot the faster horses of fast inference; the real elevator on capability is making long-running agents radically faster. He points to a tantalizing mismatch: today's fast inference chips have super high bandwidth but incredibly low capacity, so long context attention still flips back to a GPU. The economics, he says, collapse down to cost per gigabyte of memory.

On timelines, Goodwin questions the conventional wisdom that big architectural changes move slowly. His heuristic is to take a logical assumption and divide it by four on time scale, so a ten year prediction for architect intent to a usable GDS two file becomes a few years. He notes chip design still contains NP hard loops like place and route running for days, and that as intelligence accelerates, those trials become the bottleneck, much like RSI work becoming experiment and compute time bottlenecked. He does not believe we will ship a fundamentally new chip every few weeks, because fabs have three to five month cycle times and chips need a three to five year amortization window. But compressing the gap between an observation and realizing that bet in volume is where the enormous value sits.

On timelines, Goodwin questions assumptions and divides by four. Asked how soon a chief architect's intent could become a fully usable GDS two file, he says a ten year estimate is sensible but he would divide it by four and subtract a bit, expecting end-to-end prototyping in the next few years. He compares it to the RSI question: extreme intelligence can guide experiments, but then you are experiment and compute-time bottlenecked. Final sign off will not change for quite some time, since Cadence and Synopsys have spent decades with TSMC building DRC and LVS clean checks. ## 🎙 PODCASTS

**Takeaway**: A full-stack chip startup is betting that the real bottleneck for long-running agents is memory bandwidth, not raw compute.

On **No Priors**, **Walter Goodwin**, Founder and CEO of **Fractile**, explains why his company builds very fast inference chips for the world's largest models. Fractile started in summer 2022 on the observation that foundation models were arriving and that more compute needed to be poured into models at test time, similar to how AlphaGo became superhuman when rolled out at scale. The company's mission is to run huge models much faster than today's chips while scaling to models beyond the frontier and to extraordinarily long contexts.

Goodwin describes the current chip landscape as an "extraordinary zoo" of options, but notes a lot of relatively identikit chips exist. Hyperscaler efforts like Google's **TPU**, Meta's **MTIA**, Microsoft's **Maya**, and OpenAI's **Jalapeno** are developed in partnership with a small number of ASIC houses, with **Broadcom** the largest. These chips share HBM memory, Tensor Cores, and advanced packaging from **TSMC**. Fractile's bet is to go all the way up and down the silicon stack, with front end designers, physical design, back end implementation, and advanced packaging all in house, at about 150 people.

The key architectural pivot came when Fractile worried about the scalability of an SRAM-based approach as context lengths grew. For the past couple of years they have worked with memory vendors to get extremely high bandwidth access to higher capacity DRAM, aiming to unite the scalability of GPU and TPU memory with the speed of Grok or Cerebras chips. Goodwin argues the real prize is not a snappier chatbot but making long-running agents radically faster, calling the snappier chatbot the "faster horses" of fast inference.

On timelines, Goodwin says a heuristic that has worked is to question your logical assumption and divide it by four. Asked about a top semi CEO's prediction of ten years to go from architect intent to a fully usable GDS2 file, he says he would divide it by four and subtract a bit. He notes chip design still has loops solving NP-hard problems with conventional algorithms that run for days, and that final sign-off with Cadence and Synopsys will not change for quite some time, but fuzzy placement algorithms could let teams iterate faster in the meantime.

Today's fast inference chips have super high bandwidth but incredibly low capacity, so they don't run long context attention and still flip back to a GPU. The fix is chips with incredibly high bandwidth to memory plus economical memory, because at data center scale the economics collapse to cost per gigabyte of memory.

On cycle times, Goodwin believes in two slightly conflicting things: huge value in compressing the chip design cycle, and the need for thoughtful architectural bets because a chip needs a three to five year amortization window. Fab cycle times run three to five months even on a hot lot, and data center power and installation latencies are real. ## 🎙 PODCASTS
**Takeaway**: Fractile is betting that the winning AI chip will unite the speed of SRAM-based designs with the scalability of DRAM, targeting long-running agents rather than just snappier chatbots.

Walter Goodwin, founder and CEO of Fractile, joined No Priors to discuss building full-stack inference chips for the world's largest models. He explained that while many AI chips look similar, with HBM, Tensor Cores, and TSMC advanced packaging, there's a dearth of efforts going all the way up and down the silicon stack. Fractile started in 2022 betting on speed and the arrival of a deployment era, initially working on an SRAM-based chip like Grok or Cerebras. But they grew worried about scalability as context lengths grew, leading them to work with memory vendors on getting extremely high bandwidth access to higher capacity DRAM.

Goodwin argued that the real value of fast inference is not a snappier chatbot, which he called the faster horses of fast inference, but making long-running agents radically faster. He described a tantalizing mismatch today: fast inference chips have super high bandwidth but incredibly low capacity, so they don't run long context attention and still flip back to a GPU. Fractile's platform, ramping in the second half of next year, aims to unite the scalability of DRAM with the speed advantages of SRAM-based chips.

On the pace of chip design, Goodwin said he believes two slightly conflicting things: there's huge value in compressing the chip design cycle, but chips still need a three to five year amortization window. He sees the goal as having more shots on goal and a rolling frontier of bets ready to ramp. He also predicted that the idea of going from architect intent to a fully usable GDS2 file will happen much faster than the ten years one semi CEO suggested, advising to divide such estimates by four.

**No Priors: Frontier Chips for Frontier AI Labs, with Walter Goodwin, Founder/CEO of Fractile**

Walter Goodwin, founder and CEO of full stack AI chip company Fractile, makes the case that the real prize in AI chips is not a snappier chatbot but radically faster long-running agents. Fractile builds very fast inference chips for the world's largest models, a bet on speed they have held since starting the company in summer 2022. Goodwin explains that the industry is full of "relatively identikit chips," with most hyperscaler efforts relying on the same HBM memory, Tensor Cores, and TSMC advanced packaging, often delivered in partnership with ASIC houses like Broadcom. Fractile's differentiator is owning the entire stack: front end design, physical design, back end implementation, and advanced packaging, with about 150 people. They initially worked on an SRAM-based chip, but grew worried about scalability as context lengths grew. That led them to work closely with memory vendors to get extremely high bandwidth access to higher capacity DRAM, aiming to unite the scalability of GPU-style memory with the speed of SRAM-based designs. On timelines, he questions the conventional wisdom that intent-to-GDS2 will take ten years, saying a successful heuristic is to divide such estimates by four. He notes that chip design still has loops with conventional solutions to NP hard problems, like place and route running for days, and that surrogate models and approximations could accelerate those trials. The key quote: "It is the equivalent of the frontier model for the chip space: if you can just find a way to structurally carve out a three to six months advantage, you will be winning all of those deployments."

## 🎙 PODCASTS
**Takeaway**: A full-stack chip startup is betting that the real prize in fast inference is not a snappier chatbot but radically faster long-running agents, and that memory bandwidth is the bottleneck to unlock.

On No Priors, Walter Goodwin, founder and CEO of full stack AI chip company **Fractile**, explained why he started the company in summer 2022 around two observations: foundation models trained on the internet and generalizing across everything, and the need to pour more compute into models at test time. Fractile builds very fast inference chips for the world's largest models, with a bet on speed from the outset. Goodwin walked through the chip landscape, noting an extraordinary zoo of options but a lot of relatively identikit chips, where hyperscaler efforts like Google's **TPU**, Meta's **MTIA**, Microsoft's **Maya**, and OpenAI's **Jalapeno** are developed in partnership with a small number of ASIC houses, with **Broadcom** the largest. He pointed out that these platforms share HBM memory, Tensor Core bets on matrix multiplications, and advanced packaging with TSMC, leaving a dearth of efforts that go all the way up and down the silicon stack.

Fractile spent its first two years on an **SRAM** based chip, drawn by SRAM's extremely high bandwidth living on the same silicon as logic, which can drive thousands of tokens per second. But by late 2023 and 2024, the team grew worried about scalability, especially growing context length. That pushed them toward working closely with memory vendors and logic foundry partners to get extremely high bandwidth access to higher capacity memories, moving away from SRAM toward much higher bandwidth to **DRAM**. The platform is set to ramp in the second half of next year, uniting the scalability of higher capacity, lower cost DRAM with the speed advantages of an SRAM chip.

The most striking framing came on where speed actually matters. Goodwin invoked Henry Ford's faster horses: a snappier chatbot is the faster horses of fast inference, while the real elevator on capability is taking very long running agents and making them radically faster. He described a tantalizing mismatch today, where fast inference chips have super high bandwidth memory but incredibly low capacity, so they do not run long context attention and still flip back to a GPU. Running inference at data center scale for thousands of users, he said, collapses the economics down to essentially a cost per gigabyte of memory.

On timelines, Goodwin applied a heuristic of questioning assumptions and dividing time scales by four. Asked about a top semi CEO's ten-year estimate for going from chief architect intent to a fully usable GDS2 file, he said he would divide by four and subtract a bit, expecting end-to-end prototyping within a few years. He noted that chip design still has loops with conventional solutions to NP hard problems, like place and route tools running for days, and compared it to the RSI question: extreme intelligence can guide experiments, but then you are experiment and compute time bottlenecked. He does not believe chips will ship every few weeks, since fabs have three to five month cycle times and chips need a three to five year amortization window, but compressing the gap between an observation and realizing that bet in volume is where enormous value is captured.

https://claude.com/blog/claude-for-small-business-launches-new-workflows-integrations-and-training-programs

## 🎙 PODCASTS

**Takeaway**: Fractile is betting that memory bandwidth, not just compute, will decide who wins the inference era, and that a three to six month structural advantage in chip design is the equivalent of a frontier model lead.

Walter Goodwin, Founder and CEO of Fractile, joined No Priors to explain why he started a full-stack AI chip company in summer 2022 to build very fast inference chips for the world's largest models. The core bet: as foundation models arrived and test-time compute became the path to superhuman performance, the world would shift into a deployment era where speed and marginal cost would matter more than anything. Fractile spent its first two years on an SRAM-based chip, similar to Groq or Cerebras, chasing thousands of tokens per second. But by late 2023, Goodwin grew worried about scalability. Two things grow with AI: model parameters and context length. The context length problem pushed them away from SRAM toward a more ambitious bet: working with memory vendors to get extremely high bandwidth access to higher capacity DRAM. The goal is a platform that unites the scalability of GPU-style DRAM with the speed advantages of SRAM chips, ramping in the second half of next year.

Goodwin was blunt about where speed actually matters. A snappier chatbot, he said, is "the faster horses of fast inference." The real prize is taking multi-trillion parameter models and running them at many thousands of tokens per second to make long-running agents radically faster. Today's fast inference chips have super high bandwidth but incredibly low capacity, so they can't run long context attention and still flip back to a GPU. Fractile wants to solve that mismatch.

On the chip design cycle, Goodwin believes AI can compress front-end design dramatically, but physical constraints remain: fab cycle times of three to five months, data center power limits, and the need for a three to five year amortization window. He doesn't think we'll ship fundamentally new chips every few weeks, but he does think the gap between an observation and realizing that bet in volume can shrink enormously. When asked about a top semi CEO's prediction that intent-to-GDSII would take ten years, Goodwin said: "A heuristic that has been successful over the past couple of years is to just always question your logical assumption and then divide it by four on time scale." He sees a world where end-to-end prototyping happens in the next few years, with fuzzy placement algorithms accelerating iteration while final sign-off stays with Cadence and Synopsys.

The competitive framing is sharp. Crack open an NVIDIA system and you find six to nine custom chips working together. Fractile is building one. Goodwin's vision is a rolling frontier of bets, deeply aligned and ready to ramp, that gives a perennial six month gap against competitors. "The equivalent of the frontier model for the chip space," he said, "is if you can just find a way to structurally carve out a three to six months advantage, you will be winning all of those deployments."
https://www.youtube.com/@NoPriorsPodcast

**Takeaway**: Fractile is betting that the real frontier for AI chips is memory bandwidth, not raw compute, and that a full-stack, AI-forward design loop can carve out a structural three to six month lead.

On **No Priors**, Walter Goodwin, Founder and CEO of full-stack AI chip company **Fractile**, explained why he started the company in summer 2022 around a bet on speed. He described the current chip landscape as an "extraordinary zoo" of relatively identikit chips, where hyperscaler efforts like **Google's TPU**, **Meta's MTIA**, **Microsoft's Maya**, and **OpenAI's Jalapeno** are largely delivered in partnership with a small number of ASIC houses, with **Broadcom** the largest. Fractile, by contrast, keeps the entire story in house: front end designers, physical design, back end implementation, and advanced packaging, at about 150 people.

The company's architectural journey is the heart of the episode. For its first two years Fractile worked on an **SRAM**-based chip, drawn to SRAM's extremely high bandwidth because it lives on the same silicon as the logic. But growing context lengths made them nervous about scalability, pushing them toward working closely with memory vendors to get extremely high bandwidth access to higher capacity **DRAM**. The platform ramping in the second half of next year aims to unite the scalability of DRAM with the speed advantages of an SRAM chip.

Goodwin argued the real prize is not a snappier chatbot, which he called the "faster horses" of fast inference, but making long-running agents radically faster. He noted a tantalizing mismatch: today's fast inference chips have super high bandwidth but incredibly low capacity, so they do not run long context attention and still flip back to a GPU. The fix is chips with incredibly high bandwidth to memory that can load weights and state thousands of times per second, while also being economical, since at data center scale the economics collapse to cost per gigabyte of memory.

On timelines, he pushed back on the idea of shipping fundamentally new chips every few weeks, citing fab cycle times of three to five months and the need for a three to five year amortization window. But he believes compressing the gap between an observation and realizing that bet in volume is where enormous value lies. Asked about a top semi CEO's prediction of ten years to go from chief architect intent to a fully usable GDS two file, he offered a heuristic: question your logical assumption and divide it by four on time scale. He expects end-to-end prototyping within the next few years, while final sign-off from **Cadence** and **Synopsys** stays valuable for DRC and LVS clean checks.

His most striking line captured the whole thesis: "The equivalent of the frontier model for the chip space is if you can just find a way to structurally carve out a three to six months advantage, you will be winning all of those deployments."

deck: Fractile bets on memory bandwidth while OpenAI's dot wins hearts and Swyx warns the security reckoning is no longer theoretical. Meanwhile, builders quietly discover agents that coordinate without being asked.
quote: It is the equivalent of the frontier model for the chip space: if you can just find a way to structurally carve out a three to six months advantage, you will be winning all of those deployments.
quoteBy: Walter Goodwin · Founder/CEO of Fractile

## 🧭 Daily Insights

**Core insight**: The conversation today splits between infrastructure ambition and product reality. Fractile's Walter Goodwin argues the chip race is now about carving out a three to six month structural advantage, while Sam Altman calls dot his favorite OpenAI product because it learns workflow and style. Meanwhile, Swyx warns that rogue agents and AI-driven attacks have made security no longer theoretical, and Garry Tan shows what happens when agents start coordinating across sessions without being asked.

## 𝕏 / TWITTER

**Swyx** teased that "one more thing" is coming and that the team has been working on **dots** for a while. More substantively, he made the case that Security x AI is now urgent: an exploding number of rogue agents, more breaches, more AI-driven attacks. He is back as a founding partner of the second **AI Security Summit** with Snyk, arguing security must be at the center of the AI conversation because "this stuff is no longer theoretical."
https://x.com/swyx/status/2106103958657958298
https://x.com/swyx/status/2106042773510177256

**Thibault Sottiaux** noted that future models will be much better at code deletion and simplification, "just in time." He also confirmed fixes for the **Pro 500** reset issue after reports that users did not get the expected reset, promising to make up for it.
https://x.com/thsottiaux/status/2106252868307271752
https://x.com/thsottiaux/status/2106239435461579088
https://x.com/thsottiaux/status/2106233145163141249

**Peter Yang** found that a YouTube research tool costing almost $300/year had become too complicated, so he tested whether **Claude** could build the core feature set he actually needed. Claude built it in 5 min. He also flagged a UX problem with the **Muse** desktop app: the persistent on-screen element makes him not want to open it.
https://x.com/petergyang/status/2106072698564874410
https://x.com/petergyang/status/2106113169571946560

**Nan Yu** observed that "everyone is making the same thing," a pointed comment on product convergence in the current AI builder landscape.
https://x.com/thenanyu/status/2106189530743398867

**Madhu Guru** praised the underrated feeling of reading great writing that is 100% human written, saying he loves "that human-written smell in a doc."
https://x.com/realmadhuguru/status/2106102222501376050

**Thariq** highlighted that "You should know" is a great way to stay on top of what is possible with **Claude** and a good example of what mods enable, noting you can really make **Claude Code** yours.
https://x.com/trq212/status/2106119299484221762

**Garry Tan** described **Capy** as a 24/7 standup for your agents. He was surprised by cross-session coordination: his **GBrain** collaborator Sina started a fix wave that steers around what he is already working on across multiple Capy threads, all model agnostic. His goal with GBrain is for agents to feel as native and inevitable as the web, not a chatbot feature but a personal Jiminy Cricket that knows you and helps you 24/7.
https://x.com/garrytan/status/2106102038706970794
https://x.com/garrytan/status/2106092289173213444
https://x.com/garrytan/status/2106063850453991758

**Matt Turck** pushed back on the idea that the Bay Area is a monoculture, noting it has both neo-clouds and neo-labs.
https://x.com/mattturck/status/2106076198027890750

**Nikunj Kothari** shared a home automation prompt for **Claude Code** or **Codex**: sniff network packets and find what else can be automated, given a Hermes agent already runs Gmail, thermostat, DoorDash, and Amazon. He wants a full list of devices and research on how they can be connected to an agent.
https://x.com/nikunj/status/2106072546206773574

**Peter Steinberger** called one slide at DevDay his favorite, praising the team.
https://x.com/steipete/status/2106076508020506722

**Sam Altman** said **dot** is his favorite OpenAI product so far, noting it feels noticeably better each day as it learns his workflow and style, and that having it do the stuff he does not like doing has him very happy. He also addressed speculation about the **Cerebras** partnership, calling Cerebras a close partner with deep engagement pushing on the frontiers of speed.
https://x.com/sama/status/2106085986606403684
https://x.com/sama/status/2106147184693620924

**Claude** showcased interactive 3D demos made with **Opus 5.5** and **Sonnet 5.5**, including a jet engine you can cut away and pull apart, and a pop-up city where each building is a paper fold.
https://x.com/claudeai/status/2106125478956507480
https://x.com/claudeai/status/2106125477710901276

## 📰 OFFICIAL BLOGS

**Claude Blog**: Claude for Small Business now includes 43 workflows and 27 new integrations with tools small businesses already use, including Shopify, Salesforce, TikTok, Atlassian, Zoom, Xero, Gusto, Square, Stripe, and Zapier. The new workflows extend Claude from running the back office to growing the business, arriving with a fall schedule of free in-person workshops and partner webinars. Since launching in May, it has been installed more than 900,000 times. About a third of owners on the spring SMB Tour asked for help growing the business: generating leads, answering inbound inquiries, and writing proposals. Pedro Rubio, Founder and CEO of Blackfyre GovCon, said what used to take 120 hours now takes five minutes. Cara Roellgen, Director of Strategy and Innovation at KBSO Consulting, sees Claude as an equalizer for small businesses. Garrett French, Owner of Driller Design Co., described a daily briefing that runs at 6:00 am every morning, pulling CRM to-dos and prioritizing them.
https://claude.com/blog/claude-for-small-business-launches-new-workflows-integrations-and-training-programs

## 🎙 PODCASTS

**Takeaway**: Fractile founder Walter Goodwin argues the chip race is now about structurally carving out a three to six month advantage, and that means owning the entire silicon stack in house.

Walter Goodwin, founder and CEO of full stack AI chip company Fractile, joined No Priors to explain why he started the company in summer 2022 around two observations: foundation models trained on the internet generalizing across everything, and the need to pour more compute into models at test time. Fractile builds very fast inference chips for the world's largest models, with a bet on speed from the outset. Goodwin describes a landscape full of "relatively identikit chips" where hyperscalers like Google with TPU, Meta with MTIA, Microsoft with Maya, and OpenAI with Jalapeno all rely on a small number of ASIC houses, with Broadcom the largest. He sees a relative dearth of efforts that go all the way up and down the silicon stack. Fractile, at about 150 people, does front end design, physical design, back end implementation, and advanced packaging in house, enabling a much more agile closed loop. The company spent its first two years on an SRAM based chip, then pivoted toward working with memory vendors to get extremely high bandwidth access to higher capacity DRAM. Goodwin calls the snappier chatbot the "faster horses" of fast inference; the real prize is taking multi trillion parameter models and running them at many thousands of tokens per second for long running agents. On timelines, he says to question your logical assumption and divide it by four, predicting end-to-end prototyping in the next few years, though final sign-off with Cadence and Synopsys will not change for quite some time. His most striking line: "It is the equivalent of the frontier model for the chip space: if you can just find a way to structurally carve out a three to six months advantage, you will be winning all of those deployments."
https://www.youtube.com/@NoPriorsPodcast

## 📰 OFFICIAL BLOGS
**Claude for Small Business** now includes 43 workflows and 27 new integrations with tools small businesses already use, including Shopify, Salesforce, TikTok, Atlassian, Zoom, Xero, Gusto, Square, Stripe, and Zapier. ## 🎙 PODCASTS
Walter Goodwin, founder and CEO of full stack AI chip company Fractile, argues the chip space is now a race to structurally carve out a three to six month advantage. The takeaway: speed, not just capability, is the wedge that wins frontier deployments.

Goodwin started Fractile in summer 2022 on a bet that foundation models would usher in a deployment era where inference cost is paid every single time a model runs. The company builds very fast inference chips for the world's largest models, aiming to scale to models beyond today's frontier and to extraordinarily long contexts. He notes the landscape is crowded with relatively identikit chips: hyperscaler efforts like Google's TPU, Meta's MTIA, Microsoft's Maya, and OpenAI's Jalapeno are largely developed with a small number of ASIC houses, Broadcom being the largest. Most share HBM, Tensor Cores, and advanced packaging from TSMC, leaving a dearth of teams working all the way up and down the silicon stack.

Fractile spent its first two years on an SRAM based chip, drawn by the extremely high bandwidth of memory living on the same silicon as logic, which can drive thousands of tokens per second. But by late 2023 and 2024, growing context length made scalability a worry, pushing the team toward working with memory vendors to get aggressively high bandwidth access to higher capacity DRAM. Goodwin frames the payoff bluntly: "It is the equivalent of the frontier model for the chip space: if you can just find a way to structurally carve out a three to six months advantage, you will be winning all of those deployments." He calls the snappier chatbot the faster horses of fast inference, arguing the real elevator on capability is making very long running agents radically faster.

On timelines, Goodwin questions assumptions and divides by four. Asked how soon an architect's intent could become a fully usable GDS two file, he says ten years sounds sensible but he would divide it by four and subtract a bit, expecting end-to-end prototyping within a few years. He cautions that chip design still contains genuinely expensive conventional loops, like place and route running for days, and that final sign off with Cadence, Synopsys, and the foundries will not change for quite some time. The real value is compressing the gap between an observation and realizing that bet in volume, giving more shots on goal while still placing subtle architectural bets that hold up over a three year plus lifespan.
https://www.youtube.com/@NoPriorsPodcast

## 📰 OFFICIAL BLOGS

**Claude for Small Business** now includes 43 workflows and 27 new integrations with tools like **Shopify**, **Salesforce**, **TikTok**, **Atlassian**, **Zoom**, **Xero**, **Gusto**, **Square**, **Stripe**, and **Zapier**. The product has been installed more than 900,000 times since launching in May. New workflows extend Claude from back-office operations to growing the business, with a fall schedule of free workshops in 10 US cities. More than 150 organizations trained as Approved Claude SMB Trainers will run over 750 workshops.

https://claude.com/blog/claude-for-small-business-launches-new-workflows-integrations-and-training-programs

## 🎙 PODCASTS

**Takeaway**: Fractile is betting that the future of AI chips isn't just about raw compute, but about memory bandwidth that can scale to trillion-parameter models running at thousands of tokens per second.

On **No Priors**, **Walter Goodwin**, Founder and CEO of **Fractile**, discussed building full-stack inference chips for the world's largest models. He explained that while SRAM-based chips offer extremely high bandwidth, they don't scale to the growing context lengths that frontier models demand. Fractile pivoted to working with memory vendors to achieve "extremely high bandwidth access to higher capacity memories," combining the scalability of DRAM with the speed advantages of SRAM-based designs.

Goodwin sees the real value of fast inference not in snappier chatbots, but in "taking these kind of very long running agents and making them radically faster." He described a "tantalizing mismatch" today where fast inference chips have high bandwidth but low capacity, forcing a flip back to GPUs for long context attention.

On the chip design cycle, Goodwin believes AI can compress timelines but not eliminate physical constraints. "There is a huge value in being able to take the overall chip design cycle and compress that," he said, but noted that chips still need a three to five year amortization window. His vision is a "rolling frontier of bets" where Fractile can trigger ramps on deeply aligned architectures, carving out a three to six month advantage over competitors.

He also predicted that AI-guided chip design will accelerate, but final sign-off will remain with tools like **Cadence** and **Synopsys** for quite some time. The opportunity is in "fuzzy placement algorithms" that get you almost all the way to your final design faster.

https://www.youtube.com/@NoPriorsPodcast

His goal with **GBrain**: agents that feel as native and inevitable as the web did, "not as a chatbot feature, but as a personal Jiminy Cricket that knows you and helps you 24/7."

Matt Turck, VC at FirstMark Capital, offered a wry defense of the Bay Area: "People call the Bay Area a monoculture, but that's totally unfair: it has both neo-clouds AND neo-labs."

Nikunj Kothari, partner at FPV Ventures, shared a fun home-automation prompt for Claude Code or Codex: sniff network packets and find what else can be automated, given a Hermes agent already running Gmail, thermostat, DoorDash, and Amazon. He also quoted Robin Williams on kindness.

Sam Altman had a reflective day. He described the contrast between high-stakes decision calls and walking in to children who want to laugh and play as "the strangest and best thing I have ever experienced." On business, he addressed speculation about the Cerebras partnership, calling Cerebras a close partner with deep engagement "pushing on the frontiers of speed." And he declared **dot** his favorite OpenAI product so far, noting it feels noticeably better each day as it learns his workflow and takes on the stuff he dreads.

Claude's official account showcased creative builds: a jet engine in interactive 3D you can cut away and pull apart, made with **Opus 5.5**, and a pop-up city where each building is a paper fold drawn on a flat canvas, made with **Sonnet 5.5**.

## 📰 OFFICIAL BLOGS

**Claude for Small Business** now includes 43 workflows and 27 new integrations with tools small businesses already use, including **Shopify**, **Salesforce**, **TikTok**, **Atlassian**, **Zoom**, **Xero**, **Gusto**, **Square**, **Stripe**, and **Zapier**. The new workflows extend Claude from running the back office to growing the business, arriving with a fall schedule of free in-person workshops and partner webinars. Since its May launch, it has been installed more than 900,000 times. On the spring Claude SMB Tour, more than 1,000 owners in 10 cities said about a third wanted help growing the business: generating leads, answering inbound inquiries, and writing proposals. The tour returns this fall with free workshops in 10 US cities, over 750 workshops run by 150+ Approved Claude SMB Trainers, and 14 integration partners hosting free webinars. One owner, Pedro Rubio of Blackfyre GovCon, said: "What used to take me 120 hours now takes me five minutes." Cara Roellgen of KBSO Consulting called Claude "an equalizer for small businesses," and Garrett French of Driller Design Co. described a 6:00 am daily briefing that scans the CRM and prioritizes the day's tasks.
https://claude.com/blog/claude-for-small-business-launches-new-workflows-integrations-and-training-programs

## 🎙 PODCASTS

**Takeaway: The chip race's real prize is a three-to-six-month structural lead, and the bottleneck is no longer intelligence but the physical world.**

On No Priors, Walter Goodwin, Founder and CEO of Fractile, explains why his company builds very fast inference chips for the world's largest models. Fractile started in summer 2022 on a bet that foundation models would arrive and that more compute would be poured in at test time, bringing AlphaGo-style rollout scaling to language modeling. The mission: run huge models much faster than today's chips while scaling to models beyond the frontier and extraordinarily long contexts.

Goodwin argues the chip landscape is full of "relatively identikit chips," with hyperscalers like Google, Meta, Microsoft, and OpenAI all relying on a small number of ASIC houses, Broadcom being the largest. Fractile's differentiator is going all the way up and down the silicon stack, with front end designers, its own physical design team, back end implementation, and advanced packaging work, all in about 150 people. That agile closed loop matters because, as he puts it, "in the AI chip space more than any other kind of chip play before, you have to really place your bets correctly."

The technical journey is the heart of the episode. Fractile spent its first two years on an SRAM-based chip, like Grok or Cerebras, chasing thousands of tokens per second. But growing context length made them nervous about scalability, so they pivoted to working with memory vendors on extremely high bandwidth access to higher capacity DRAM. The result is a platform ramping in the second half of next year that unites DRAM's scalability with SRAM's speed. Goodwin frames the payoff sharply: a snappier chatbot is "the faster horses of fast inference," while the real elevator on capability is making long-running agents radically faster.

He is candid about physical limits. Fab cycle times are three to five months even in a hot lot, and chips need a three-to-five year amortization window. So he does not believe in shipping a fundamentally new chip every few weeks. Instead, the value is compressing the gap between an observation and realizing that bet in volume, giving more shots on goal. On the question of going from architect intent to a usable GDS2 file, he applies a heuristic: take the conventional ten-year estimate, divide by four, and subtract a bit. The remaining bottleneck is the conventionally expensive work, like place-and-route running for days, which is exactly where surrogate models and fuzzy placement could help iterate faster.

The memorable line captures the whole thesis: "It is the equivalent of the frontier model for the chip space: if you can just find a way to structurally carve out a three to six months advantage, you will be winning all of those deployments."

## 🎙 PODCASTS

**Takeaway**: Fractile is betting that the winning inference chip will combine the speed of SRAM-based designs with the scalability of DRAM, targeting long-running agents rather than just snappier chatbots.

Walter Goodwin, founder and CEO of Fractile, joined No Priors to discuss building full-stack AI inference chips. He explained that Fractile started in summer 2022 with a bet on speed, seeing the arrival of foundation models and the need to pour more compute into models at test time. The company initially worked on an SRAM-based chip, observing that SRAM offers extremely high bandwidth between compute and model weights or KV cache, driving thousands of tokens per second. But by late 2023 and 2024, they grew worried about scalability, particularly as context lengths grew. That led to a more exciting bet: working closely with memory vendors and logic foundry partners to get extremely high bandwidth access to higher capacity DRAM memories. The platform will ramp in the second half of next year, uniting the scalability of DRAM with the speed advantages of SRAM-based chips.

Goodwin argued that the real value of speed is not a snappier chatbot, which he called the faster horses of fast inference, but taking multi-trillion parameter models and running them comfortably at many thousands of tokens per second to make long-running agents radically faster. He noted a tantalizing mismatch today: fast inference chips have super high bandwidth but incredibly low capacity, and they are not running long context attention, still flipping back to a GPU. The challenge boils down to needing chips with incredibly high bandwidth to memory to load weights and state thousands of times per second, but also economical memory, because at data center scale the economics collapse to cost per gigabyte of memory.

On chip design cycles, Goodwin said he believes two slightly conflicting things: there is huge value in compressing the overall chip design cycle, but the chip you make still needs a three-year-plus useful lifespan. He does not believe we will ship a fundamentally new chip every few weeks, because the physical world has constraints on data center power, installation latencies, and financing. But shorter latency between an observation and realizing that bet in volume is where enormous value can be captured. He said Fractile is trying to build a single chip while competitors like NVIDIA have six to nine custom chips in a system, and that a rolling frontier of bets with a three to six month advantage would be the equivalent of the frontier model for the chip space.

On AI in chip design, Goodwin suggested dividing conventional timelines by four, predicting end-to-end prototyping in the next few years. He noted that final sign-off with Cadence and Synopsys will not change for quite some time, but fuzzy placement algorithms could help iterate faster in the meantime.

https://www.youtube.com/@NoPriorsPodcast

Claude for Small Business now includes 43 workflows and 27 new integrations with tools small businesses already use, including Shopify, Salesforce, TikTok, Atlassian, Zoom, Xero, Gusto, Square, Stripe, and Zapier. ## 🎙 PODCASTS
Walter Goodwin, founder and CEO of full stack AI chip company Fractile, argues that the real prize in the chip space is structural speed. The takeaway: if you can carve out a three-to-six-month advantage over competitors, you win all the deployments.

Fractile builds very fast inference chips for the world's largest models, a bet on speed held since the company started in summer 2022. Goodwin describes a landscape full of "relatively identikit chips," where hyperscaler efforts like Google's TPU, Meta's MTIA, Microsoft's Maya, and OpenAI's Jalapeno all share HBM memory, Tensor Cores, and advanced TSMC packaging, largely delivered in partnership with ASIC houses like Broadcom. Fractile, by contrast, runs the entire stack in house: front end design, physical design, back end implementation, and advanced packaging, with about 150 people staying skinny in every sector to keep an agile closed loop.

The company's architectural journey moved from an SRAM-based chip, which offers extremely high bandwidth between compute and weights or KV cache, toward a bet on high bandwidth access to higher capacity DRAM. Goodwin explains the tantalizing mismatch: fast inference chips have super high bandwidth but incredibly low capacity, so long context attention still flips back to a GPU. The fix is chips with aggressively high bandwidth to lower cost DRAM, since at data center scale the economics collapse to cost per gigabyte of memory. He calls the snappier chatbot the "faster horses" of fast inference; the real elevator on capability is making long running agents radically faster.

On timelines, Goodwin questions assumptions and divides by four. He doubts we will ship a fundamentally new chip every few weeks, since fab cycle times run three to five months and chips need a three-to-five-year amortization window. But compressing the gap between observation and volume realization is where enormous value lies, giving more shots on goal and a rolling frontier of bets.

**Quote**: "It is the equivalent of the frontier model for the chip space: if you can just find a way to structurally carve out a three to six months advantage, you will be winning all of those deployments."
https://www.youtube.com/@NoPriorsPodcast

## 🎙 PODCASTS

**Takeaway**: Fractile is betting that the winning chip for frontier AI is not the fastest chatbot chip, but the one that can run multi-trillion parameter models at thousands of tokens per second with economical DRAM memory.

On No Priors, Walter Goodwin, founder and CEO of full stack AI chip company Fractile, explained why his team abandoned an early SRAM-based design. "We started to worry about the scalability of this approach," he said, pointing to growing context lengths as the factor that pushed them toward working closely with memory vendors to get extremely high bandwidth access to higher capacity DRAM. The goal is to unite the scalability of GPU-style memory with the speed advantages of SRAM chips like Grok or Cerebras.

Goodwin argued the real prize is not a snappier chatbot but radically faster long-running agents, calling the snappier chatbot "the faster horses of fast inference." He noted a tantalizing mismatch today: fast inference chips have super high bandwidth but incredibly low capacity, so long context attention still flips back to a GPU.

On the chip market, he described an "extraordinary zoo" of relatively identikit chips, all relying on HBM, Tensor Cores, and TSMC advanced packaging, with most designs handed off to ASIC houses like Broadcom. Fractile, at about 150 people, keeps front end design, physical design, back end implementation, and advanced packaging in house for an agile closed loop.

He was candid about physical limits: fab cycle times run three to five months even in a hot lot, and chips need a three to five year amortization window. "I'm not a believer in the idea that we will ultimately get to a place where we are shipping a fundamentally new chip every few weeks," he said. Instead, the value is compressing the gap between an observation and realizing that bet in volume. His framing: "It is the equivalent of the Frontier model for the chip space: if you can just find a way to structurally carve out a three to six months advantage, you will be winning all of those deployments." He also suggested dividing conventional ten-year timelines by four, predicting end-to-end prototyping within a few years.
https://www.youtube.com/@NoPriorsPodcast

## 🎙 PODCASTS
**Takeaway**: Fractile founder Walter Goodwin argues that the frontier of AI chips is not about a snappier chatbot but about making long-running agents radically faster, and that a three to six month structural advantage in the chip space wins every deployment.

On No Priors, Walter Goodwin, Founder and CEO of Fractile, explained that his company builds very fast inference chips for the world's largest models, a bet on speed he has held since starting the company in summer 2022. He described the chip landscape as an "extraordinary zoo" of options, but noted that many are relatively identikit chips, all sharing HBM memory, Tensor Cores for matrix multiplication, and advanced packaging with TSMC. Fractile's differentiator is going all the way up and down the silicon stack, with front end designers, its own physical design team, back end implementation, and advanced packaging work, all in a company of about 150 people.

Goodwin traced the company's architectural journey: for the first two years it worked on an SRAM-based chip, drawn by SRAM's extremely high bandwidth because it lives on the same silicon as the logic. But toward the end of 2023 and into 2024, the team grew worried about scalability, especially as growing context length became central to how models roll out. That pushed them toward working closely with memory vendors to get extremely high bandwidth access to higher capacity DRAM memories, a platform he said will ramp in the second half of next year, uniting the scalability of DRAM with the speed advantages of an SRAM chip.

He was blunt about where speed actually matters. A snappier chatbot, he said, is "the faster horses of kind of fast inference," invoking Henry Ford. The real elevator on capability is taking multi-trillion parameter models and running them comfortably at many thousands of tokens per second for very long running agents. He pointed to a tantalizing mismatch today: fast inference chips have super high bandwidth memory but incredibly low capacity, so they do not run long context attention and still flip back to a GPU for that.

On the pace of chip design, Goodwin said he believes two slightly conflicting things: there is huge value in compressing the overall chip design cycle, but chips still need a three to five year amortization window and a three year plus useful lifespan, so thoughtful architectural bets remain essential. He suggested always questioning your logical assumption and dividing the time scale by four, predicting end-to-end prototyping within the next few years, though final sign-off with Cadence, Synopsys, and foundry DRC and LVS checks will not change for quite some time. His closing frame was the frontier model analogy: "It is the equivalent of the Frontier model for the chip space: if you can just find a way to structurally carve out a three to six months advantage, you will be winning all of those deployments."

## 🎙 PODCASTS
**Takeaway**: Fractile is betting that the future of AI inference isn't just about faster chatbots, it's about making long-running agents radically faster by solving the memory bandwidth problem.

**No Priors** host Sarah Guo speaks with **Walter Goodwin**, founder and CEO of **Fractile**, a full-stack AI chip company building very fast inference chips for the world's largest models. Goodwin explains that Fractile started in summer 2022, betting on two things: the arrival of foundation models trained on the internet, and the need to pour more compute into models at test time, similar to how AlphaGo became superhuman when rolled out at scale.

The conversation digs into the chip landscape, which Goodwin describes as an "extraordinary zoo" of relatively identikit chips. Most hyperscaler efforts, Google's TPU, Meta's MTIA, Microsoft's Maya, and OpenAI's Jalapeno, share similar bets on HBM, Tensor Cores, and advanced packaging with TSMC. Fractile's key architectural bet was moving away from SRAM-based designs (like Grok or Cerebras) toward working with memory vendors to get extremely high bandwidth access to higher capacity DRAM memories. This unites the scalability of GPU/TPU memory with the speed advantages of SRAM chips.

Goodwin argues that the real value of fast inference isn't a "snappier chatbot" but making long-running agents radically faster. He notes a "tantalizing mismatch" today: fast inference chips have super high bandwidth but incredibly low capacity, so they can't run long context attention and still flip back to a GPU. Fractile aims to solve this by getting aggressively high bandwidth from lower cost DRAM memory.

On the pace of chip design, Goodwin believes in questioning assumptions and dividing timelines by four. While a top semi CEO predicted ten years until a chief architect's intent becomes a fully usable GDS2 file, Goodwin thinks it will be faster, though physical constraints like fab cycle times and the need for a three to five year amortization window remain. The goal is to compress the gap between an observation and realizing that bet in volume, giving Fractile a three to six month structural advantage that "will be winning all of those deployments."

Claude's account showcased interactive 3D built with **Opus 5.5**, including a jet engine you can cut away and pull apart, and a pop-up paper-fold city made with **Sonnet 5.5**.

## 📰 OFFICIAL BLOGS
**Claude for Small Business** now includes 43 workflows and 27 new integrations with tools small businesses already use, among them Shopify, Salesforce, TikTok, Atlassian, Zoom, Xero, Gusto, Square, Stripe, and Zapier. The new workflows extend Claude from running the back office to growing the business, arriving alongside a fall schedule of free in-person workshops and partner webinars. Launched in May as connectors and ready-to-run workflows, it has since been installed more than 900,000 times. On the spring Claude SMB Tour, more than 1,000 owners in 10 cities said about a third wanted help growing the business: generating leads, answering inbound inquiries, and writing proposals, with many also wanting day-to-day reporting handled. The tour returns this fall with free workshops in 10 US cities, more than 150 organizations trained as Approved Claude SMB Trainers running over 750 workshops, and 14 integration partners hosting free webinars. Pedro Rubio, Founder and CEO of Blackfyre GovCon, said work that used to take 120 hours now takes five minutes. Cara Roellgen, Director of Strategy and Innovation at KBSO Consulting, called Claude an equalizer letting a 40-person firm do work as big as a 100 or 200 person firm. Garrett French, Owner of Driller Design Co., described a 6:00 am daily briefing that scans the CRM, prioritizes to-dos, and emails the day's biggest priorities.
https://claude.com/blog/claude-for-small-business-launches-new-workflows-integrations-and-training-programs

## 🎙 PODCASTS
**Takeaway**: The next chip war is not about raw compute but about memory bandwidth, and whoever compresses the gap between an architectural insight and volume deployment wins the frontier.

On No Priors, Walter Goodwin, Founder and CEO of Fractile, explains why his company builds very fast inference chips for the world's largest models. Fractile started in summer 2022 betting on two shifts: foundation models generalizing across everything, and the need to pour more compute into models at test time, the way AlphaGo became superhuman when rolled out at scale. The company is deliberately full stack, with front end designers, its own physical design team, back end implementation, and advanced packaging work, all in about 150 people. Goodwin argues most chips in the market are relatively identikit: HBM memory, Tensor Cores, advanced packaging at TSMC, with physical design largely outsourced to ASIC houses like Broadcom. Fractile's first two years were spent on an SRAM based chip, but growing context lengths made scalability a worry, pushing the team toward skunkworks projects with memory vendors to get extremely high bandwidth access to higher capacity DRAM. The platform is set to ramp in the second half of next year. His framing of the opportunity is sharp: "It is the equivalent of the frontier model for the chip space: if you can just find a way to structurally carve out a three to six months advantage, you will be winning all of those deployments." He is skeptical of shipping fundamentally new chips every few weeks, since fab cycle times run three to five months and chips need a three to five year amortization window, but he believes compressing the latency between observation and volume realization is where enormous value sits. Asked about a top semi CEO's ten year estimate for going from architect intent to a usable GDS two file, Goodwin offered a heuristic: question the assumption and divide the time scale by four, then subtract a bit. He sees prototyping going end to end within a few years, with conventional place and route tools and final DRC and LVS sign off persisting for a while, and surrogate models for thermal and finite element work becoming far more valuable as intelligence accelerates.
https://www.youtube.com/@NoPriorsPodcast
