keywords: AI agents | product simplicity | AI infrastructure
headline: The Agent Adoption Gap Nobody Wants to Admit
deck: Coding agents race ahead while the rest of knowledge work waits for rebuilt workflows. Meanwhile, the infrastructure layer feeding GPUs quietly becomes a $30B giant, and Claude merges its tools into one.
quote: I am very uncomfortable about people trying to ascribe religious force or a surrender of human judgment to AI models, and think it is a real safety issue.
quoteBy: Sam Altman · The mission of OpenAI is to ensure that AGI benefits all of humanity

## 🧭 Daily Insights

**Core insight**: The conversation today centers on a widening gap between AI capability and AI adoption. Coding agents have taken off, but real agentic adoption across the rest of knowledge work remains very early because workflows, governance, and accountability models still need to be rebuilt. At the same time, product leaders are converging on the same diagnosis: AI products are too complicated, and simplification is the next competitive frontier.

## 𝕏 / TWITTER

**Thibault Sottiaux** announced a strategic reset at OpenAI, stating that the only things being worked on are simplifications, efficiency for more usage, and groundbreaking features or new models. He acknowledged that while investing ahead of the curve matters, user feedback is clear that people want things to get simpler. He also shared a personal experiment where he used his agent to achieve inbox zero for the first time, having it delete unnecessary email categories, label work emails, and walk him through replies needing attention.

**Madhu Guru** argued that AI adoption is largely a product problem today. Even among the 2% of people paying for AI, usage depth is shallow, mainly because most AI products resemble airplane cockpits with 100 levers covering connectors, permissions, model selection, and token usage. He expects this to change materially in the next 12 months as product teams make AI products easier to use.

**Guillermo Rauch** predicted that security will become a larger and larger function in software companies, describing it as both verification engineering and capital allocation. He framed it as a challenge and opportunity for startups, asking how you can trust a 2-person-and-a-dog company as AI adversaries grow more sophisticated. He also made a bold claim that AI will make everything free, including itself, with free energy as humanity's final frontier.

**Aaron Levie** laid out why AI agent adoption is still bimodal. Coding and coding-adjacent tasks have taken off while everything else lags, and even within coding there is a wide continuum from developers running background agents in parallel to everyone else working 1:1 with agents. He argued that most knowledge work workflows still need to be reengineered for agents, requiring rebuilt processes, new data wiring, accountability practices, governance changes, and security upgrades, which is why he expects 100X more agent adoption from what we have seen so far.

**Ryo Lu** wrote a long reflection on convergence to the mean, arguing that when everyone looks at everyone else to decide what to make, we eventually stop making anything of our own. He observed that AI makes this loop frictionless because it can draw from more references than we could see in a lifetime, but access to every perspective is not the same as having one. He called for approaching software more like artists, where a piece of software expresses beliefs about how life should feel, and warned against a world where everyone becomes a more efficient distributor of the same ideas.

**Nikunj Kothari** flagged an innovator's dilemma playing out as personal agents become inevitable, noting that Amazon is protecting its ads cash cow and brand while DoorDash, albeit smaller, is opening the gates with CLIs and allowing orders via text. He also cautioned that tokenmaxxing for its own sake is not honestly useful in this era.

**Peter Steinberger** joked about how everyone is building the same thing, and flagged that OpenClaw's Android app has been stuck in review limbo for over a week, asking if anyone at Google could help.

**Aditya Agarwal** pointed out a common misconception that being super rich grants unlimited access to the world's best professionals, noting that a leading cancer doctor will still only see you for 20-30 minutes. He argued this is why AI is so crazy: it both democratizes access and makes the amount of time available unlimited for every individual, the practical effect of intelligence too cheap to meter.

**Sam Altman** stated he is very uncomfortable about people trying to ascribe religious force or a surrender of human judgment to AI models, and thinks it is a real safety issue.

**Zara Zhang** posed a simple but provocative question: how will the world change if coding agents get 10x better?

## 📰 OFFICIAL BLOGS

**Claude Blog** announced that Claude Cowork and chat are merging into one Claude, rolling out on Pro and Max plans over the next few weeks. Claude Docs and Claude Slides are new, and Claude Design now works inside conversations. Users can ask for a document and write it together with Claude, or ask for a presentation and have Claude draft the slides, then edit directly, present from Claude, or download as PowerPoint or PDF. All three are in beta on paid plans, with Enterprise admins controlling when to turn them on. The blog explained that Cowork was built as a separate place for bigger work and Design for visual work, but people used both and found deciding where a task belonged frustrating, and work started in one did not carry into the other. Claude can now figure out what a task needs, making Cowork and Design capabilities available from any conversation with existing context, skills, and connectors. A Senior Economist, Andrew Keller, described having Claude pull up his legal research database, read all the cases, figure out which other cases he might need, download them, and store them in a folder for his personal review.
https://claude.com/blog/cowork-is-now-claude

## 🎙 PODCASTS

**Takeaway**: The layer feeding data to GPUs is quietly becoming a $30 billion business, and its founder believes the next decade will bring more change than the last thousand years.

On The MAD Podcast with Matt Turck, Renen Hallak, founder and CEO of VAST Data, explained why the software infrastructure layer sitting between hardware and models is the operating system for the AI era. He described how data centers have shifted from 10 kilowatt racks to 500 kilowatt racks, requiring new power density, extremely fast networks, and very large SSDs, with every layer of the stack being redone. He shared a striking anecdote about the pace of demand: a customer, one of the AI clouds, initially said they would need about 500 petabytes over three years, then came back the next week saying they would need an extra two exabytes on top of that.

Hallak traced his path from spending six months trying to prove whether P equals NP, concluding he was not nearly smart enough, to joining a startup acquired by EMC, and then founding VAST in 2016 after realizing neural nets could finally do something useful once given faster access to more data. He explained the core architectural bet: the old shared nothing approach based on sharding breaks down at AI scale because communication grows quadratically and resilience suffers, so VAST built the opposite, a disaggregated shared everything architecture where SSDs sit on the other side of a fast network and all nodes see all information as if directly attached. He noted one customer system today spans multiple exabytes in a single cluster delivering tens of terabytes per second across tens of thousands of nodes.

On agents and enterprise IP, Hallak argued that over time every organization's IP will be distilled into models and weights, much like the human brain starts with a base model and fine tunes through experience. He described agents as artificial people that will fine tune based on experiences with us, and said enterprises will not want to expose proprietary processes to big model builders, creating a need for an intelligence marketplace where capabilities can be leased without exposing weights. He announced VAST's model management work, including confidential computing with encrypted memory and help from NVIDIA, enabling enterprises to run inference on prem without exposing model builders' weights, which he hopes expands the total addressable market into regulated industries. He also reflected on the recent news that AI has begun solving long-open millennium problems, saying that for the first time AI has proven it can do things we do not know how to do.
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=awoR908Yu5Y

## 📰 OFFICIAL BLOGS

**Claude Blog** announced that Claude Cowork and chat are merging into one Claude. Users can bring a quick question or hand over a report due at noon, and Claude takes it from there, even after the laptop is closed. It is rolling out on Pro and Max plans over the next few weeks. Claude Docs and Claude Slides are new today, and Claude Design now works inside conversations. Ask for a document and you and Claude write it together; ask for a presentation and Claude drafts the slides. You can edit directly, present straight from Claude, or download as PowerPoint or PDF. All three are in beta on paid plans, with Enterprise admins choosing when to turn them on. The blog quotes Andrew Keller, Senior Economist: "I could have Claude pull up my legal research database, and it would pull all the cases, read them, figure out which other cases I might need, download them, and store them in a folder for my personal review." The team explained they built Cowork as a separate place for bigger work and Design for visual work, but people used both and said the frustrating part was deciding where a task belonged. So they stopped making users choose.

## 🎙 PODCASTS

**Takeaway**: The software infrastructure layer feeding GPUs is quietly becoming a $30B business, and the next wave of enterprise AI will be about owning your own weights, not renting someone else's.

On The MAD Podcast with Matt Turck, Renen Hallak, founder and CEO of VAST Data, explained why the middle layer of the AI stack is the least visible but most critical. VAST Data is valued at $30,000,000,000 and powers top AI players like xAI and some of the biggest AI clouds. Hallak described a customer that initially projected needing 500 petabytes over three years, then came back and said they needed an extra two exabytes on top of that.

Hallak positioned VAST Data in the software infrastructure layer of Jensen Huang's five-layer cake, calling it "the operating system for this new era." He explained that the old stack was built for 10 kilowatt racks and 10 gig ethernet, while today you need 500 kilowatt racks, extremely fast networks, and very large SSDs. The architecture VAST built, called disaggregated shared everything, was the opposite of traditional shared nothing systems. Instead of SSDs attached directly to CPUs, the media sits on the other side of the network, allowing all nodes to see all information as if it were directly attached. One customer system today spans multiple exabytes within a single cluster delivering tens of terabytes per second across tens of thousands of nodes.

On agents and fine-tuning, Hallak argued that over time every organization's IP will be distilled into models and weights they own. He compared it to the human brain: "we were all born with a base model but then over time as we travel the world we learn new things, we infer during the day, we fine tune at night, and tomorrow we'll be a little bit smarter than we were today." He predicted that agents will fine-tune models through reinforcement learning, and that enterprises will not want to expose proprietary information to big model builders. This led to VAST's announcement around model management and confidential computing, enabling enterprises to run inference on prem without exposing model builders' weights, with help from Nvidia and encrypted memory.

Hallak also shared that he spent six months trying to prove P=NP as a student, hoping to claim the $7,000,000 bounty on the seven millennium problems, before realizing he was not nearly smart enough to do it. He noted that AI has now proven it can do things we do not know how to do, referencing OpenAI's claimed solution to Navier Stokes and rumors of two more millennium problems being close to solved.
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=awoR908Yu5Y

He walks through how the AI factory differs from the old stack: 10 kilowatt racks became 500 kilowatt racks, CPUs became GPUs, 10 gig ethernet and old hard drives became extremely fast networks and very large SSDs, because we are no longer analyzing numbers and columns but pictures, video, sound, and natural language. He notes one AI cloud customer that expected to need about 500 petabytes over three years and came back last week asking for an extra two exabytes on top of that.

The most striking part is his argument that enterprises will not just rent intelligence but own it. He compares base models to a human brain we are all born with, then says we infer during the day and fine tune at night, so every organization's IP will be distilled into models and weights they own. He is explicit that you do not want to expose your proprietary information, processes, and secret sauce to somebody else, and that this is why the infrastructure layer must enforce trust so an enterprise does not expose its data and a model builder does not expose its weights. He imagines an intelligence marketplace where a carpentry shop with the best carpenter robots could lease that brain module for a week without ever revealing the weights. VAST's new announcement is about model management, including confidential computing with encrypted memory underneath, so enterprises can run inference on prem without exposing model builders' weights, which he hopes expands the addressable market into regulated industries.

He also tells the origin story: as a student he spent six months trying to prove whether P equals NP, hoping to claim the Clay Institute's million dollar bounty, and concluded he was not nearly smart enough. He notes that AI has now proven it can do things we do not know how to do, with rumors that OpenAI and Anthropic are close on more of the seven millennium problems. VAST started in 2016 on a bet that neural nets needed both fast and very large systems, building a disaggregated shared everything architecture that is the opposite of shared nothing sharding, and he credits pitching storage to skeptical VCs for giving the company far less competition today.
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=awoR908Yu5Y

headline: AI's Next Frontier Is Making Itself Simple
deck: Builders agree agent adoption is still bimodal and products look like airplane cockpits, while the infrastructure layer feeding GPUs quietly scales toward exabytes.
quote: I am very uncomfortable about people trying to ascribe religious force or a surrender of human judgment to AI models, and think it is a real safety issue.
quoteBy: Sam Altman · The mission of OpenAI is to ensure that AGI benefits all of humanity

## 🧭 Daily Insights
**Core insight**: The dominant thread today is that AI's bottleneck has shifted from capability to product. Madhu Guru argues adoption is largely a product problem, Aaron Levie says real agentic adoption outside coding is still very early, and Thibault Sottiaux says OpenAI is locking in on simplification. Meanwhile the infrastructure underneath keeps compounding: VAST Data's Renen Hallak describes customers jumping from 500 petabytes to an extra two exabytes in a single week.

## 𝕏 / TWITTER
**Thibault Sottiaux** says the team is locking in, with only simplifications, more efficiency for more usage, groundbreaking features or new models being worked on, noting feedback is clear that users want things simpler. He also described using his dot to reach inbox zero for the first time, having it delete unneeded email categories, label work emails, and walk him through replies while searching for context in the background.

**Madhu Guru** argues AI adoption is largely a product problem today: even among the 2% paying for AI, usage depth is shallow because most products look like airplane cockpits with 100 levers such as connectors, permissions, model selection and token usage. He expects this to change materially in the next 12 months as product teams make AI easier to use.

**Amjad Masad** shared a deep and somewhat technical conversation with Alex Atallah of **OpenRouter**, and teased something called **Replit Drift**.

**Guillermo Rauch** predicts security will become a larger and larger function in software companies, framing it as verification engineering plus capital allocation, and asks how anyone can trust a 2-person-and-a-dog company as AI adversaries grow more sophisticated. He also argues AI will make everything free, including itself, with free energy as the last domino.

**Aaron Levie** says AI agent adoption is still very bimodal: coding and coding-adjacent tasks have taken off while everything else lags, and even within coding only a small percentage of developers deploy background agents working in parallel. He argues most knowledge-work workflows still need to be reengineered for agents, requiring rebuilt data wiring, new accountability and liability practices, governance and compliance changes, and security upgrades, which is why he expects 100X more agent adoption than seen so far.

**Ryo Lu** wrote a long essay on convergence to the mean: when everyone looks at everyone else to decide what to make, everything becomes polished and interchangeable, and AI makes this loop frictionless because access to every perspective is not the same as having one. He argues we should approach making things more like artists, developing a perspective through the work, and asks what the point is of everyone being able to make something if we all end up making the same thing.

**Zara Zhang** asked how the world will change if coding agents get 10x better.

**Nikunj Kothari** flagged the innovator's dilemma as personal agents become inevitable, noting Amazon is protecting its ads cash cow and brand while DoorDash is slowly opening the gates with CLIs and text ordering. He also cautioned that tokenmaxxing for its own sake is not honestly useful in this era.

**Peter Steinberger** laughed about how everyone is building the same thing, and asked if anyone at Google could help with **OpenClaw**'s Android app, now over a week in review limbo.

**Aditya Agarwal** notes a common misconception that being super rich buys unlimited access to the world's best doctor or lawyer, when in reality the leading cancer doctor still sees you for 20-30min. He says this is why AI is so crazy: it both democratizes access and makes time unlimited for every individual, the practical effect of intelligence too cheap to meter.

**Sam Altman** said he is very uncomfortable about people trying to ascribe religious force or a surrender of human judgment to AI models, and thinks it is a real safety issue.

## 📰 OFFICIAL BLOGS
**Claude Blog** announced that **Claude Cowork** and chat are merging into one Claude, rolling out on Pro and Max plans over the next few weeks. Claude Docs and Claude Slides are new, and Claude Design now works inside conversations, so you can ask for a document and write it together or ask for a presentation and Claude drafts the slides, then edit directly, present straight from Claude, or download as PowerPoint or PDF. All three are in beta on paid plans, with Enterprise admins choosing when to turn them on. The team says people used Cowork and Design separately and found deciding where a task belonged frustrating, and work started in one did not carry into the other, so Claude now figures out what a task needs with the context, skills and connectors you already have. Senior Economist Andrew Keller described having Claude pull up his legal research database, read the cases, figure out which other cases he might need, download them, and store them in a folder for his personal review.
https://claude.com/blog/cowork-is-now-claude

## 🎙 PODCASTS
The takeaway: the unglamorous software infrastructure layer in the middle of the AI stack is where the next $30B of value quietly accumulates.

On The MAD Podcast with Matt Turck, Renen Hallak, founder and CEO of **VAST Data**, explains why the layer between GPUs and models matters more than it gets credit for. He describes the AI factory as the culmination of a fully rebuilt stack, where racks went from 10 kilowatts to 500 kilowatts and data is now pictures, video, sound and natural language rather than columns of a database. The scale is startling: one AI cloud customer projected 500 petabytes over three years, then came back a week later needing an extra two exabytes on top, and VAST runs a single cluster of multiple exabytes delivering tens of terabytes per second across tens of thousands of nodes.

Hallak traces the company back to 2015, when neural nets that could tell which videos had cats convinced him that faster access to more data, not new algorithms, was the unlock. He spent six months as a student trying to prove P=NP, reasoning that proving equality would also solve the other six millennium problems for $7,000,000, and concluded he was not nearly smart enough. His architecture bet was the opposite of shared nothing sharding: disaggregated shared everything, with SSDs on the other side of a fast network so every node sees all information as if directly attached. He notes the timing was brutal, telling early VCs there was no plan B if the underlying technologies did not arrive, and that storage was simply not sexy.

On agents, he thinks of them as artificial people that will fine tune models from experience, meaning each organization's IP becomes weights they own rather than something the big labs capture. That leads to VAST's new model management push, including confidential computing with encrypted memory so enterprises can run inference on prem without exposing model builders' weights, and his vision of an intelligence marketplace where a carpentry shop could lease its best carpenter-robot brain module for a week without revealing the weights. His line on the stakes: "I think in the next ten years, we'll see more difference than we did in the last thousand years."
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=awoR908Yu5Y

deck: Coding agents race ahead while the rest of knowledge work waits for rebuilt workflows. Meanwhile, the infrastructure layer feeding all those GPUs quietly becomes a $30B business.
quote: I am very uncomfortable about people trying to ascribe religious force or a surrender of human judgment to AI models, and think it is a real safety issue.
quoteBy: Sam Altman · The mission of OpenAI is to ensure that AGI benefits all of humanity

## 🧭 Daily Insights

**Core insight**: The conversation today centers on a widening gap between AI capability and AI adoption. Coding agents have taken off, but real agentic adoption across the rest of knowledge work is still early because workflows need to be rebuilt, not just augmented with chat. At the same time, builders are pushing for simpler products, arguing that today's AI tools look like airplane cockpits with too many levers.

## 𝕏 / TWITTER

**Thibault Sottiaux** announced a strategic reset at OpenAI, stating that the only things being worked on are simplifications, more efficiency for more usage, and groundbreaking features or new models. He acknowledged that feedback is clear users want things to get simpler. He also shared a personal milestone: using his dot to achieve inbox zero for the first time, with the agent deleting unnecessary email categories, labeling work emails, and walking him through replies that needed context.

**Madhu Guru** argued that AI adoption is largely a product problem today. Even among the 2% paying for AI, usage depth is shallow. The main reason: most AI products look like airplane cockpits with 100 levers including connectors, permissions, model selection, and token usage. He expects things to look materially different in the next 12 months as product teams make AI easier to use.

**Guillermo Rauch** predicted that security will become a larger function in software companies, describing it as verification engineering and capital allocation. He raised the challenge for startups: as AI adversaries grow more sophisticated, how can you trust a 2-person-and-a-dog company? He also declared that AI will make everything free, including itself, with free energy as humanity's final frontier.

**Aaron Levie** described AI agent adoption as bimodal: coding and coding-adjacent tasks have taken off, while everything else lags. Even within coding, only a small percentage of developers deploy background agents working in parallel. He emphasized that most knowledge work workflows still need to be reengineered for agents, requiring new practices for accountability, governance, and security. He expects 100X more agent adoption from what we have seen so far.

**Ryo Lu** published a long reflection on convergence to the mean, warning that when everyone looks at everyone else to decide what to make, we eventually stop making anything of our own. He argued that AI makes this loop frictionless, drawing from more references than we could see in a lifetime, but access to every perspective is not the same as having one. He called for approaching software more like artists, asking what you are trying to let someone feel, understand, or do.

**Aditya Agarwal** pointed out a common misconception that wealth buys unlimited access to the world's best professionals. In reality, the world's leading cancer doctor will still see you for 20-30 minutes. He argued this is why AI is so transformative: it both democratizes access and makes the amount of time available unlimited for every individual, the practical effect of intelligence too cheap to meter.

**Sam Altman** stated he is very uncomfortable about people trying to ascribe religious force or a surrender of human judgment to AI models, and thinks it is a real safety issue.

**Nikunj Kothari** observed an innovator's dilemma playing out as personal agents become inevitable. Amazon is protecting its ads cash cow and brand, while DoorDash is slowly opening the gates with CLIs and allowing orders via text. He also cautioned against tokenmaxxing for its own sake, calling it not honestly useful in this era.

**Peter Steinberger** noted the irony of everyone building the same thing, and flagged that OpenClaw's Android app has been stuck in review limbo for over a week.

**Zara Zhang** posed a simple question: how will the world change if coding agents get 10x better?

**Amjad Masad** shared a podcast conversation with Alex Atallah of OpenRouter, going deep and technical. He also teased Replit Drift.

## 📰 OFFICIAL BLOGS

**Claude Blog** announced that Claude Cowork and chat are merging into one Claude. Users can bring a quick question or hand over a report due at noon, and Claude takes it from there, even after the laptop is closed. It is rolling out on Pro and Max plans over the next few weeks. Claude Docs and Claude Slides are new today, and Claude Design now works inside conversations. All three are in beta on paid plans, with Enterprise admins controlling when to turn them on. The blog quoted Andrew Keller, Senior Economist: "I could have Claude pull up my legal research database, and it would pull all the cases, read them, figure out which other cases I might need, download them, and store them in a folder for my personal review."

https://claude.com/blog/cowork-is-now-claude

## 🎙 PODCASTS

**Takeaway**: The software infrastructure layer feeding GPUs is becoming the operating system for the AI era, and it is a $30 billion business hiding in plain sight.

Matt Turck interviewed Renen Hallak, founder and CEO of VAST Data, on The MAD Podcast. Hallak described VAST as sitting right in the middle of Jensen Huang's five-layer cake: power, hardware, software infrastructure, models, and applications. He called the software infrastructure layer "the operating system for this new era," managing compute, storage, networking, databases, and the tools needed as the industry shifts from training to inference, agents, and reinforcement learning.

Hallak shared a striking anecdote about the pace of demand: "We had a customer, one of these AI clouds, they said we're probably going to need about 500 petabytes over the next three years. Last week, came back to us and said, we're gonna need an extra two exabytes on top of that 500 petabytes." He predicted that in the next ten years, we will see more difference than in the last thousand years.

On the AI factory concept, Hallak explained that data centers are being rebuilt from 10 kilowatt racks to 500 kilowatt racks, with GPUs replacing CPUs and extremely fast networks replacing 10 gig ethernet. He argued that enterprises will eventually need their own AI factories because their IP will be distilled into models and weights. Drawing an analogy to the human brain, he said we are all born with a base model but fine-tune through experience: "we infer during the day, we fine tune at night, and tomorrow we'll be a little bit smarter than we were today."

Hallak also discussed VAST's new model management announcement, including confidential computing that allows enterprises to run inference on prem without exposing model builders' weights. He envisioned an intelligence marketplace where a carpentry shop with the best carpenter robots could lease that brain module for a week without revealing the weights. He noted that AI has now proven it can do things we do not know how to do, referencing OpenAI's claimed solution to Navier-Stokes and rumors of more Millennium Prize problems being tackled.

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=awoR908Yu5Y

keywords: agent adoption | AI factories | product simplicity
headline: AI's Real Bottleneck Is Product, Not Models
deck: Builders agree agents have barely started, while OpenAI trims Codex and a $30B data layer steps out of the shadows. The next 12 months will decide who makes AI simple enough to actually use.
quote: I am very uncomfortable about people trying to ascribe religious force or a surrender of human judgment to AI models, and think it is a real safety issue.
quoteBy: Sam Altman · The mission of OpenAI is to ensure that AGI benefits all of humanity

## 🧭 Daily Insights
**Core insight**: The loudest thread today is that AI's bottleneck has shifted from capability to product. Madhu Guru argues most AI products look like airplane cockpits with 100 levers, and Aaron Levie says agent adoption is bimodal, with coding far ahead of everything else. Meanwhile Thibault Sottiaux says OpenAI is locking in on simplification and efficiency for Codex and ChatGPT, and Renen Hallak describes the invisible software infrastructure layer that feeds the GPUs.

## 𝕏 / TWITTER
Thibault Sottiaux, Codex & ChatGPT at OpenAI, says the team is locking in on simplifications, more efficiency for more usage, and groundbreaking features or new models, noting feedback is clear that users want things simpler. He also described using his dot to reach inbox zero: it deleted unneeded email categories in batch, labeled work emails, and walked him through replies while searching for context in the background.

Madhu Guru, Sr Director of AI at Meta, argues AI adoption is largely a product problem today. Even among the 2% paying for AI, usage depth is shallow because most products look like airplane cockpits with 100 levers such as connectors, permissions, model selection, and token usage. He expects this to change materially in the next 12 months as product teams make AI easier to use.

Amjad Masad, CEO of Replit, shared a technical conversation with Alex Atallah of OpenRouter and teased **Replit Drift**.

Guillermo Rauch, CEO of Vercel, predicts security will become a larger function in software companies, framing it as verification engineering plus capital allocation, and asks how you trust a 2-person-and-a-dog company as AI adversaries grow more sophisticated. He also claims AI will make everything free, including itself, with free energy as the last domino.

Aaron Levie, CEO of Box, says AI agent adoption is still very bimodal: coding and coding-adjacent tasks have taken off while everything else lags. Even within coding, only a small percentage of developers deploy background agents in parallel, and the rest of knowledge work needs workflows rebuilt, data rewired, new accountability and liability practices, governance changes, and security upgrades. He expects 100X more agent adoption from what we have seen so far.

Ryo Lu, who designed Cursor, Notion, and Stripe, wrote a long essay on convergence to the mean: when everyone looks at everyone else to decide what to make, we copy what works and everything becomes polished and interchangeable. He argues AI makes this loop frictionless, producing a tidal wave of mid, and that builders should approach making things more like artists, developing a perspective through the work rather than borrowing a competitor's roadmap.

Nikunj Kothari, partner at FPV Ventures, sees an innovator's dilemma as personal agents become inevitable: Amazon is protecting its ads cash cow and brand, while DoorDash is slowly opening the gates with CLIs and text ordering. He also warns that tokenmaxxing for its own sake is not useful in this era.

Peter Steinberger, building OpenClaw, laughed about how everyone is building the same thing and asked for help at Google, noting OpenClaw's Android app has been stuck in review limbo for over a week.

Aditya Agarwal, General Partner at SPC and co-founder of Bevel Health, notes that even the world's leading cancer doctor will still only see you for 20-30 minutes no matter how rich you are. AI is crazy because it both democratizes access and makes time unlimited for every individual, the practical effect of intelligence too cheap to meter.

Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI, said he is very uncomfortable about people trying to ascribe religious force or a surrender of human judgment to AI models, and thinks it is a real safety issue.

## 📰 OFFICIAL BLOGS
Claude Cowork and chat are now one Claude. Starting today, Cowork and chat merge into a single Claude that can take a task from a quick question to a report due at noon, even after you close your laptop. It rolls out on Pro and Max plans over the next few weeks. Claude Docs and Claude Slides are new, and Claude Design now works inside conversations, so you can write a document together, draft slides, edit directly, present from Claude, or download as PowerPoint or PDF. All three are in beta on paid plans, and Enterprise admins choose when to turn them on. The team says people used Cowork and Design separately and found deciding where a task belonged frustrating, so Claude now figures out what a task needs, with context, skills, and connectors available from any conversation. Senior Economist Andrew Keller described having Claude pull up his legal research database, read the cases, find others he might need, download them, and store them in a folder for personal review.
https://claude.com/blog/cowork-is-now-claude

## 🎙 PODCASTS
Takeaway: the least visible layer of the AI stack, the software infrastructure that feeds data to GPUs, may be where the biggest fortunes are being quietly made.

On The MAD Podcast with Matt Turck, Renen Hallak, founder and CEO of VAST Data, describes a company valued at $30,000,000,000 that powers top AI players like xAI yet stays surprisingly under the radar. He places VAST right in the middle of Jensen Huang's five layer cake: power, hardware, software infrastructure, models, applications. He calls his layer the operating system for this new era, managing compute, storage, networking, databases, training, inference, and the tools that make agents simple, safe, fast, and resilient.

Hallak explains why the old stack breaks. Data centers went from 10 kilowatt racks to 500 kilowatt racks, and shared nothing architectures with sharding top out around 100 nodes because communication grows quadratically. VAST built the opposite: disaggregated shared everything, with SSDs on the other side of a fast network using NVMe over Fabrics, so all nodes see all information as if directly attached. One customer runs multiple exabytes in a single cluster delivering tens of terabytes per second across tens of thousands of nodes.

On demand, he says: "We had a customer, one of these AI clouds, they said we're probably going to need about 500 petabytes over the next three years. Last week, came back to us and said, we're gonna need an extra two exabytes on top of that 500 petabytes."

He argues every organization's IP will be distilled into weights, with agents fine tuning through reinforcement learning over time, and that enterprises will want to own that IP rather than expose it to model builders. VAST's new announcement is model management, including confidential computing with encrypted memory and Nvidia, so enterprises can run inference on prem without exposing model builders' weights, opening regulated industries to these models. He also recalls spending six months trying to prove P=NP as a student, and notes that AI is now solving problems like Navier Stokes that people could not.
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=awoR908Yu5Y

## 📰 OFFICIAL BLOGS

**Claude Blog** announced that Claude Cowork and chat are merging into one Claude, rolling out on Pro and Max plans over the next few weeks with more plans to follow. https://claude.com/blog/cowork-is-now-claude

## 🎙 PODCASTS

**Takeaway**: The layer feeding data to GPUs is the least visible and most valuable part of the AI stack, and it is being rebuilt from scratch.

On The MAD Podcast with Matt Turck, Renen Hallak, founder and CEO of VAST Data, walks through the software infrastructure layer that sits in the middle of Jensen Huang's five layer cake, between hardware below and models above. He calls it the operating system for this new era, managing compute, storage, networking, databases, and the tools that make training, inference, and agents simple, safe, fast, scalable, and resilient.

Hallak describes how data centers have changed: old stacks had 10 kilowatt racks, today you need 500 kilowatt racks, GPUs instead of CPUs, extremely fast networks, and very large SSDs instead of 10 gig ethernet and old hard drives. Because we are no longer analyzing numbers and columns but pictures, video, sound, and natural language, every layer of the cake needs to be redone, and the culmination is what he calls the AI factory. He expects AI factories to be for everyone eventually, not just the big labs, and argues that once you reach a certain scale it is more cost effective to buy than to rent.

His analogy for enterprise model work is the human brain: we are all born with a base model, we infer during the day and fine tune at night, and tomorrow we are a little smarter. He predicts every organization's IP will be distilled into models and weights they own, and that agents will fine tune based on experiences with us, learn from each other, and generate the next level of artificial intelligence. He also wants an intelligence marketplace where an enterprise can lease a brain module for a week without exposing its weights, which is where VAST's new model management and confidential computing announcement comes in, using Nvidia encrypted memory so enterprises can run inference on prem without exposing model builders' weights.

On the storage architecture, Hallak explains that old shared nothing systems break down past about 100 nodes because communication grows quadratically, while AI needs systems with many millions of nodes. VAST built the opposite: disaggregated shared everything, with SSDs on the other side of a fast network using NVMe over Fabrics, so all nodes see all information as if directly attached. He notes one customer site runs multiple exabytes in a single cluster delivering tens of terabytes per second across tens of thousands of nodes, and that pitching storage to VCs in 2016 was hard but left far less competition.

A memorable line from the episode: "I think in the next ten years, we'll see more difference than we did in the last thousand years."

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=awoR908Yu5Y

On the infrastructure side, the layer between GPUs and models is emerging as a $30B business nobody talks about, and the argument is that enterprises will eventually own their own weights and agents rather than renting intelligence from a handful of labs.

**Aditya Agarwal** points out that even the world's leading cancer doctor will still only see you for 20-30 minutes no matter how rich you are, which is why AI is so crazy: it democratizes access and makes time unlimited for every individual, the practical effect of intelligence too cheap to meter.

**Sam Altman** said he is very uncomfortable about people trying to ascribe religious force or a surrender of human judgment to AI models, and thinks it is a real safety issue.

**Nikunj Kothari** sees an innovator's dilemma playing out as personal agents become inevitable: Amazon is protecting its ads cash cow and brand, while DoorDash, albeit smaller, is opening the gates slowly with CLIs and text ordering. ## 📰 OFFICIAL BLOGS

**Claude Blog** announced that Claude Cowork and chat are merging into one Claude, so a task started in one place carries into the other with the context, skills, and connectors you already have. Claude Docs and Claude Slides are new, and Claude Design now works inside conversations: ask for a document and you write it together, ask for a presentation and Claude drafts the slides, editable directly, presentable from Claude, or downloadable as PowerPoint or PDF. All three are in beta on paid plans, rolling out on Pro and Max over the next few weeks, with Enterprise admins choosing when to turn them on. Andrew Keller, Senior Economist, described having Claude pull up his legal research database, read all the cases, figure out which other cases he might need, download them, and store them in a folder for personal review. The blog's example: a weekly report due at noon, drafted as a doc with teammate notes and matching slides from the same conversation, then scheduled to run every Monday without being asked.

https://claude.com/blog/cowork-is-now-claude

## 🎙 PODCASTS

**Takeaway: the unglamorous middle layer between GPUs and models is quietly becoming a $30B business, and the next fight is over who owns the weights.**

On The MAD Podcast, Matt Turck spoke with Renen Hallak, founder and CEO of VAST Data, about the software infrastructure layer that feeds data to GPUs. Hallak places VAST right in the middle of Jensen Huang's five layer cake: power, hardware, software infrastructure, models, applications. He calls his layer "the operating system for this new era," managing compute, storage, networking, databases, and increasingly the tools for inference, agents, and reinforcement learning.

The scale numbers are the story. One AI cloud customer told VAST they would need about 500 petabytes over three years, then came back and said they needed an extra two exabytes on top. VAST has a single cluster at a customer site that is multiple exabytes across tens of thousands of nodes, delivering tens of terabytes per second. Hallak explains why the old shared-nothing architecture breaks: communication grows quadratically within the cluster, and you cannot really exceed 100 nodes, while AI needs millions. VAST's answer is disaggregated shared everything, with SSDs on the other side of a fast network using NVMe over Fabrics, so every node sees all the information as if it were directly attached.

On agents, Hallak thinks of them as artificial people that will fine tune models based on experiences with us, and that each organization will own the IP generated through that fine tuning rather than letting the big model builders own everything. He wants an intelligence marketplace where a carpentry shop with the best carpenter robots can lease that brain module for a week without ever exposing the weights. VAST's announcement this week is about model management, including confidential computing with Nvidia encrypted memory so enterprises can run inference on prem without exposing model builders' weights, expanding their addressable market into regulated industries.

The memorable line: "I think in the next ten years, we'll see more difference than we did in the last thousand years." Hallak also admits he spent six months of his life trying to prove P=NP, hoping to collect the $7 million in millennium prizes, before concluding he was not nearly smart enough. He notes that AI has now proven it can do things we do not know how to do, with rumors that OpenAI and Anthropic are close on more of the seven millennium problems.

## 📰 OFFICIAL BLOGS

**Claude Blog** announced that Claude Cowork and chat are merging into one Claude, so a quick question or a report due at noon can be handed over and Claude takes it from there even after you close your laptop. It is rolling out on Pro and Max plans over the next few weeks, with more plans to follow. Claude Docs and Claude Slides are new, and Claude Design now works inside conversations, so you can ask for a document and write it together or ask for a presentation and Claude drafts the slides, then edit directly, present from Claude, or download as PowerPoint or PDF. All three are in beta on paid plans, and Enterprise admins choose when to turn them on. The post notes people used Cowork and Design separately and said the frustrating part was deciding where a task belonged, and what they started in one did not carry into the other, so Claude now figures out what a task needs with the context, skills, and connectors you already have. Senior Economist Andrew Keller is quoted: "I could have Claude pull up [my legal research database], and it would pull all the cases, read them, figure out which other cases I might need, download them, and store them in a folder for my personal review."

https://claude.com/blog/cowork-is-now-claude

## 🎙 PODCASTS

**Takeaway**: The layer between models and GPUs is where the next $30B of AI value hides, and it is being rebuilt from scratch.

On The MAD Podcast with Matt Turck, Renen Hallak, founder and CEO of VAST Data, explains why the software infrastructure layer in the middle of Jensen's five layer cake is being redone end to end. He describes the shift from 10 kilowatt racks to 500 kilowatt racks, from CPUs to GPUs, from 10 gig ethernet and old hard drives to extremely fast networks and very large SSDs, and from analyzing numbers and columns to pictures, video, sound, and natural language. One customer, an AI cloud, first projected 500 petabytes over three years, then came back needing an extra two exabytes on top of that.

Hallak traces the founding intuition to 2015 and 2016, before the Transformers paper and long before the ChatGPT moment: neural nets could suddenly recognize which videos had cats, and it was clear the enabling factor was faster access to far more data, not new algorithms. Existing systems assumed you needed fast or big, but AI needed both fast and very large, so VAST built the opposite of shared nothing sharding, a disaggregated shared everything architecture where media sits on the other side of a fast network and every node sees all information as if directly attached. He notes one customer site today runs multiple exabytes in a single cluster delivering tens of terabytes per second across tens of thousands of nodes, and that old architectures break down past roughly 100 nodes because communication grows quadratically.

On agents, he thinks of them as artificial people that will fine tune models through reinforcement learning over time, so each organization's IP gets distilled into weights they own rather than the big model builders owning everything. He compares it to the human brain: we are born with a base model, infer during the day, fine tune at night, and tomorrow we are a little smarter, with each person's model of the universe slightly different. That leads to his vision of an intelligence marketplace, where a carpentry shop with the best carpenter robots could lease that brain module for a week without ever exposing the weights.

The week's announcement is model management as part of the operating system, understanding which model is good at coding, which at images, which is expensive, and routing tasks accordingly, plus confidential computing with Nvidia and encrypted memory so enterprises can run inference on prem without exposing model builders' weights. His most memorable line: "I think in the next ten years, we'll see more difference than we did in the last thousand years."

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=awoR908Yu5Y

keywords: AI agents | product simplicity | AI factories
headline: AI's Next Frontier Is Simplicity, Not More Levers
deck: Builders agree agent adoption is still bimodal and AI products feel like airplane cockpits. Meanwhile the infrastructure layer feeding the GPUs quietly becomes a $30B story.
quote: I am very uncomfortable about people trying to ascribe religious force or a surrender of human judgment to AI models, and think it is a real safety issue.
quoteBy: Sam Altman · The mission of OpenAI is to ensure that AGI benefits all of humanity

## 🧭 Daily Insights

**Core insight**: Today's conversation converges on one theme: AI has a product problem, not a capability problem. Madhu Guru argues even the 2% paying for AI use it shallowly because products resemble airplane cockpits with 100 levers, while Aaron Levie notes agent adoption is bimodal, with coding far ahead of everything else. The counterweight comes from infrastructure: VAST Data's Renen Hallak describes an AI factory layer where enterprises will own their own weights and fine-tuned intelligence.

## 𝕏 / TWITTER

Thibault Sottiaux, working on Codex and ChatGPT at OpenAI, says the team is locking in on simplifications, more efficiency for more usage, and groundbreaking features or new models, acknowledging that feedback is clear users want things simpler. He also described using his dot to reach inbox zero for the first time, deleting unneeded email categories in batch, auto-labeling work emails, and walking through replies with background context search.

Madhu Guru, Sr Director of AI at Meta, argues AI adoption is largely a product problem today: even among the 2% paying for AI, usage depth is shallow, mainly because most AI products look like airplane cockpits with 100 levers covering connectors, permissions, model selection, and token usage. He expects this to change materially in the next 12 months as product teams make AI easier to use.

Guillermo Rauch, CEO of Vercel, predicts security will become a larger function in software companies, framing it as verification engineering plus capital allocation, and asks how anyone can trust a 2-person-and-a-dog company as AI adversaries grow more sophisticated. He also argues AI will make everything free, including itself, with free energy as the last domino and humanity's final frontier.

Aaron Levie, CEO of Box, says AI agent adoption is still very bimodal: coding and coding-adjacent tasks have taken off while the rest of knowledge work is very early, because most workflows still need to be reengineered for agents. That requires rebuilt workflows, newly wired data, new accountability and liability practices, governance and compliance changes, and security upgrades, which is why he expects 100X more agent adoption from what we have seen so far.

Ryo Lu, who designed at Cursor, Notion, and Stripe, wrote a long essay on convergence to the mean: when everyone looks at everyone else to decide what to make, we eventually stop making anything of our own, and AI makes this loop frictionless. He argues access to every perspective is not the same as having one, warns of a tidal wave of mid, and calls for approaching software more like artists, asking what you are trying to let someone feel, understand, or do.

Aditya Agarwal, General Partner at SPC and Co-Founder of Bevel Health, notes that even the super rich cannot get unlimited time from the world's best doctor or lawyer, since a leading cancer doctor will still see you for 20-30min. AI changes this by both democratizing access and making time unlimited for every individual, the practical effect of intelligence too cheap to meter.

Sam Altman, whose mission at OpenAI is to ensure that AGI benefits all of humanity, says he is very uncomfortable about people trying to ascribe religious force or a surrender of human judgment to AI models, and thinks it is a real safety issue.

Nikunj Kothari, partner at FPV Ventures, frames an innovator's dilemma as personal agents become inevitable: Amazon is protecting its ads cash cow and brand, while DoorDash, albeit smaller, is opening the gates slowly with CLIs and text ordering. He also warns that tokenmaxxing for its own sake is not honestly useful in this era.

Peter Steinberger, building OpenClaw, laughed about how everyone is building the same thing and flagged that OpenClaw's Android app has been stuck over a week in review limbo at Google.

Zara Zhang, a builder, posed a single question: how will the world change if coding agents get 10x better?

## 📰 OFFICIAL BLOGS

Claude Cowork and chat are now one Claude. Starting today, Cowork and chat merge into a single Claude, so you can bring a quick question or hand over a report due at noon and Claude takes it from there, even after you have closed your laptop. It rolls out on Pro and Max plans over the next few weeks, with more plans to follow. Claude Docs and Claude Slides are new today, and Claude Design now works inside conversations too: ask for a document and you and Claude write it together, ask for a presentation and Claude drafts the slides, then edit directly, present straight from Claude, or download as PowerPoint or PDF. All three are in beta on paid plans, and Enterprise admins choose when to turn them on. The team says people used Cowork and Design separately and told them the frustrating part was deciding where a task belonged, and what they started in one did not carry into the other, so they stopped making users choose. Claude can now figure out what a task needs, with the context, skills, and connectors you already have. Senior Economist Andrew Keller described having Claude pull up his legal research database, pull all the cases, read them, figure out which other cases he might need, download them, and store them in a folder for personal review. Anything you make with Claude Design, Slides, or Docs lives at one shareable link you can open on your phone.
https://claude.com/blog/cowork-is-now-claude

## 🎙 PODCASTS

The takeaway: the least visible layer of the AI stack, the software infrastructure feeding the GPUs, may be where the most durable moat gets built.

He places VAST right in the middle of Jensen Huang's five layer cake, between hardware below and model builders above, managing compute, storage, networking, databases, and the tooling for training, inference, agents, and reinforcement learning. The scale is startling: one AI cloud customer projected about 500 petabytes over three years, then came back needing an extra two exabytes on top of that.

Existing systems assumed you needed things fast or big, while AI needed both fast and very large, so VAST built the opposite of shared nothing sharding: disaggregated shared everything, with SSDs on the other side of a fast network using NVMe over Fabrics, so all nodes see all information as if directly attached. One customer site today runs multiple exabytes in a single cluster delivering tens of terabytes per second across tens of thousands of nodes, before the agentic revolution.

His most striking line: "I think in the next ten years, we'll see more difference than we did in the last thousand years." He extends the analogy to agents as artificial people that fine tune on their experiences with you, meaning each organization's IP gets distilled into weights it owns, which is why he wants an intelligence marketplace where enterprises do not expose data and model builders do not expose weights. ## 🎙 PODCASTS

**Takeaway**: The layer between GPUs and models is quietly becoming the operating system of the AI era, and whoever owns the weights owns the future.

On The MAD Podcast with Matt Turck, Renen Hallak, founder and CEO of VAST Data, explains where his company sits in Jensen Huang's five layer cake: right in the middle, the software infrastructure layer that manages compute, storage, networking, databases, and the tools for training, inference, and agents. He calls it the operating system for this new era. The AI factory concept, he says, is not just for big labs: the old stack of 10 kilowatt racks, 10 gig ethernet, and hard drives is being replaced by 500 kilowatt racks, extremely fast networks, and very large SSDs, because AI now processes pictures, video, sound, and natural language rather than columns of a database. He gives a striking example of demand: one AI cloud customer said it would need about 500 petabytes over three years, then came back and said it needed an extra two exabytes on top of that.

Hallak's view of agents is that they are artificial people that will fine tune models through reinforcement learning over time, so every organization's IP gets distilled into its own weights. He compares it to the human brain: we are all born with a base model, we infer during the day and fine tune at night, and tomorrow we are a little smarter. That is why he argues enterprises will not want to expose proprietary processes to a model builder, and model builders will not want to expose their weights, which is what VAST's new model management and confidential computing announcement addresses, using encrypted memory with help from Nvidia so enterprises can run inference on prem without either side seeing what it should not. He imagines an intelligence marketplace where a carpentry shop with the best carpenter robots could lease that brain module for a week without revealing the weights.

On the architecture, Hallak explains that old shared nothing systems break down past roughly 100 nodes because communication grows quadratically, while AI needs systems with many millions of nodes; VAST's disaggregated shared everything design puts SSDs on the other side of a fast network using NVMe over Fabrics so all nodes see all information as if directly attached. One customer system is multiple exabytes in a single cluster delivering tens of terabytes per second. He also recalls spending six months trying to prove P=NP as a student, and notes that AI is now being used on millennium problems like Navier Stokes that have been open for nearly a hundred years.

**Takeaway**: The layer between GPUs and models, worth roughly $30B, is quietly becoming the operating system of the AI era, and whoever owns model management and confidential computing may decide how enterprises adopt AI at all.

He later joined a startup acquired by EMC, and in 2015 saw that neural nets were finally showing they could do something, recognizing that faster access to more data was the key enabler. He started VAST in early 2016, three years before the Transformers paper. "We don't have a plan B," he told early VCs who asked what would happen if the underlying technologies didn't materialize. That forward bet became VAST's moat.

keywords: AI agents | product design | AI infrastructure
headline: AI's Missing Middle: Why Agents Stall and Products Confuse
deck: Adoption stays bimodal as builders debate whether AI's real bottleneck is product design or the infrastructure feeding GPUs, while one founder warns against a tidal wave of sameness.
quote: I am very uncomfortable about people trying to ascribe religious force or a surrender of human judgment to AI models, and think it is a real safety issue.
quoteBy: Sam Altman · The mission of OpenAI is to ensure that AGI benefits all of humanity

## 🧭 Daily Insights

**Core insight**: The conversation today splits between two camps: those arguing AI adoption is a product problem, not a capability problem, and those building the invisible infrastructure layer that makes it all possible. Madhu Guru and Aaron Levie both point to the same gap, that most AI products still look like airplane cockpits and real agentic adoption outside coding is barely started. Meanwhile, Renen Hallak's podcast makes the case that the layer feeding GPUs is where the next $30B of value sits, and Ryo Lu warns that frictionless AI generation risks a "tidal wave of mid" if builders stop having a point of view.

## 𝕏 / TWITTER

**Thibault Sottiaux** announced a strategic reset at OpenAI, saying the team is locking in on simplifications, more efficiency for more usage, and groundbreaking features or new models, noting that feedback is clear users want things simpler. He also shared a personal win: achieving inbox zero for the first time by making it an active goal for his dot, which deleted unneeded email categories in batch, labeled work emails, and walked him through replies needing context.

**Madhu Guru** argued that AI adoption is largely a product problem today. Even among the 2% paying for AI, usage depth is shallow because most products look like airplane cockpits with 100 levers: connectors, permissions, model selection, token usage. He expects this to change materially in the next 12 months as product teams make AI easier to use.

**Guillermo Rauch** predicted security will become a larger function in software companies, framing it as verification engineering plus capital allocation, and asked how anyone can trust a 2-person-and-a-dog company as AI adversaries grow more sophisticated. He also declared that AI will make everything free, including itself, with free energy as humanity's final frontier.

**Aaron Levie** described AI agent adoption as still very bimodal: coding and coding-adjacent tasks have taken off, everything else lags. Even within coding, only a small percentage of developers deploy background agents working in parallel while most work 1:1. He argued the rest of knowledge work needs workflows rebuilt, data rewired, new accountability and governance paradigms, and security upgrades, which is why he expects 100X more agent adoption from what we've seen so far.

**Ryo Lu** published a long essay on convergence to the mean, warning that when everyone looks at everyone else to decide what to make, we stop making anything of our own. He argued AI makes this loop frictionless but access to every perspective isn't the same as having one, and that software should be approached like art, expressing beliefs about how life should feel. He closed with a question: what is the point of everyone being able to make something, if we all end up making the same thing?

**Nikunj Kothari** flagged an innovator's dilemma as personal agents become inevitable, noting Amazon is protecting its ads cash cow while DoorDash is slowly opening the gates with CLIs and text ordering. He also cautioned that tokenmaxxing for its own sake is not honestly useful in this era.

**Aditya Agarwal** pushed back on the idea that wealth buys unlimited access to top professionals, noting the world's leading cancer doctor still sees you for 20-30 minutes. He argued AI both democratizes access and makes time unlimited for every individual, the practical effect of intelligence too cheap to meter.

**Sam Altman** said he is very uncomfortable about people trying to ascribe religious force or a surrender of human judgment to AI models, calling it a real safety issue.

**Peter Steinberger** joked about how everyone is building the same thing, and flagged that OpenClaw's Android app has been stuck in review limbo for over a week, asking if anyone at Google could help.

**Amjad Masad** shared a deep technical conversation with Alex Atallah of OpenRouter and teased something called Replit Drift.

**Zara Zhang** posed a simple question: how will the world change if coding agents get 10x better?

## 📰 OFFICIAL BLOGS

**Claude Blog** announced that Claude Cowork and chat are merging into one Claude, rolling out on Pro and Max plans over the next few weeks. Claude Docs and Claude Slides are new, and Claude Design now works inside conversations. Users can ask for a document and write it together with Claude, or ask for a presentation and Claude drafts the slides, editable directly, presentable from Claude, or downloadable as PowerPoint or PDF. All three are in beta on paid plans, with Enterprise admins controlling when to turn them on. The blog explained that Cowork was built as a separate place for bigger work and Design for visual work, but people used both and found deciding where a task belonged frustrating, and work started in one didn't carry into the other. Now Claude figures out what a task needs, with context, skills, and connectors available from any conversation. Andrew Keller, Senior Economist, is quoted: "I could have Claude pull up [my legal research database], and it would pull all the cases, read them, figure out which other cases I might need, download them, and store them in a folder for my personal review."

https://claude.com/blog/cowork-is-now-claude

## 🎙 PODCASTS

**Takeaway**: The layer between GPUs and models is where AI's next $30B of value hides, and it's being rebuilt from scratch.

Matt Turck interviewed Renen Hallak, founder and CEO of VAST Data, on The MAD Podcast. Hallak described VAST as sitting "right in the middle" of Jensen Huang's five-layer cake, the software infrastructure layer he sometimes calls "the operating system for this new era." He explained that the old stack of 10 kilowatt racks and 10 gig ethernet has been replaced by 500 kilowatt racks, extremely fast networks, and very large SSDs, because AI workloads are pictures, video, sound, and natural language rather than columns of a database.

The scale is staggering. One customer, an AI cloud, initially projected 500 petabytes over three years, then came back needing an extra two exabytes on top. VAST has a single cluster today at multiple exabytes delivering tens of terabytes per second across tens of thousands of nodes. Hallak explained why the old shared-nothing architecture breaks down: communication grows quadratically within the cluster, and resilience suffers when one part fails. VAST's "disaggregated shared everything" architecture puts SSDs on the other side of a fast network using NVMe over Fabrics, so all nodes see all information as if directly attached.

On agents, Hallak offered a memorable analogy: "we were all born with a base model but then over time as we travel the world we learn new things, we infer during the day, we fine tune at night." He predicted every organization's IP will be distilled into models and weights they own, and that enterprises won't want to expose proprietary processes to big model builders. VAST's new announcement focuses on model management and confidential computing, letting enterprises run inference on prem without exposing model builders' weights, using Nvidia encrypted memory underneath. Hallak also recalled spending six months trying to prove P=NP as a student, realizing he wasn't nearly smart enough, and noted that AI is now solving millennium problems humans couldn't crack in a century.

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=awoR908Yu5Y

## 🎙 PODCASTS

**Takeaway**: The layer between GPUs and models is where the next $30B of AI value hides, and whoever owns the operating system for AI factories will decide how enterprises keep their intelligence private.

On The MAD Podcast with Matt Turck, Renen Hallak, founder and CEO of VAST Data, explains the software infrastructure layer that feeds massive amounts of data to GPUs. He describes a customer, one of the AI clouds, that said it would need about 500 petabytes over three years and came back last week asking for an extra two exabytes on top. "I think in the next ten years, we'll see more difference than we did in the last thousand years," he says. Hallak places VAST right in the middle of Jensen Huang's five layer cake, calling his company's work the operating system for this new era, and notes that racks have gone from 10 kilowatts to 500 kilowatts, requiring new power density, extremely fast networks, and very large SSDs.

He argues the AI factory will eventually be for everyone, not just the big labs, and that enterprises will own their own models, weights, and agents rather than letting model builders own everything. His analogy: we are all born with a base model, but as we travel the world we learn new things, infer during the day, and fine tune at night. He wants a world where an enterprise does not expose its data and a model builder does not expose its weights, which is why VAST announced model management with confidential computing, using Nvidia encrypted memory so both sides can rest assured. He even imagines an intelligence marketplace where a carpentry shop could lease its best carpenter-robot brain module for a week without revealing the weights.

On his own path, Hallak recalls spending six months trying to prove whether P=NP, hoping to solve all seven millennium problems and collect $7,000,000, before concluding he was not nearly smart enough. He notes that AI has now proven it can do things we do not know how to do, with rumors that OpenAI and Anthropic are close on more of those century-old problems. He founded VAST in early 2016, before the Transformers paper and ChatGPT, betting on disaggregated shared everything architecture when the underlying parts did not yet exist. "We don't have a plan b," he told skeptical VCs. That bet is now his moat, and he credits the unsexiness of storage for keeping competition away.

**Aaron Levie** says AI agent adoption is still very bimodal: coding and coding-adjacent tasks have taken off while everything else lags, and even within coding only a small percentage of developers deploy background agents working in parallel. Most knowledge work workflows still need to be reengineered for agents, requiring new data wiring, accountability and liability practices, governance changes, and security upgrades, which is why he expects 100X more agent adoption from what we have seen so far.

**Ryo Lu** wrote a long essay on convergence to the mean: when everyone looks at everyone else to decide what to make, we copy what works and everything becomes polished but interchangeable. He argues AI makes this loop frictionless because access to every perspective is not the same as having one, and calls for approaching software more like artists, developing a point of view through the work rather than borrowing answers from a competitor's roadmap.

**Aditya Agarwal** points out that even the super rich cannot get unlimited access to the world's best doctor or lawyer, since a leading cancer doctor will still see you for 20-30min. He argues AI both democratizes access and makes the amount of time available unlimited for every individual, the practical effect of intelligence too cheap to meter.

**Sam Altman** says he is very uncomfortable about people trying to ascribe religious force or a surrender of human judgment to AI models, and thinks it is a real safety issue.

**Nikunj Kothari** sees an innovator's dilemma playing out as personal agents become inevitable: Amazon is protecting its ads cash cow and brand, while DoorDash, albeit smaller, is opening the gates slowly with CLIs and ordering via text. He also warns that tokenmaxxing for its own sake is not honestly useful in this era.

**Peter Steinberger** is over a week into review limbo for OpenClaw's Android app and is asking if anyone at Google can help.

**Zara Zhang** asks how the world will change if coding agents get 10x better.

**Amjad Masad** shared Replit Drift and a deep, somewhat technical conversation with Alex Atallah of OpenRouter.

## 📰 OFFICIAL BLOGS

**Claude Blog** announced that Claude Cowork and chat are merging into one Claude, so a quick question or a report due at noon can be handed over and Claude takes it from there even after you close your laptop. Claude Docs and Claude Slides are new, and Claude Design now works inside conversations, letting you write documents together, draft slides, edit directly, present from Claude, or download as PowerPoint or PDF. All three are in beta on paid plans, with Enterprise admins choosing when to turn them on. The post notes that people used both Cowork and Design and found deciding where a task belonged frustrating, so Claude can now figure out what a task needs, with context, skills, and connectors available from any conversation. Senior Economist Andrew Keller is quoted describing Claude pulling up his legal research database, reading cases, finding related ones, downloading them, and storing them in a folder for his review.
https://claude.com/blog/cowork-is-now-claude

## 🎙 PODCASTS

**Takeaway**: The layer between models and GPUs is quietly becoming a $30B business, and the next battleground is model management and confidential computing.

On The MAD Podcast with Matt Turck, Renen Hallak, founder and CEO of VAST Data, walks through the software infrastructure layer he calls the operating system for the AI era. He describes the shift from 10 kilowatt racks to 500 kilowatt racks, from CPUs to GPUs, and from 10 gig ethernet and old hard drives to extremely fast networks and very large SSDs, arguing every layer of the stack has to be redone because we are no longer analyzing numbers and columns but pictures, video, sound, and natural language. He recounts a customer, one of the AI clouds, saying they would need about 500 petabytes over the next three years, then coming back last week to say they needed an extra two exabytes on top of that.

Hallak explains VAST's disaggregated shared everything architecture as the opposite of shared nothing sharding, where SSDs sit on the other side of a fast network and all nodes see all information as if directly attached. He notes one customer site runs multiple exabytes in a single cluster delivering tens of terabytes per second across tens of thousands of nodes, and that old architectures cannot scale past roughly 100 nodes because communication grows quadratically. On agents, he predicts every organization's IP will be distilled into models and weights they own, with agents fine tuning through reinforcement learning over time, and he wants an intelligence marketplace where a carpentry shop could lease its best carpenter robot brain module for a week without exposing the weights. The company's new announcement is about model management and confidential computing, letting enterprises run inference on prem without exposing model builders' weights, using Nvidia encrypted memory underneath.

Memorable quote: "I think in the next ten years, we'll see more difference than we did in the last thousand years."
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=awoR908Yu5Y
