deck: Coding agents race ahead while the rest of knowledge work waits for workflows to be rebuilt. Meanwhile, a $30B infrastructure layer bets on confidential computing to unlock the enterprise.
quote: I am very uncomfortable about people trying to ascribe religious force or a surrender of human judgment to AI models, and think it is a real safety issue.
quoteBy: Sam Altman · The mission of OpenAI is to ensure that AGI benefits all of humanity

## 🧭 Daily Insights

**Core insight**: The conversation today splits between two camps: those shipping agent products and those asking why adoption remains so shallow. Aaron Levie argues real agentic adoption outside coding is still very early because workflows need to be rebuilt, not just chat interfaces deployed. Meanwhile, Madhu Guru frames AI adoption as a product problem: even among the 2% paying for AI, usage depth is shallow because products look like airplane cockpits with 100 levers.

## 𝕏 / TWITTER

**Thibault Sottiaux** announced a strategic simplification push at OpenAI, stating that only simplifications, efficiency improvements, groundbreaking features, and new models are being worked on. He also shared his experience achieving inbox zero for the first time by making it an active goal for his agent, which deleted unnecessary email categories, labeled work emails, and walked him through replies needing attention while searching for relevant context in the background.

**Madhu Guru** argued that AI adoption is largely a product problem today. Even among the 2% paying for AI, usage depth is shallow because most AI products resemble airplane cockpits with 100 levers including connectors, permissions, model selection, and token usage. He expects this to change materially in the next 12 months as product teams make AI products easier to use.

**Amjad Masad** shared a podcast conversation with Alex Atallah of OpenRouter, describing it as going deep and somewhat technical. He also teased something called Replit Drift.

**Guillermo Rauch** predicted that security will become a larger function in software companies, describing it as verification engineering and capital allocation. He noted the challenge for startups as AI adversaries grow more sophisticated, asking how you can trust a 2-person-and-a-dog company. He also stated that AI will make everything free, including itself, with free energy as humanity's final frontier.

**Aaron Levie** observed that AI agent adoption remains bimodal: coding and coding-adjacent tasks have taken off while everything else lags. Even within coding, adoption patterns vary widely, with a small percentage of developers deploying background agents working in parallel while most still work with agents 1:1. He argued that most knowledge work workflows still need to be reengineered for agents, requiring rebuilt workflows, new data wiring, accountability practices, governance changes, and security upgrades. He expects 100X more agent adoption from what we have seen so far.

**Ryo Lu** wrote a long reflection on convergence to the mean, warning that when everyone looks at everyone else to decide what to make, we eventually stop making anything of our own. He argued that AI makes this feedback loop frictionless but access to every perspective is not the same as having one. He called for approaching software more like artists, asking what you are trying to let someone feel, understand, or do, and warned against a world where everyone becomes a more efficient distributor of the same ideas.

**Zara Zhang** posed a simple question: how will the world change if coding agents get 10x better?

**Nikunj Kothari** commented on the innovator's dilemma as personal agents become inevitable, noting that Amazon is protecting its ads cash cow while DoorDash is opening the gates slowly with CLIs and allowing orders via text. He also cautioned against tokenmaxxing for its own sake, saying it is not honestly useful in this era.

**Peter Steinberger** laughed about how everyone is building the same thing. He also flagged that OpenClaw's Android app has been stuck in review limbo for over a week and asked if anyone at Google could help.

**Aditya Agarwal** challenged the misconception that being super rich grants unlimited access to the world's best professionals. He noted that the world's leading cancer doctor will still see you for 20-30 minutes no matter how much money you have. This is why AI is so crazy: it both democratizes access and makes the amount of time available unlimited for every individual, the practical effect of intelligence too cheap to meter.

**Sam Altman** stated he is very uncomfortable about people trying to ascribe religious force or a surrender of human judgment to AI models, and thinks it is a real safety issue.

## 📰 OFFICIAL BLOGS

**Claude Blog** announced that Claude Cowork and chat are merging into one Claude. Users can bring a quick question or hand over a report due at noon, and Claude takes it from there, even after the laptop is closed. It is rolling out on Pro and Max plans over the next few weeks. Claude Docs and Claude Slides are new today, and Claude Design now works inside conversations. All three are in beta on paid plans, with Enterprise admins choosing when to turn them on. The blog quoted Andrew Keller, Senior Economist, describing how he could have Claude pull up his legal research database, pull all the cases, read them, figure out which other cases he might need, download them, and store them in a folder for personal review.

https://claude.com/blog/cowork-is-now-claude

## 🎙 PODCASTS

**Takeaway**: The layer between GPUs and models is where the next $30B battle is being fought, and confidential computing may be the key that unlocks regulated enterprises.

Matt Turck interviewed Renen Hallak, founder and CEO of VAST Data, on The MAD Podcast. Hallak described VAST as sitting right in the middle of Jensen Huang's five-layer cake: power, hardware, software infrastructure, models, and applications. He called the software infrastructure layer the operating system for this new era, managing compute, storage, networking, databases, training, and inference.

Hallak shared a striking anecdote about the pace of demand: a customer, one of the AI clouds, initially said they would need about 500 petabytes over three years, then came back and said they needed an extra two exabytes on top of that. He said that in the next ten years, we will see more difference than we did in the last thousand years.

The conversation covered VAST's architecture, which Hallak described as the opposite of shared nothing systems. Instead of SSDs directly attached to CPUs, the media sits on the other side of the network, allowing all nodes to see all information as if it were directly attached. This shared everything approach enables systems with millions of nodes, with one customer site running multiple exabytes in a single cluster delivering tens of terabytes per second.

Hallak announced a new model management capability, framing models as resources that need to be managed just like GPUs or SSDs. A key aspect is confidential computing, which enables enterprises to run inference on prem without exposing model builders' weights. With help from NVIDIA and encrypted memory, neither side sees what they are not allowed to see, potentially increasing the total addressable market of model builders into regulated industries.

On agents, Hallak predicted that over time we will get attached to our agents and expect them to know things that happened yesterday or a year ago. This requires them to fine tune models based on experiences, making them smarter and able to do more. He envisioned an intelligence marketplace where, for example, a carpentry shop with the best carpenter robots could lease that brain module to others for a week without exposing the weights.

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=awoR908Yu5Y

## 🧭 Daily Insights

**Core insight**: The conversation today splits between two camps. One group is celebrating how far coding agents have come, with some builders handing off entire inboxes and reports to their AI. The other is warning that outside of coding, agent adoption is still bimodal and shallow, because most workflows have not been rebuilt for agents yet. The consensus forming is that the next 12 months belong to product teams who make AI feel simpler, not more powerful.

## 𝕏 / TWITTER

**Thibault Sottiaux** locked in a clear direction for **Codex** and **ChatGPT**: only simplifications, more efficiency for more usage, and groundbreaking features or new models. He also shared a concrete agent win, using his dot to delete unneeded email categories, auto-label work emails, and walk him through replies with background context search. The result was his first ever inbox zero, which he called a great feeling.

**Madhu Guru** argued that AI adoption is largely a product problem today. Even among the 2% paying for AI, usage depth is shallow, because most AI products look like airplane cockpits with 100 levers: connectors, permissions, model selection, token usage. He expects this to change materially in the next 12 months as product teams make AI easier to use.

**Guillermo Rauch** predicted that security will become a larger and larger function in software companies, framing it as verification engineering plus capital allocation. He noted the tension for startups: as AI adversaries grow more sophisticated, how do you trust a 2-person-and-a-dog company? He also declared that AI will make everything free, including itself, with free energy as humanity's final frontier.

**Aaron Levie** described AI agent adoption as still very bimodal. Coding and coding-adjacent tasks have taken off, with a small percentage of developers running background agents in parallel while everyone else works 1:1 with agents. The rest of knowledge work is very early because workflows must be reengineered, data rewired, and new governance, compliance, and security paradigms built. He expects 100X more agent adoption from what we have seen so far.

**Ryo Lu** wrote a long essay on convergence to the mean: when everyone looks at everyone else to decide what to make, we eventually stop making anything of our own. He argued that AI makes this loop frictionless, drawing from more references than we could see in a lifetime, but access to every perspective is not the same as having one. His prescription is to approach making things more like artists, developing a perspective through the work so software carries someone's care, humor, or curiosity.

**Nikunj Kothari** flagged an innovator's dilemma as personal agents become inevitable. Amazon is protecting its ads cash cow and brand, while DoorDash, albeit smaller, is opening the gates slowly with CLIs and text ordering. He also cautioned that tokenmaxxing for its own sake is not honestly useful in this era.

**Aditya Agarwal** pointed out a common misconception: even the super rich cannot get unlimited access to the world's best doctor, lawyer, or creative professional. The leading cancer doctor will still see you for 20-30 minutes. This is why AI is so crazy, he wrote, because it both democratizes access and makes the amount of time available unlimited for every individual, the practical effect of intelligence too cheap to meter.

**Sam Altman** said he is very uncomfortable about people trying to ascribe religious force or a surrender of human judgment to AI models, and thinks it is a real safety issue.

**Peter Steinberger** noted the review limbo for **OpenClaw**'s Android app, now over a week in review, and asked if anyone at Google could help. He also laughed about how everyone is building the same thing.

**Zara Zhang** posed a simple question: how will the world change if coding agents get 10x better?

**Amjad Masad** shared **Replit Drift** and pointed to a deep, somewhat technical conversation with Alex Atallah of **OpenRouter**.

## 📰 OFFICIAL BLOGS

**Claude Blog** announced that **Claude Cowork** and chat are merging into one Claude. Bring a quick question or hand over a report due at noon, and Claude takes it from there, even after you have closed your laptop. It is rolling out on Pro and Max plans over the next few weeks. **Claude Docs** and **Claude Slides** are new today, and **Claude Design** now works inside conversations too. Ask for a document and you and Claude write it together; ask for a presentation and Claude drafts the slides, which you can edit, present straight from Claude, or download as PowerPoint or PDF. All three are in beta on paid plans, and Enterprise admins choose when to turn them on. The team explained that people used Cowork and Design separately and told them the frustrating part was deciding where a task belonged, and what they started in one did not carry into the other. So they stopped making users choose. Claude can now figure out what a task needs, with the context, skills, and connectors you already have. Senior Economist Andrew Keller described having Claude pull up his legal research database, read the cases, figure out which other cases he might need, download them, and store them in a folder for his personal review.

https://claude.com/blog/cowork-is-now-claude

## 🎙 PODCASTS

**Takeaway**: The layer between the GPUs and the models is where the next $30B of AI value is being built, and it is being rebuilt from scratch.

On The MAD Podcast, Matt Turck spoke with Renen Hallak, founder and CEO of **VAST Data**, a company valued at $30,000,000,000 that powers top AI players like **xAI** and some of the biggest AI clouds. Hallak placed VAST right in the middle of Jensen Huang's five layer cake: power, hardware, software infrastructure, models, applications. He calls his layer the operating system for this new era, managing compute, storage, networking, databases, and the tools that make the shift from training to inference, agents, and reinforcement learning simple, safe, fast, scalable, and resilient.

The scale numbers are striking. One AI cloud customer told VAST they would need about 500 petabytes over three years, then came back and said they needed an extra two exabytes on top. Hallak described a single cluster at a customer site that is multiple exabytes, delivering tens of terabytes per second across tens of thousands of nodes, before the agentic revolution even hits. The old shared nothing architecture breaks down at that scale because communication grows quadratically and recovery is slow, which is why VAST built a disaggregated shared everything architecture, putting SSDs on the other side of a fast network with NVMe over Fabrics so every node sees all the information as if it were directly attached.

Hallak's vision for enterprises is that their IP will be distilled into models and weights. He compared it to the human brain: we are all born with a base model, then we learn as we travel the world, infer during the day, and fine tune at night. Agents will do the same, and organizations will own the IP generated through that fine tuning rather than letting the big model builders own everything. The week's announcement was about model management and confidential computing, letting enterprises run inference on prem without exposing the model builders' weights, with help from Nvidia and encrypted memory underneath. His analogy for why this matters: in the 1970s you needed a PhD in computer science to operate a computer, and today everybody can do it, not because we learned, but because the operating system made it intuitive and safe.

One memorable line from Hallak on the stakes: "I think in the next ten years, we'll see more difference than we did in the last thousand years."

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=awoR908Yu5Y

## 🎙 PODCASTS

**Takeaway**: The layer between GPUs and models is becoming the operating system for AI, and the next battle is over who owns the intelligence that gets distilled into weights.

Matt Turck talks with Renen Hallak, founder and CEO of VAST Data, about the software infrastructure layer that feeds massive amounts of data to GPUs. Hallak places VAST right in the middle of Jensen Huang's five layer cake: power, hardware, software infrastructure, models, applications. He calls his layer the operating system for this new era, managing compute, storage, networking, and increasingly making sense of data through databases and orchestrating training and inference.

On the AI factory concept, Hallak notes data centers look nothing like they did five years ago: 10 kilowatt racks have become 500 kilowatt racks, CPUs have become GPUs, and 10 gig ethernet and old hard drives have given way to extremely fast networks and very large SSDs. Every layer of the cake needs to be redone because we are no longer analyzing numbers and columns but pictures, video, sound, and natural language. He expects AI factories to be for everyone eventually, not just the big labs, and argues that once you reach a certain scale it is more cost effective to buy than rent.

His most striking idea is that every organization's IP will be distilled into models and weights. He compares it to the human brain: we are all born with a base model, we infer during the day and fine tune at night, and tomorrow we are a little smarter. Every organization's agents will fine tune through reinforcement learning over time, and that IP should belong to the enterprise, not the big model builders. This leads to his vision of an intelligence marketplace, where a carpentry shop with the best carpenter robots could lease that brain module to you for a week without ever exposing the weights.

The announcement this week is about model management: understanding which model is good at coding, which at images, which is expensive and which is cheap, and routing tasks accordingly. A key piece is confidential computing, enabling enterprises to run inference on prem without exposing model builders' weights, with help from Nvidia and encrypted memory, hopefully expanding the addressable market into regulated industries. Hallak also explains the technical bet behind VAST: the old shared nothing architecture breaks down at scale because communication grows quadratically, while VAST's disaggregated shared everything design puts SSDs on the other side of a fast network so all nodes see all information as if directly attached. One customer site runs multiple exabytes in a single cluster delivering tens of terabytes per second across tens of thousands of nodes.

On his journey, Hallak recalls spending six months trying to prove P=NP as a student, hoping to claim the Clay Institute's million dollar bounty, before realizing he was not nearly smart enough. He notes that AI has now proven it can do things we do not know how to do, with rumors that OpenAI and Anthropic are close to solving more of the millennium problems. He started VAST in early 2016, before the Transformers paper and long before ChatGPT, betting that neural nets needed both fast and very large systems. Pitching storage to VCs was hard, and he told early board members there was no plan B if the underlying technologies did not arrive. They did, across 2017 to 2019, and that forward bet is now the moat.

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=awoR908Yu5Y

keywords: AI agents | product simplicity | AI infrastructure
headline: The Agent Era's Real Bottleneck Is Product, Not Models
deck: Builders agree agent adoption is bimodal and painfully early, while the infrastructure layer feeding GPUs quietly scales toward exabytes. One CEO warns AI could make us all build the same thing.
quote: I am very uncomfortable about people trying to ascribe religious force or a surrender of human judgment to AI models, and think it is a real safety issue.
quoteBy: Sam Altman · The mission of OpenAI is to ensure that AGI benefits all of humanity

## 🧭 Daily Insights
**Core insight**: The loudest thread today is that AI's bottleneck has shifted from models to product and workflow design. Madhu Guru argues AI adoption is largely a product problem, Aaron Levie says real agentic adoption outside coding is still very early because workflows must be rebuilt, and Thibault Sottiaux says user feedback is clear: make things simpler. Meanwhile the infrastructure underneath keeps scaling, with VAST Data's founder describing customers jumping from 500 petabytes to 2.5 exabytes in a single request.

## 𝕏 / TWITTER
**Thibault Sottiaux**, who works on Codex and ChatGPT at OpenAI, says the team is locking in on only simplifications, more efficiency for more usage, and groundbreaking features or new models, noting that feedback is clear users want things simpler. He also described using his agent to reach inbox zero for the first time, having it batch-validate and delete unneeded email categories, label work emails, and walk him through replies while searching for context in the background.
https://x.com/thsottiaux/status/2106610099720720811
https://x.com/thsottiaux/status/2106603980386394123
https://x.com/thsottiaux/status/2106602729875685780

**Madhu Guru**, Sr Director of AI at Meta, argues AI adoption is largely a product problem today: even among the 2% paying for AI, usage depth is shallow because most AI products look like airplane cockpits with 100 levers such as connectors, permissions, model selection, and token usage. He expects this to change materially in the next 12 months as product teams make AI easier to use.
https://x.com/realmadhuguru/status/2106450089938157720

**Amjad Masad**, CEO of Replit, teased something called **Replit Drift** and shared a deep, somewhat technical conversation with Alex Atallah of **OpenRouter**.
https://x.com/amasad/status/2106506305875947966
https://x.com/amasad/status/2106450234369085609
https://x.com/amasad/status/2106406812316827874

**Guillermo Rauch**, CEO of Vercel, predicts security will become a larger and larger function in software companies, framing it as verification engineering plus capital allocation, and asks how anyone can trust a 2-person-and-a-dog company as AI adversaries grow more sophisticated. He also argues AI will make everything free, including itself, with free energy as humanity's final frontier.
https://x.com/rauchg/status/2106516538836856945
https://x.com/rauchg/status/2106503460384538793

**Aaron Levie**, CEO of Box, says AI agent adoption is still very bimodal: coding and coding-adjacent tasks have taken off while everything else lags, and even within coding only a small percentage of developers run background agents in parallel. He argues the rest of knowledge work needs workflows rebuilt, data wired up in new ways, new accountability and liability practices, governance and compliance changes, and security upgrades, which is why he expects 100X more agent adoption from what we've seen so far.
https://x.com/levie/status/2106583814709633413

**Ryo Lu**, who designed at Cursor, Notion, and Stripe, wrote a long essay on convergence to the mean: when everyone looks at everyone else to decide what to make, we copy what works and everything becomes polished and interchangeable. He argues AI makes this loop frictionless, since access to every perspective isn't the same as having one, and calls for approaching software more like artists, asking what you're trying to let someone feel, understand, or do.
https://x.com/ryolu_/status/2106337039201505453

**Zara Zhang**, a builder, posed a simple question: how will the world change if coding agents get 10x better?
https://x.com/zarazhangrui/status/2106405482852434359

**Nikunj Kothari**, partner at FPV Ventures, sees an innovator's dilemma playing out as personal agents become inevitable: Amazon is protecting its ads cash cow and brand, while DoorDash, albeit smaller, is opening the gates with CLIs and text ordering. He also warns that tokenmaxxing for its own sake is not useful in this era.
https://x.com/nikunj/status/2106488814940414455
https://x.com/nikunj/status/2106452873513201930

**Peter Steinberger**, who builds OpenClaw, laughed about how everyone is building the same thing and asked if anyone at Google could help, noting OpenClaw's Android app has been stuck in review limbo for over a week.
https://x.com/steipete/status/2106489264443981978
https://x.com/steipete/status/2106446147791597774

**Aditya Agarwal**, General Partner at SPC and co-founder of Bevel Health, points out that even the super rich can't get unlimited time from the world's best doctor or lawyer, which is why AI is so crazy: it democratizes access and makes time effectively unlimited. He calls this the practical effect of intelligence too cheap to meter.
https://x.com/adityaag/status/2106503075209044336

**Sam Altman**, whose mission at OpenAI is to ensure AGI benefits all of humanity, says he is very uncomfortable about people ascribing religious force or a surrender of human judgment to AI models, and thinks it is a real safety issue.
https://x.com/sama/status/2106388373221118198

## 📰 OFFICIAL BLOGS
**Claude Blog** announced that Claude Cowork and chat are merging into one Claude, so a task started in one place carries into any conversation with your existing context, skills, and connectors. Claude Docs and Claude Slides are new, and Claude Design now works inside conversations, letting you write documents together, draft slides, edit directly, present from Claude, or download as PowerPoint or PDF. All three are in beta on paid plans, rolling out on Pro and Max over the next few weeks, with Enterprise admins controlling when to turn them on. Andrew Keller, Senior Economist, described having Claude pull up his legal research database, read the cases, figure out which others he might need, download them, and store them in a folder for personal review.
https://claude.com/blog/cowork-is-now-claude

## 🎙 PODCASTS
**Takeaway**: The layer feeding GPUs is quietly becoming a $30B business, and its founder thinks the next decade will outpace the last thousand years of change.

On The MAD Podcast, Matt Turck spoke with Renen Hallak, founder and CEO of VAST Data, about the software infrastructure layer sitting in the middle of Jensen Huang's five-layer cake. Hallak described the scale shock directly: one AI cloud customer projected 500 petabytes over three years, then came back last week asking for an extra two exabytes on top. He frames the shift as a full-stack rebuild, where old 10-kilowatt racks become 500-kilowatt racks and shared-nothing architectures break down because communication grows quadratically, while AI needs systems with millions of nodes. VAST's answer is a disaggregated shared-everything architecture, with media on the other side of a fast network using NVMe over Fabrics, which lets one customer cluster span multiple exabytes and deliver tens of terabytes per second.

Hallak also sketched a future where agents are "artificial people" that fine-tune on their own experiences, meaning each organization's IP gets distilled into its own weights rather than flowing back to big model builders. He used a carpentry shop analogy: if your carpenter robots are the best in the business, you should be able to lease that brain module for a week without ever exposing the weights, which points toward an intelligence marketplace. The company's new announcement is about model management, including confidential computing with Nvidia encrypted memory so enterprises can run inference on prem without exposing model builders' weights or their own data. He also recalled spending six months on P=NP as a student, and noted that AI is now proving it can do things we don't know how to do, with rumors that more Millennium Prize problems are close to falling.
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=awoR908Yu5Y

## 📰 OFFICIAL BLOGS

**Claude Blog** announced that Claude Cowork and chat are merging into one Claude. Users can bring a quick question or hand over a report due at noon, and Claude takes it from there, even after the laptop is closed. It is rolling out on Pro and Max plans over the next few weeks. Claude Docs and Claude Slides are new today, and Claude Design now works inside conversations. Ask for a document and you and Claude write it together; ask for a presentation and Claude drafts the slides. All three are in beta on paid plans, and Enterprise admins choose when to turn them on. The blog noted that people used both Cowork and Design and told them the frustrating part was deciding where a task belonged, and what they started in one did not carry into the other. Claude can now figure out what a task needs, so what Cowork and Design can do is available from any conversation, with the context, skills, and connectors already in place.

https://claude.com/blog/cowork-is-now-claude

## 🎙 PODCASTS

**Takeaway**: The software infrastructure layer feeding GPUs is a surprisingly under-the-radar $30B business, and its founder thinks AI factories will eventually belong to everyone, not just the big labs.

Matt Turck interviewed Renen Hallak, founder and CEO of VAST Data, on The MAD Podcast. Hallak positioned VAST right in the middle of Jensen Huang's five-layer cake: power, hardware, software infrastructure, models, applications. He called the software infrastructure layer the operating system for this new era, managing compute, storage, networking, databases, training and inference functions, and increasingly tools for agents and reinforcement learning.

Hallak described how AI factories differ from old data centers: 10 kilowatt racks have become 500 kilowatt racks, CPUs have become GPUs, and 10 gig ethernet and old hard drives have become extremely fast networks and very large SSDs. The data itself has shifted from numbers and columns to pictures, video, sound, and natural language, which takes far more space. He said the big labs are leading the way, but anybody who stays with the old stack will get left behind.

On agents, Hallak offered a striking analogy: we were all born with a base model, but over time as we travel the world we learn new things, we infer during the day, we fine tune at night, and tomorrow we will be a little bit smarter. He predicted that every organization's IP will be distilled into models and weights they own, and that agents will fine tune based on experiences with us, making them smarter and more familiar over time. He also described an intelligence marketplace where a carpentry shop with the best carpenter robots could lease that brain module to you for a week without exposing the weights.

The episode also covered VAST's new model management announcement, including confidential computing that lets enterprises run inference on prem without exposing model builders' weights, with help from Nvidia and encrypted memory underneath. Hallak said this should increase the total addressable market of model builders into regulated industries and large enterprises.

A memorable line from Hallak on the scale of demand: "We had a customer, one of these AI clouds, they said we're probably going to need about 500 petabytes over the next three years. Last week, came back to us and said, we're gonna need an extra two exabytes on top of that 500 petabytes."

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=awoR908Yu5Y

**Takeaway**: The software infrastructure layer feeding GPUs is a surprisingly under-the-radar $30 billion business, and its founder believes we will see more change in the next ten years than in the last thousand.

On The MAD Podcast with Matt Turck, Renen Hallak, founder and CEO of VAST Data, explained the five-layer AI cake where his company sits right in the middle: the software infrastructure layer that manages compute, storage, networking, databases, and increasingly model management. He described the shift from 10 kilowatt racks to 500 kilowatt racks, from CPUs to GPUs, from hard drives to very large SSDs, and from analyzing numbers to processing pictures, video, sound, and natural language. One customer, an AI cloud, initially projected needing 500 petabytes over three years, then came back needing an extra two exabytes on top of that.

Hallak shared a striking anecdote about his early days: he spent six months trying to prove P=NP, hoping to solve all seven Millennium Problems and collect $7 million. After six months, he realized he wasn't nearly smart enough. But the experience shaped his conviction that if computers could help with hard problems, that was the way forward. He founded VAST in 2016, three years before the Transformers paper, betting on forward-looking technologies that didn't exist yet. When VCs asked what the plan B was if those parts never materialized, he told them there was no plan B.

The conversation turned to agents and fine-tuning. Hallak envisions agents as artificial people that will fine-tune models based on experiences, making them smarter over time. Every organization's IP will be distilled into models and weights they own. He gave the analogy of a carpentry shop with the best carpenter robots: you should be able to lease that brain module for a week without exposing the weights. This led to VAST's announcement around confidential computing and model management, enabling enterprises to run inference on prem without exposing model builders' weights, with help from Nvidia and encrypted memory.

On the AI factory concept, Hallak argued it will eventually be for everyone, not just big labs. Enterprises that stay with old business information systems will get left behind. The physical location can be on prem, in a colo, or in an AI cloud, but the key distinction is ownership: owning the information, models, weights, and agents. He compared it to the 1970s when you needed a PhD to operate a computer, and the operating system made it intuitive and safe for everyone.

keywords: AI agents | model management | AI factories
headline: The Middle Layer Nobody Sees Is Eating AI
deck: Builders split between agent adoption that is still bimodal and a $30B infrastructure layer quietly feeding every GPU. Meanwhile OpenAI promises simplification, and one designer asks whether we are all just building the same thing.
quote: I am very uncomfortable about people trying to ascribe religious force or a surrender of human judgment to AI models, and think it is a real safety issue.
quoteBy: Sam Altman · The mission of OpenAI is to ensure that AGI benefits all of humanity

## 🧭 Daily Insights
**Core insight**: The loudest thread today is that AI adoption is still a product problem, not a capability problem. Builders agree the models are good enough, but the interfaces are cockpit-like and the workflows underneath have not been rebuilt, so real agentic usage outside coding remains early. Underneath that, a quieter conversation is forming about the infrastructure and judgment layers: who manages the models, who owns the fine-tuned weights, and whether faster making leads to more originality or just more sameness.

## 𝕏 / TWITTER
**Thibault Sottiaux**, working on Codex and ChatGPT at OpenAI, says the team is locking in on simplifications, more efficiency for more usage, and groundbreaking features or new models, noting that feedback is clear people want things to get simpler. He also described using his agent to reach inbox zero for the first time, with it deleting unneeded email categories in batch, labeling work emails, and walking him through replies while searching for context in the background.
https://x.com/thsottiaux/status/2106610099720720811
https://x.com/thsottiaux/status/2106603980386394123

**Madhu Guru**, Sr Director of AI at Meta, argues AI adoption is largely a product problem today: even among the 2% paying for AI, usage depth is shallow because most products look like airplane cockpits with 100 levers such as connectors, permissions, model selection, and token usage. He expects this to change materially in the next 12 months as product teams make AI easier to use.
https://x.com/realmadhuguru/status/2106450089938157720

**Guillermo Rauch**, CEO of Vercel, predicts security will become a larger function in software companies, framing it as verification engineering plus capital allocation, and asks how anyone can trust a 2-person-and-a-dog company as AI adversaries get more sophisticated. He also argues AI will make everything free, including itself, with free energy as the last domino and humanity's final frontier.
https://x.com/rauchg/status/2106516538836856945
https://x.com/rauchg/status/2106503460384538793

**Aaron Levie**, CEO of Box, says AI agent adoption is still very bimodal: coding and coding-adjacent tasks have taken off while everything else lags, and even within coding only a small percentage of developers run background agents in parallel while the rest work 1:1. He argues the rest of knowledge work needs workflows rebuilt, data wired up in new ways, new accountability and liability practices, governance changes, and security upgrades, which is why he expects 100X more agent adoption from what we have seen so far.
https://x.com/levie/status/2106583814709633413

**Ryo Lu**, who designed at Cursor, Notion, and Stripe, wrote a long essay on convergence to the mean: when everyone looks at everyone else to decide what to make, we copy what works and everything becomes polished, interchangeable, and nothing alive. He argues AI makes this loop frictionless because access to every perspective is not the same as having one, and that we should approach making things more like artists, since software can express beliefs about how life should feel.
https://x.com/ryolu_/status/2106337039201505453

**Nikunj Kothari**, partner at FPV Ventures, sees an innovator's dilemma playing out as personal agents become inevitable: Amazon is protecting its ads cash cow and brand, while DoorDash, albeit smaller, is opening the gates slowly with CLIs and ordering via text. He also warns that tokenmaxxing for its own sake is not useful in this era.
https://x.com/nikunj/status/2106488814940414455
https://x.com/nikunj/status/2106452873513201930

**Peter Steinberger**, building OpenClaw and working with OpenAI, notes wryly that everyone is building the same thing, and says OpenClaw's Android app has been stuck in review limbo for over a week.
https://x.com/steipete/status/2106489264443981978
https://x.com/steipete/status/2106446147791597774

**Aditya Agarwal**, General Partner at SPC and co-founder of Bevel Health, points out that even the world's leading cancer doctor will still only see you for 20-30 minutes no matter how rich you are. He argues AI is crazy precisely because it both democratizes access and makes time unlimited for every individual, the practical effect of intelligence too cheap to meter.
https://x.com/adityaag/status/2106503075209044336

**Sam Altman**, whose mission at OpenAI is to ensure AGI benefits all of humanity, says he is very uncomfortable about people trying to ascribe religious force or a surrender of human judgment to AI models, and thinks it is a real safety issue.
https://x.com/sama/status/2106388373221118198

## 📰 OFFICIAL BLOGS
**Claude Blog** announced that Claude Cowork and chat are merging into one Claude, so a quick question or a report due at noon can be handed over even after you close your laptop, rolling out on Pro and Max plans over the next few weeks. Claude Docs and Claude Slides are new, and Claude Design now works inside conversations, letting you write a document together, draft slides, edit directly, present straight from Claude, or download as PowerPoint or PDF. The team says people used both Cowork and Design and found the frustrating part was deciding where a task belonged, so Claude now figures out what a task needs with the context, skills, and connectors you already have. Senior Economist Andrew Keller described having Claude pull up his legal research database, read the cases, find others he might need, download them, and store them in a folder for his review.

## 🎙 PODCASTS
**Takeaway**: The layer between models and GPUs is a $30B business most people have never heard of, and its founder thinks every organization's IP will eventually be distilled into weights it owns.

On The MAD Podcast, Matt Turck talks with Renen Hallak, founder and CEO of VAST Data, about the software infrastructure layer that feeds data to GPUs. Hallak places VAST right in the middle of Jensen Huang's five layer cake, calling it the operating system for this new era, and describes how AI factories differ from the old stack: 500 kilowatt racks instead of 10 kilowatt racks, GPUs instead of CPUs, and very large SSDs instead of old hard drives. He recalls a customer that projected 500 petabytes over three years and came back needing an extra two exabytes on top, adding that in the next ten years we will see more difference than in the last thousand.

The core of the conversation is model management. Hallak argues models have become a resource like a GPU or an SSD, and resources need managing, which is why VAST announced confidential computing so enterprises can run inference on premises without exposing model builders' weights, with help from Nvidia and encrypted memory underneath. He extends the analogy of agents as artificial people: we will get attached to our agents, expect them to remember yesterday and a year ago, and that requires them to fine tune models based on experiences with us, which means each organization owns the IP generated through fine tuning rather than letting big model builders own everything. He even imagines an intelligence marketplace where a carpentry shop with the best carpenter robots could lease that brain module for a week without revealing the weights.

On his background, Hallak says he spent six months trying to prove whether P equals NP, hoping to collect the Clay Institute's million dollar bounty, and concluded he was not nearly smart enough. He notes that AI has now proven it can do things we do not know how to do, citing rumors that OpenAI and Anthropic are close to solving more of the millennium problems. He also explains the technical bet behind VAST: instead of shared nothing sharding, which breaks down past roughly 100 nodes, VAST built a disaggregated shared everything architecture with media on the other side of a fast network using NVMe over Fabrics, enabling clusters of tens of thousands of nodes and multiple exabytes. Pitching storage to VCs in 2016 was hard, he admits, but that scarcity became the moat.

Memorable quote: "I kept telling them we don't have a plan b, which they didn't like and so, I was not their favorite person in those days."
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=awoR908Yu5Y

keywords: AI agents | model management | product simplicity
headline: AI's Real Bottleneck Is Product, Not Intelligence
deck: Builders agree agents have barely started, while OpenAI promises simpler tools and VAST Data bets on the layer that feeds every GPU. The next 12 months will decide who makes AI usable.
quote: I am very uncomfortable about people trying to ascribe religious force or a surrender of human judgment to AI models, and think it is a real safety issue.
quoteBy: Sam Altman · The mission of OpenAI is to ensure that AGI benefits all of humanity

## 🧭 Daily Insights
**Core insight**: The conversation has shifted from raw model capability to the unglamorous work of making AI actually usable. Aaron Levie argues agent adoption is bimodal and 100X more is coming once workflows are rebuilt, while Madhu Guru says AI is largely a product problem because even paying users barely scratch the surface. Meanwhile Thibault Sottiaux promises OpenAI is locking in on simplification and efficiency, and VAST Data's Renen Hallak makes the case that the real money sits in the software infrastructure layer feeding all those GPUs.

## 𝕏 / TWITTER
Thibault Sottiaux, working on Codex and ChatGPT at OpenAI, says the team is locking in on simplifications, more efficiency for more usage, and groundbreaking features or new models, noting feedback is clear that users want things simpler. He also described using his agent to reach inbox zero for the first time, having it delete unneeded email categories in batch, label work emails, and walk him through replies while searching for context in the background.

Madhu Guru, Sr Director of AI at Meta, argues AI adoption is largely a product problem today. Even among the 2% paying for AI, usage depth is shallow, mainly because most AI products look like airplane cockpits with 100 levers such as connectors, permissions, model selection, and token usage. He expects this to change materially in the next 12 months as product teams make AI easier to use.

Amjad Masad, CEO of Replit, shared a deep and somewhat technical conversation with Alex Atallah of OpenRouter, and teased something called Replit Drift.

Guillermo Rauch, CEO of Vercel, predicts security will become a larger function in software companies, framing it as verification engineering plus capital allocation, and sees a challenge and opportunity for startups as AI adversaries grow more sophisticated. He also declared that AI will make everything free, including itself, with free energy as humanity's final frontier.

Aaron Levie, CEO of Box, says AI agent adoption is still very bimodal: coding and coding-adjacent tasks have taken off while everything else lags. Even within coding, only a small percentage of developers deploy background agents working in parallel, with most still working 1:1. He argues the rest of knowledge work needs workflows rebuilt, data wired up in new ways, new accountability and liability practices, governance and compliance changes, and security upgrades, which is why he expects 100X more agent adoption from what we've seen so far.

Ryo Lu, who designed Cursor, Notion, and Stripe, wrote a long essay on convergence to the mean: when everyone looks at everyone else to decide what to make, we eventually stop making anything of our own, and AI makes this loop frictionless. He argues access to every perspective isn't the same as having one, and that we should approach making things more like artists, asking what we're trying to let someone feel, understand, or do.

Zara Zhang, a builder, posed a simple question: how will the world change if coding agents get 10x better?

Nikunj Kothari, partner at FPV Ventures, flagged an innovator's dilemma as personal agents become inevitable, noting Amazon is protecting its ads cash cow while DoorDash is slowly opening the gates with CLIs and text ordering. He also cautioned that tokenmaxxing for its own sake is not honestly useful in this era.

Peter Steinberger, who works on OpenClaw and with OpenAI, laughed about how everyone is building the same thing, and asked if anyone at Google could help with OpenClaw's Android app, which has been stuck over a week in review limbo.

Aditya Agarwal, General Partner at SPC and co-founder of Bevel Health, points out that even the world's leading cancer doctor will still only see you for 20-30 minutes no matter how rich you are. AI both democratizes access and makes the amount of time available unlimited for every individual, the practical effect of intelligence too cheap to meter.

Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI, said he is very uncomfortable about people trying to ascribe religious force or a surrender of human judgment to AI models, and thinks it is a real safety issue.

## 📰 OFFICIAL BLOGS
Claude Cowork and chat are now one Claude, merging the separate spaces for bigger work and visual work into a single experience. People used both and said the frustrating part was deciding where a task belonged, and what they started in one didn't carry into the other. Now Claude figures out what a task needs, with context, skills, and connectors available from any conversation. Claude Docs and Claude Slides are new, and Claude Design now works inside conversations too: ask for a document and you write it together, ask for a presentation and Claude drafts the slides, editable directly, presentable straight from Claude, or downloadable as PowerPoint or PDF. All three are in beta on paid plans, with Enterprise admins choosing when to turn them on. The rollout hits Pro and Max plans over the next few weeks, with more plans to follow. Andrew Keller, Senior Economist, described having Claude pull up his legal research database, read all the cases, figure out which other cases he might need, download them, and store them in a folder for his personal review. In the example workflow, a weekly report due at noon gets drafted from a single conversation, with slides matching the report, a comment left for Claude on a slide, and a recurring Monday schedule so Claude starts without being asked. Anything you make lives at one shareable link you can open on your phone.
https://claude.com/blog/cowork-is-now-claude

## 🎙 PODCASTS
**Takeaway**: The layer between models and GPUs is where the next $30B infrastructure battle is being fought, and VAST Data's founder thinks every enterprise will eventually need its own AI factory.

On The MAD Podcast with Matt Turck, Renen Hallak, founder and CEO of VAST Data, explained where his company sits in Jensen Huang's five layer cake of AI: right in the middle, the software infrastructure layer, which he sometimes calls the operating system for this new era. He described how the old stack of 10 kilowatt racks, 10 gig ethernet, and old hard drives has been replaced by 500 kilowatt racks, extremely fast networks, and very large SSDs, because we're no longer analyzing columns of a database but pictures, video, sound, and natural language. One customer, an AI cloud, told him they'd need about 500 petabytes over three years, then came back last week asking for an extra two exabytes on top. Hallak's analogy for enterprise AI is the human brain: we're all born with a base model, we infer during the day and fine tune at night, and every organization's IP will be distilled into models and weights they own. He argues enterprises won't want to expose their proprietary processes to model builders, and model builders won't want to expose their weights, which is why VAST announced model management with confidential computing, using Nvidia encrypted memory so enterprises can run inference on prem without either side seeing what they're not allowed to see. He also floated an intelligence marketplace, where a carpentry shop with the best carpenter robots could lease that brain module to you for a week without ever showing the weights. On his own path, he spent six months trying to prove P=NP as a student, hoping to collect the Clay Institute's $7 million, before concluding he wasn't nearly smart enough. He noted that AI has now proven it can do things we don't know how to do, with rumors that OpenAI and Anthropic are close on more of the seven millennium problems. On pitching storage in 2016, he told VCs there was no plan B, and credits that bet for giving VAST its moat: "I think in the next ten years, we'll see more difference than we did in the last thousand years."

## 🎙 PODCASTS

**Takeaway**: The software infrastructure layer feeding GPUs is a surprisingly under-the-radar $30B business, and its founder believes every organization will eventually need its own AI factory.

In this episode of The MAD Podcast, Matt Turck speaks with Renen Hallak, founder and CEO of VAST Data, about the crucial layer between models and compute. Hallak describes his company as sitting right in the middle of Jensen Huang's five-layer cake: power, hardware, software infrastructure, models, and applications. He calls this middle layer the operating system for the new era, managing compute, storage, networking, databases, and the tools needed as the industry shifts from training to inference, agents, and reinforcement learning.

Hallak shares a striking anecdote about the pace of demand: a customer, one of the AI clouds, initially said they would need about 500 petabytes over three years, then came back last week saying they needed an extra two exabytes on top of that. He notes that data centers look completely different today, moving from 10 kilowatt racks to 500 kilowatt racks, requiring extremely fast networks and very large SSDs. On the AI factory concept, he argues it will eventually be for everyone, not just big labs, and that enterprises will need their own AI factories in the medium term as they shift from people-based organizations to augmenting them with agents.

A key thread is how enterprises will own their intelligence. Hallak predicts that all organizations' IP will be distilled into models and weights, comparing it to the human brain: we are all born with a base model, but over time we learn, infer during the day, and fine tune at night. He argues enterprises will not want to expose proprietary information and processes to model builders, and model builders will not want to expose their weights, so the software infrastructure layer is the right place to enforce that trust. He envisions an intelligence marketplace where, for example, a carpentry shop with the best carpenter robots could lease that brain module to someone else for a week without revealing the weights.

The episode also covers VAST's new announcement around model management and confidential computing, enabling enterprises to run inference on prem without exposing model builders' weights, with help from Nvidia and encrypted memory. Hallak explains the technical foundation of VAST, describing how the old shared nothing architecture breaks down at scale because communication grows quadratically, while VAST's disaggregated shared everything architecture puts SSDs on the other side of a fast network so all nodes see all information as if directly attached. He notes one customer site today runs multiple exabytes within a single cluster delivering tens of terabytes per second across tens of thousands of nodes.

On his background, Hallak recalls spending six months trying to prove whether P equals NP, hoping to solve all seven millennium problems and collect $7 million, before realizing he was not nearly smart enough. He reflects that AI has now proven it can do things we do not know how to do, referencing rumors that OpenAI and Anthropic are close to solving additional millennium problems. He also jokes that pitching a storage company to VCs in 2016 was hard, but VAST now reaps the benefits of having far less competition.

## 🧭 Daily Insights

**Core insight**: The conversation today splits between two uncomfortable truths. First, AI agent adoption remains deeply bimodal: coding has taken off, but everything else is still waiting for workflows to be rebuilt from scratch. Second, the infrastructure layer feeding those agents, storage, databases, model management, is becoming the real bottleneck and opportunity, with VAST Data now valued at $30 billion. The trend forming: as models commoditize into "resources," the operating system layer that manages them, secures them, and lets enterprises own their fine-tuned weights becomes the next platform war.

## 𝕏 / TWITTER

**Thibault Sottiaux** announced a strategic reset at OpenAI: the team is locking in on simplifications, efficiency for more usage, and groundbreaking features or new models. He acknowledged that while investing ahead of the curve matters, user feedback is clear that people want things simpler. He also demonstrated the power of agentic workflows by achieving inbox zero for the first time, using his agent to batch-delete unnecessary email categories, auto-label work emails, and surface replies needing context from background searches. The experience, he noted, let him process a backlog of direct feedback and requests in a single Saturday.

**Madhu Guru** argued that AI adoption is largely a product problem, not a technology one. Even among the 2% of users paying for AI, usage depth remains shallow because most products resemble airplane cockpits with 100 levers: connectors, permissions, model selection, token usage. He predicts this will change materially in the next 12 months as product teams assert themselves and make AI products genuinely easier to use.

**Guillermo Rauch** made two provocative claims. First, security will become a larger function at software companies, framing it as both verification engineering ("my code is probably memory-safe") and capital allocation ("what surface should I throw most tokens at?"). He sees opportunity for small teams to disrupt vast areas of cybersecurity as AI adversaries grow more sophisticated. Second, he declared that AI will make everything free, including itself, with free energy as humanity's final frontier.

**Aaron Levie** laid out the bimodal reality of agent adoption: coding and coding-adjacent tasks have taken off, while the rest of knowledge work remains early. Even within coding, adoption varies widely, with a small percentage of developers deploying background agents in parallel while most still work 1:1 with agents. The bottleneck outside coding is that workflows need to be reengineered, data rewired, accountability and liability practices rebuilt, and governance and compliance paradigms changed. He expects 100X more agent adoption from what we've seen so far.

**Ryo Lu** wrote a long meditation on convergence to the mean: when everyone looks at everyone else to decide what to make, we eventually stop making anything of our own. He argued that AI makes this loop frictionless, drawing from more references than we could see in a lifetime, but access to every perspective isn't the same as having one. He called for approaching software more like artists, where a piece of software expresses beliefs about how life should feel, and warned that if we can make almost anything, deciding what deserves to exist becomes more important, not less.

**Aditya Agarwal** pointed out a common misconception: even the super rich can't get unlimited access to the world's best doctor or lawyer. The leading cancer doctor will still see you for 20-30 minutes. This is why AI is so transformative, he argued: it both democratizes access and makes the amount of time available unlimited for every individual, the practical effect of intelligence too cheap to meter.

**Sam Altman** expressed discomfort about people ascribing religious force or a surrender of human judgment to AI models, calling it a real safety issue.

**Nikunj Kothari** flagged an innovator's dilemma playing out as personal agents become inevitable: Amazon is protecting its ads cash cow and brand, while DoorDash, albeit smaller, is opening the gates slowly with CLIs and text-based ordering. He also cautioned against tokenmaxxing for its own sake, noting it's useful to explore edges but not honestly useful as an end in itself.

**Peter Steinberger** laughed about how everyone is building the same thing, and flagged that OpenClaw's Android app has been stuck in review limbo for over a week.

**Zara Zhang** posed a simple but loaded question: how will the world change if coding agents get 10x better?

**Amjad Masad** shared a podcast conversation with Alex Atallah of OpenRouter, going deep and technical, and teased something called Replit Drift.

## 📰 OFFICIAL BLOGS

**Claude Blog** announced that Claude Cowork and chat are merging into one Claude. Starting today, users can bring a quick question or hand over a report due at noon, and Claude takes it from there, even after the laptop is closed. It's rolling out on Pro and Max plans over the next few weeks. Claude Docs and Claude Slides are new today, and Claude Design now works inside conversations. Ask for a document and you and Claude write it together; ask for a presentation and Claude drafts the slides. You can edit directly, present straight from Claude, or download as PowerPoint or PDF. All three are in beta on paid plans, with Enterprise admins controlling when to turn them on. The blog quoted Andrew Keller, Senior Economist: "I could have Claude pull up my legal research database, and it would pull all the cases, read them, figure out which other cases I might need, download them, and store them in a folder for my personal review." The core insight: people used both Cowork and Design and told Anthropic the frustrating part was deciding where a task belonged, and what they'd started in one didn't carry into the other. So Anthropic stopped making users choose. Claude can now figure out what a task needs, with context, skills, and connectors available from any conversation.
https://claude.com/blog/cowork-is-now-claude

## 🎙 PODCASTS

**Takeaway**: The layer between GPUs and models, software infrastructure, is quietly becoming a $30 billion business, and its founder thinks we'll see more change in the next ten years than in the last thousand.

Matt Turck interviewed Renen Hallak, founder and CEO of VAST Data, on The MAD Podcast. Hallak positioned VAST right in the middle of Jensen Huang's five-layer cake: power, hardware, software infrastructure, models, applications. He calls this middle layer "the operating system for this new era," managing compute, storage, networking, databases, and increasingly model management. The scale is staggering: one customer, an AI cloud, initially projected 500 petabytes over three years, then came back needing an extra two exabytes on top. VAST has one system at a customer site that is multiple exabytes within a single cluster delivering tens of terabytes per second across tens of thousands of nodes.

Hallak explained why the old shared-nothing architecture breaks down: communication grows quadratically within the cluster, and resilience suffers when any part fails. VAST's disaggregated shared-everything architecture puts SSDs on the other side of a fast network using NVMe over Fabrics, so all nodes see all information as if directly attached. This let them build storage, then a database, then compute orchestration for AI.

The big announcement this week is model management: treating models as resources like GPUs or SSDs, understanding which model is good at coding versus images, which is expensive versus cheap, and routing tasks accordingly. A key piece is confidential computing, enabling enterprises to run inference on prem without exposing model builders' weights, with help from Nvidia and encrypted memory. Hallak's vision: enterprises will fine-tune models through reinforcement learning over time, distilling their IP into weights they own. He compared it to the human brain: "we were all born with a base model but then over time as we travel the world we learn new things, we infer during the day, we fine tune at night, and tomorrow we'll be a little bit smarter than we were today." He envisions an intelligence marketplace where a carpentry shop with the best carpenter robots could lease that brain module for a week without exposing the weights.

On the current AI moment, Hallak noted that for the first time, AI has proven it can do things we don't know how to do, referencing OpenAI's claimed solution to Navier-Stokes and rumors of more Millennium Prize problems being tackled. He spent six months in school trying to prove P=NP before realizing he wasn't nearly smart enough. His conclusion: if we want these problems solved in our lifetime, we need computers to speed us up.
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=awoR908Yu5Y

**Takeaway**: The software infrastructure layer feeding GPUs is becoming the operating system for the AI era, and whoever owns the data, models, and weights owns the future.

On The MAD Podcast with Matt Turck, Renen Hallak, founder and CEO of VAST Data, explained why the middle layer of the AI stack is both under the radar and critically important. VAST Data is valued at $30 billion and powers top AI players including xAI. Hallak described a customer, one of the AI clouds, that initially projected needing 500 petabytes over three years, then came back needing an extra two exabytes on top. The entire stack is new, and the culmination is what he calls the AI factory.

Hallak thinks of agents as artificial people that will work for us and organizations, and over time we will expect them to remember what happened yesterday or a year ago. He gave a memorable analogy for the intelligence marketplace: "If I run a carpentry shop and my carpenter robots are the best in the business, I should be able to lease to you that brain module such that you can build a chair or whatever it is that you're trying to do, but I'm only giving it to you for a week."

**Guillermo Rauch** predicted that security will become a larger function in software companies, framing it as verification engineering and capital allocation. He noted the challenge for startups: as AI adversaries grow more sophisticated, how can you trust a 2-person-and-a-dog company? He also declared that AI will make everything free, including itself, with free energy as humanity's final frontier.

**Aaron Levie** observed that AI agent adoption is still very bimodal: coding and coding-adjacent tasks have taken off, while everything else lags. Even within coding, adoption patterns vary widely, with some developers deploying background agents in parallel while most still work 1:1 with agents. He argued that real agentic adoption in knowledge work requires workflows to be rebuilt, data wired up in new ways, new accountability practices, governance changes, and security upgrades. He expects 100X more agent adoption from what we've seen so far.

**Ryo Lu** published a long reflection on convergence to the mean, warning that when everyone looks at everyone else to decide what to make, we eventually stop making anything of our own. He argued that AI makes this loop frictionless but access to every perspective isn't the same as having one. He called for approaching software more like artists, where a piece of software expresses beliefs about how life should feel, and warned against a tidal wave of mid.

**Aditya Agarwal** pointed out a common misconception: even super rich people can't get unlimited access to the world's best doctor or lawyer. He argued this is why AI is so crazy: it both democratizes access and makes the amount of time available unlimited for every individual, calling it the practical effect of intelligence too cheap to meter.

**Sam Altman** stated he is very uncomfortable about people trying to ascribe religious force or a surrender of human judgment to AI models, and thinks it is a real safety issue.

**Nikunj Kothari** commented on the innovator's dilemma as personal agents become inevitable, noting Amazon is protecting its ads cash cow while DoorDash is slowly opening the gates with CLIs and text ordering. He also cautioned against tokenmaxxing for its own sake.

**Peter Steinberger** joked about how everyone is building the same thing, and asked if anyone at Google could help with OpenClaw's Android app, which has been in review limbo for over a week.

**Amjad Masad** shared a link asking who's building something, promoted a deep technical conversation with Alex Atallah of OpenRouter, and mentioned Replit Drift.

**Zara Zhang** posed a simple question: how will the world change if coding agents get 10x better?

## 📰 OFFICIAL BLOGS

**Claude Blog** announced that Claude Cowork and chat are merging into one Claude. Starting today, users can bring a quick question or hand over a report due at noon, and Claude takes it from there, even after you've closed your laptop. It's rolling out on Pro and Max plans over the next few weeks. Claude Docs and Claude Slides are new today, and Claude Design now works inside conversations too. Ask for a document and you and Claude write it together; ask for a presentation and Claude drafts the slides. You can edit directly, present straight from Claude, or download as PowerPoint or PDF. All three are in beta on paid plans. The blog explains that Cowork was built as a separate place for bigger work and Design for visual work, but people used both and found it frustrating to decide where a task belonged. So Claude now figures out what a task needs, with context, skills, and connectors available from any conversation. The post includes a quote from Andrew Keller, Senior Economist, describing how Claude pulled legal research, read cases, identified related cases, downloaded them, and stored them in a folder for personal review. A weekly report example shows Claude asking clarifying questions, checking progress from your phone, and delivering a doc with notes and slides ready to open, adjust, and download as PowerPoint. You can schedule it for every Monday and Claude starts without being asked. Anything you make lives at one shareable link.

https://claude.com/blog/cowork-is-now-claude

## 🎙 PODCASTS

**Takeaway**: The software infrastructure layer between GPUs and models is the hidden $30B battleground, and the next frontier is model management and confidential computing.

In this episode of The MAD Podcast with Matt Turck, Renen Hallak, founder and CEO of VAST Data, explains why the middle layer of the AI stack is the operating system for this new era. He describes how a customer initially estimated needing 500 petabytes over three years, then came back needing an extra two exabytes on top of that. He argues that in the next ten years we'll see more difference than in the last thousand years.

Hallak positions VAST Data right in the middle of Jensen Huang's five-layer cake: power, hardware, software infrastructure, models, applications. He explains that everything from the old stack needs to be redone for AI, from 10 kilowatt racks to 500 kilowatt racks, from CPUs to GPUs, from 10 gig ethernet to extremely fast networks and large SSDs. He calls the culmination of this stack the AI factory, which he believes will eventually be for everyone, not just big labs.

A key insight is that enterprises will need to own their own AI factories because their IP will be distilled into models and weights. He uses the analogy of the human brain: we're all born with a base model, but over time we learn, infer during the day, fine-tune at night, and tomorrow we're a little smarter. Every organization's IP will be distilled into models they own. He argues this requires a way for enterprises to fine-tune without exposing data and for model builders to monetize without exposing weights, leading to what he calls an intelligence marketplace.

The episode also covers VAST Data's new announcement around model management and confidential computing, enabling enterprises to run inference on prem without exposing model builders' weights, with help from Nvidia and encrypted memory. Hallak explains that models have become a resource, just like a GPU or SSD, and need to be managed. He predicts that as we have hundreds and thousands of agents generating new derivatives of models, model management will become a much bigger task.

A memorable quote from Hallak: "I think in the next ten years, we'll see more difference than we did in the last thousand years."

## 🎙 PODCASTS
The hidden layer feeding the GPUs is now a $30B business, and its founder thinks every enterprise will eventually need its own AI factory.

On The MAD Podcast with Matt Turck, Renen Hallak, founder and CEO of VAST Data, walks through the software infrastructure layer he calls the operating system for this new era. He describes a customer, one of the AI clouds, that first projected 500 petabytes over three years and came back needing an extra two exabytes on top. The old stack of 10 kilowatt racks and 10 gig ethernet is gone, replaced by 500 kilowatt racks, extremely fast networks, and very large SSDs, because we are no longer analyzing columns of a database but pictures, video, sound, and natural language.

Hallak's central argument is about where intelligence accumulates. He compares organizations to the human brain: we are all born with a base model, we infer during the day and fine tune at night, and every organization's IP will be distilled into models and weights they own. That is why he does not want enterprises sending their secret sauce to a model builder, and why VAST's announcement centers on model management and confidential computing, using Nvidia encrypted memory so enterprises can run inference on prem without exposing the model builder's weights and without exposing their own data. He imagines an intelligence marketplace where a carpentry shop with the best carpenter robots could lease that brain module for a week without ever revealing the weights.

The company's technical bet goes back to 2016, before the Transformers paper and long before ChatGPT, when Hallak concluded that sharding and shared nothing architectures would break down as data grew orders of magnitude. VAST built the opposite: disaggregated shared everything, with media on the other side of a fast network using NVMe over Fabrics, so all nodes see all information as if directly attached. One customer system today spans multiple exabytes in a single cluster delivering tens of terabytes per second across tens of thousands of nodes. Pitching storage to VCs in 2016 was brutal, and when they asked what happens if the underlying technologies never arrive, he told them there was no plan B. That bet is now the moat.

Memorable line: "I think in the next ten years, we'll see more difference than we did in the last thousand years."

**Nikunj Kothari** noted an innovator's dilemma playing out as personal agents become inevitable: Amazon is protecting its ads cash cow and brand, while DoorDash, albeit smaller, is opening the gates slowly with CLIs and allowing ordering via text. He also cautioned against tokenmaxxing for its own sake, saying it is not honestly useful in this era.

**Peter Steinberger** joked about how everyone is building the same thing, and flagged that OpenClaw's Android app has been stuck in review limbo for over a week, asking if anyone at Google could help.

**Zara Zhang** posed a simple question: how will the world change if coding agents get 10x better?

**Amjad Masad** shared a podcast conversation with Alex Atallah of OpenRouter, going deep and technical, and teased something called Replit Drift.

**Nan Yu** simply posted "The man has spoken" with a link.

## 📰 OFFICIAL BLOGS

**Claude Blog** announced that Claude Cowork and chat are merging into one Claude. Starting today, you can bring a quick question or hand over a report due at noon, and Claude takes it from there, even after you have closed your laptop. It is rolling out on Pro and Max plans over the next few weeks. Claude Docs and Claude Slides are new today, and Claude Design now works inside conversations. Ask for a document and you and Claude write it together; ask for a presentation and Claude drafts the slides. You can edit directly, present straight from Claude, or download as PowerPoint or PDF. All three are in beta on paid plans, and Enterprise admins choose when to turn them on. The blog explained that Cowork was built as a separate place for bigger work and Design for visual work, but people used both and said the frustrating part was deciding where a task belonged. So Claude can now figure out what a task needs, with context, skills, and connectors available from any conversation. Andrew Keller, Senior Economist, shared: "I could have Claude pull up my legal research database, and it would pull all the cases, read them, figure out which other cases I might need, download them, and store them in a folder for my personal review." A weekly report scenario shows Claude asking clarifying questions, checking progress from your phone, and delivering a doc with teammate notes plus slides ready to adjust and download as PowerPoint, all from the same conversation. You can schedule it for every Monday and Claude starts on the report without being asked. Anything you make lives at one shareable link you can open on your phone.

https://claude.com/blog/cowork-is-now-claude

## 🎙 PODCASTS

**The MAD Podcast with Matt Turck** featured Renen Hallak, founder and CEO of VAST Data, in an episode titled "Who Feeds the GPUs? Inside AI's Hidden $30B Layer." The takeaway: the software infrastructure layer between hardware and models is becoming the operating system for the AI era, and it is surprisingly under the radar despite powering top AI players.

Hallak described VAST Data as sitting right in the middle of Jensen Huang's five-layer cake: power, hardware, software infrastructure, models, applications. He calls this middle layer "the operating system for this new era," managing compute, storage, networking, databases, training, and inference. The AI factory concept, he explained, requires rethinking every layer: 500 kilowatt racks instead of 10 kilowatt racks, GPUs instead of CPUs, extremely fast networks, and very large SSDs. "In the next ten years, we'll see more difference than we did in the last thousand years," he said.

A striking anecdote: one AI cloud customer initially projected 500 petabytes over three years, then came back needing an extra two exabytes on top. Hallak argued that enterprises will eventually need their own AI factories, not just API access, because their IP will be distilled into models and weights. He used a human brain analogy: we are all born with a base model, but over time we learn, infer during the day, fine-tune at night, and tomorrow we are a little smarter. Every organization's IP will be distilled into models they own.

On agents, Hallak sees them as artificial people that will fine-tune models based on experiences with us, making them smarter and creating the next level of AI. He warned that enterprises do not want to expose proprietary information, processes, or secret sauce to model builders, which is why confidential computing matters. VAST Data's announcement focuses on model management and confidential computing, enabling enterprises to run inference on prem without exposing model builders' weights, with help from Nvidia and encrypted memory. He also floated the idea of an intelligence marketplace where a carpentry shop with the best carpenter robots could lease that brain module for a week without revealing the weights.

On his journey, Hallak spent six months trying to prove P=NP as a student, hoping to solve all seven millennium problems and collect $7 million. He joined a startup acquired by EMC in 2012, then founded VAST Data in 2016, betting on forward-looking technologies that were not yet available. "We don't have a plan B," he told skeptical VCs. That bet became their moat: the only ones with this architecture. He noted that storage was not sexy, which meant less competition, and thanked VCs for the difficulty.

Madhu Guru and Aaron Levie both argue the bottleneck is no longer model capability but product design and workflow reengineering, with Levie predicting 100X more agent adoption once the rest of knowledge work catches up to coding. Underneath it all, the infrastructure layer that feeds the GPUs is quietly becoming a $30B business.
