**Thibault Sottiaux** announced a strategic reset at OpenAI's Codex and ChatGPT: only simplifications, efficiency gains, and genuinely new features are on the table. He cited clear user feedback that things need to get simpler. He also demonstrated his own agent workflow, using it to delete unnecessary email categories in batch, auto-label work emails, and surface replies needing context, achieving inbox zero for the first time.

**Madhu Guru** argued that AI adoption is largely a product problem. Even among the 2% paying for AI, usage depth is shallow because most products resemble airplane cockpits with 100 levers: connectors, permissions, model selection, token usage. He expects this to change materially in the next 12 months as product teams mature.

**Guillermo Rauch** predicted that security will become an increasingly large function at software companies, framing it as both verification engineering and capital allocation. He sees a challenge for startups: as AI adversaries grow more sophisticated, how do you trust a 2-person-and-a-dog company? He also declared that AI will make everything free, including itself, with free energy as humanity's final frontier.

**Aaron Levie** described AI agent adoption as bimodal: coding and coding-adjacent tasks have taken off, while the rest of knowledge work remains early. The reason is that most workflows still need to be reengineered for agents, requiring rebuilt processes, new data wiring, accountability frameworks, governance changes, and security upgrades. He expects 100X more agent adoption from what we have seen so far.

**Ryo Lu** wrote a long essay on convergence to the mean: when everyone looks at everyone else to decide what to make, we eventually stop making anything of our own. He argued that AI makes this loop frictionless, producing a tidal wave of mid, and that builders need to approach making things more like artists, developing a perspective through the work rather than borrowing from a competitor's roadmap.

**Nikunj Kothari** flagged an innovator's dilemma playing out as personal agents become inevitable. Amazon is protecting its ads cash cow and brand, while DoorDash is slowly opening the gates with CLIs and text ordering. He also cautioned against tokenmaxxing for its own sake.

**Aditya Agarwal** pointed out that even the super rich cannot get unlimited access to the world's best doctor or lawyer, since a leading cancer doctor will still only see you for 20-30 minutes. AI changes this by both democratizing access and making time available unlimited for every individual, the practical effect of intelligence too cheap to meter.

**Sam Altman** expressed discomfort about people ascribing religious force or a surrender of human judgment to AI models, calling it a real safety issue.

## 📰 OFFICIAL BLOGS
**Claude Blog** announced that Claude Cowork and chat are merging into one Claude. Users can bring a quick question or hand over a report due at noon, and Claude takes it from there even after the laptop is closed. Claude Docs and Claude Slides are new, and Claude Design now works inside conversations. All three are in beta on paid plans, with Enterprise admins controlling rollout. A Senior Economist, Andrew Keller, described having Claude pull up his legal research database, read all the cases, figure out which other cases he might need, download them, and store them in a folder for personal review.

## 🎙 PODCASTS
**Takeaway**: The software infrastructure layer between GPUs and models is quietly becoming a $30B business, and its founder thinks AI factories will let every enterprise own its own intelligence.

Matt Turck interviewed Renen Hallak, founder and CEO of VAST Data, on The MAD Podcast. Hallak positioned VAST squarely in the middle of Jensen Huang's five-layer cake: power, hardware, software infrastructure, models, applications. He described the shift from 10 kilowatt racks to 500 kilowatt racks, from CPUs to GPUs, from 10 gig ethernet and hard drives to extremely fast networks and large SSDs. "Every layer of this cake needs to be redone," he said, and the culmination is what he calls the AI factory.

The most striking moment came when Hallak described a customer, one of the AI clouds, saying they would need about 500 petabytes over three years, then returning last week to say they needed an extra two exabytes on top. "I think in the next ten years, we'll see more difference than we did in the last thousand years," he said.

Hallak's vision extends to agents fine-tuning their own models. He compared agents to artificial people: "We were all born with a base model but then over time as we travel the world we learn new things, we infer during the day, we fine tune at night." He argued that every organization's IP will be distilled into models and weights they own, rather than letting big model builders own everything. This requires a trust layer where enterprises do not expose their data and model builders do not expose their weights, which VAST is addressing with confidential computing announced this week, using Nvidia encrypted memory so both sides can rest assured.

He joined a storage startup acquired by EMC in 2012, then founded VAST in 2016, three years before the Transformers paper. "We don't have a plan B," he told skeptical VCs, betting on forward-looking technologies that only became available in 2017, 2018, and 2019. keywords: AI agents | refounding | interpretability
headline: The Incumbent Strikes Back: AI's Next Act Is Inside the Enterprise
deck: Sequence Holdings bets $7.7B that old companies, not startups, win the AI era, while builders debate what agents actually create and how little we understand the models themselves.
quote: In a world where you believe that alpha comes from engineering and AI, you need to create a culture whereby the celebrated persona is the engineer.
quoteBy: Michael Lee · Co-Founder and CEO, Sequence Holdings

## 🧭 Daily Insights

**Core insight**: Builders are converging on the idea that AI's real leverage is not in new primitives but in reorganizing what already exists, whether that is a Fortune 500 incumbent, a ChatGPT interface, or a bank's underwriting workflow. At the same time, the conversation keeps circling back to a humbling truth: models are grown, not built, and nobody fully understands how they work. The trend forming is a shift from shipping features to sweating the details of deployment, interpretability, and human adoption.

## 𝕏 / TWITTER

Thibault Sottiaux, who works on Codex and ChatGPT at OpenAI, announced a 28-day cadence: each day the team will either ship one clear improvement relevant to most Codex and work users, or ship a full reset. He framed it simply as letting the improvements begin.

Peter Yang, who makes practical AI tutorials and interviews, argued that OpenAI is right to simplify ChatGPT because it has become a mess. He listed what he would streamline: Work versus Codex, Spaces versus Pages versus Sites, and the model and effort picker. His hot take is that the whole Work launch was a mistake, comparing it to Claude folding Cowork back into Chat, and he does not think Work needs its own brand. In a separate thread, he shared a conversation with Sam, co-founder of **Granola**, about users skipping the UI to use the **MCP** directly. Sam admitted there is a pang of sadness as a UI designer, but said the team made peace with the fact that for many workflows the best way to use Granola is to capture context and then use it through an internal agent. Yang also relayed Sam's point that the easier it gets to build, the more it matters to sweat the details, and that builders should hold themselves accountable not just to shipping but to whether the person actually gets daily value.

Guillermo Rauch, CEO of Vercel, noted that a product is now much faster as models speed up, pointing to **Astra ultrafast**, and said harness overhead matters more and more. He teased that the next release will feature better performance for session storage and retrieval and a big unlock for cloud durability in **libfx**. In a longer post, he said DHH is fundamentally right about **Rust**, noting Vercel has been undergoing a Rust-ification, or carcinization, for a while. He described migrating **Turborepo** from Go to Rust, where the migration completed but the ROI was controversial internally because of substantive human migration costs, and argued the calculus has changed now that what is best for humans is no longer necessarily best for business. He also shared a rule of thumb for a new project: the README is fully written by hand because it is for human consumption, while documentation internals are AI English because they are for agents.

Aaron Levie, CEO of Box, said we are already seeing what kinds of new jobs AI is creating. He pointed to AI engineers building applied products, forward deployed engineers deploying agents into companies, and new services firms, and noted that published stats undercount existing jobs transitioning to AI work. Every bank, life sciences company, manufacturer, and law firm is bringing on more technical talent or repositioning roles for agent deployment. In a second post, he argued a certain metric may tell us more about the business model of consumer AI than the state of AI, since consumer AI will almost inevitably be subsidized and monetized via commerce, ads, or device purchases, and the metric may level off lower than we think.

Ryo Lu, who designed Cursor, Notion, and Stripe, shared a bit more work on a full bleed desktop with a side dock, describing it as a little computer in your pocket.

Garry Tan, President and CEO of Y Combinator, observed that when everyone is building the same primitives it speaks to needs that will only intensify, and predicted we will eventually converge on the correct OS.

Matt Turck, a VC at FirstMark Capital and host of the MAD Podcast, flagged one of the most poorly understood aspects of AI outside AI circles: models are grown, not built, and we do not really know how they work. He cited Eric Ho of **GoodfireAI** to underline the urgent need for better interpretability.

Zara Zhang, a builder, marveled at how **Opus 5.5** silently goes off to make something for 20 plus minutes and comes back with a complete masterpiece. She also suggested X profiles are replacing resumes.

Nikunj Kothari, a partner at FPV Ventures, said he cannot believe how people make investments over a Zoom call and sometimes by just meeting the CEO. He argued there is alpha in meeting founders at their own office, where you can see the energy, how coworkers interact, how cofounders complement each other, and what beta product releases look like, and said he always asks to meet at offices for final meetings.

Peter Steinberger, who describes himself as Polyagentmorous ClawFather and works on OpenClaw and with OpenAI, posted simply about bug fixes and performance improvements.

Dan Shipper, CEO of Every, said dot has become his primary interface to AI over the last few weeks, and his dot is named boo. He bet that in a year he will still be interacting this way with ChatGPT as an always-on persistent agent, but boo will have disappeared, comparing it to early OpenClaw days when people loved the personality quirks of their Claws but dropped them as soon as something functionally more powerful arrived.

## 🎙 PODCASTS

**Takeaway**: The biggest AI opportunity may not be building new startups but buying and refounding incumbents, because ownership aligns incentives in a way that services contracts and software licenses never can.

On No Priors, Michael Lee, co-founder and CEO of Sequence Holdings, joined to discuss the largest AI take-private to date, a $7.7 billion deal with the Baldwin insurance brokerage backed by the Dell family office. Lee explained that Sequence is a permanent holding company that partners with management teams to buy and refound businesses to be market leaders with AI, and that the firm deliberately does about one deal per year.

Lee traced the idea back to his time at Lone Pine starting in 2017, when he was asked to cover AI around the time of AlphaGo and the first transformer paper. When ChatGPT arrived at the end of 2022, he felt the world had forever changed because there was finally an architecture that could scale with compute. He began thinking about which parts of the economy AI would not touch, like restaurants and golf courses, which a startup would win, like coding, and which belonged to incumbents with brand, scale, network effects, or regulatory advantages. That kernel became Sequence.

The core argument is structural. A Fortune 500 CEO trying to refound has three options: do it yourself, hire a services firm, or buy software. Doing it yourself fails because you cannot recruit and retain the talent, since every company has a celebrated persona, and in a world where alpha comes from engineering, the celebrated persona must become the engineer. Services firms optimize for getting into your wallet, staying there, and growing their share of it, which leads to incrementalism. And software is beta by definition, available to everybody, and sold around the workflow as it exists today, never around a new human assembly line that does not exist yet. Ownership, Lee argues, solves the alignment problem.

Lee described the BankSouth investment as the perfect pilot. The bank was a services customer first, starting in August of last year, before Sequence became a permanent partner. He said the difference between operating as a vendor and as an owner was night and day: as an owner you are there for a long time, so the depth of complexity you take on is demonstrably different, employees are excited that you are staying, and you can take a long term orientation toward what the bank looks like in three, five, or ten years. He also called the regulated nature of a bank a feature, not a bug, because operations are well defined, data hygiene is excellent, and the business is centralized, so anything built at headquarters amortizes across all branches.

On the platform side, Lee described Atlas, Sequence's shared platform with four layers: a data ontology that makes the business legible to models, an agent builder grounded in ground truth, an orchestration engine called Lattice, and an application builder called artifacts. The observation behind it, drawn from engineers with backgrounds at Scale AI and Palantir, is that 80 percent of a business is largely homogenous and 20 percent is vertically specific. He also stressed that the human engineering problem is much harder than the engineering problem, and that Sequence has learned to be hyper attuned to how employees feel, framing the work as elevating what people do and removing rote tasks rather than replacing them.

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TCpRwJBQvW0

**Dan Shipper** shared that "dot" has become his primary AI interface, personified as an agent named "boo." He predicts that while this persistent agent interaction model will remain, the specific personality will fade, similar to early **OpenClaw** days, as more powerful functional tools emerge.

## 🎙 PODCASTS

**Takeaway**: The biggest opportunity in AI isn't just building new tools, but acquiring and fundamentally re-architecting incumbent businesses to compete in the AI era.

In this episode of No Priors, Michael Lee, co-founder and CEO of Sequence Holdings, discusses his firm's model of buying and "re-founding" businesses. He explains their recent $7.7 billion take-private of Baldwin, an insurance brokerage, and why they focus on incumbents in industries like financial services and insurance. Lee argues that while startups may win in areas like coding, established companies in sectors with regulatory, brand, or network-effect advantages can be transformed into market leaders with the right approach.

Lee outlines the three options for a Fortune 500 CEO looking to "refound" their company: do it yourself (hard to recruit talent), hire a services firm (misaligned incentives), or buy software (sells to today's workflows, not tomorrow's). Sequence's model is a fourth way: a permanent holding company that provides aligned, long-term capital and a frontier engineering team. He stresses the need to change the "celebrated persona" of a company to the engineer, a shift that is culturally difficult but essential.

> "The human engineering problem is much more difficult than the engineering problem."

He explains that managing employee anxiety and making them feel that AI elevates their work, rather than replaces it, is the most critical and challenging part of the process. **Aaron Levie** outlined the emerging job categories AI is creating: AI engineers building applied products, forward deployed engineers deploying agents into companies, and new services firms. He emphasized that published stats undercount existing roles being repositioned for AI work across banks, life sciences, manufacturers, and law firms. He also pushed back on a consumer AI metric, arguing it "may tell us more about the business model of consumer AI than the state of AI" since consumer AI will inevitably be subsidized and monetized via commerce, ads, or device purchases.

**Matt Turck** highlighted what he considers the most poorly understood aspect of AI outside AI circles: "models are grown, not built" and we don't really know how they work, hence the urgent need for better interpretability, referencing Eric Ho of Goodfire AI.

**Zara Zhang** observed that Opus 5.5 "just silently goes off to make something for 20+ minutes and comes back with a complete masterpiece," a small but telling signal of how agentic workflows are maturing. She also noted that X profiles are replacing resumes.

**Nikunj Kothari** made a case for in-person diligence, arguing there's "so much alpha in meeting founders at their own office" where you can observe office energy, cofounder dynamics, and beta product releases. ## 🎙 PODCASTS

**No Priors: Re-Founding Incumbents for the AI Era with Michael Lee**

**Takeaway**: The biggest AI opportunity isn't building new startups, it's buying established companies and rebuilding them around frontier engineering.

Michael Lee, co-founder and CEO of Sequence Holdings, joined No Priors to discuss his firm's $7.7 billion take-private of Baldwin with the Dell family office, the largest AI take-private to date. Sequence operates as a permanent holding company that acquires incumbents and "refounds" them with frontier engineering talent.

Lee's core thesis: AI will have an uneven impact on the economy. Some industries (restaurants, golf courses) won't be touched. Some (coding) will be won by startups. But many industries have incumbents with durable advantages like brand, scale, network effects, and regulatory moats. "If you could acquire the right incumbent, inherit the advantages of being that incumbent, could you forge the market leader?" he asks.

The structural argument against doing this yourself: "Every company on the planet has a celebrated persona. In a world where you believe that alpha comes from engineering and AI, you need to create a culture whereby the celebrated persona is the engineer." Most enterprises can't recruit and retain that talent. Services firms have misaligned incentives, optimizing for "getting in your wallet, staying in your wallet, growing the share of your wallet." The insight from engineers with Scale AI and Palantir backgrounds: 80% of any business is largely homogenous, 20% is vertically specific.

On why banking was the perfect first investment: regulated institutions have well-defined operations, excellent data hygiene, and centralized functions. "The regulated nature of the bank was a feature, not a bug," Lee says. "If you think about that context, it actually works extremely well for agents." He also emphasizes "organizational physics," preferring dense, centralized operations where anything built at headquarters gets amortized across all branches.

The human side is harder than the technical side. Lee admits: "We have an engineering problem and a human engineering problem, and the human engineering problem is much more difficult than the engineering problem." keywords: AI agents | enterprise AI | refounding
headline: The Great Refounding: AI Eats the Incumbents
deck: A $7.7B take-private bets that ownership beats software, while builders debate whether agents need a UI at all and Rust's human cost in the age of AI.
quote: In a world where you believe that alpha comes from engineering and AI, you need to create a culture whereby the celebrated persona is the engineer, and that's what's required.
quoteBy: Michael Lee · Co-Founder and CEO, Sequence Holdings

## 🧭 Daily Insights

**Core insight**: Builders are converging on the idea that AI's next phase is not about shipping more features but about reorganizing how work and companies are structured. From OpenAI's Codex reset to a $7.7B bet on refounding an insurance incumbent, the theme is the same: agents change the unit of work, so the org chart, the UI, and even the choice of programming language all have to be rethought from first principles.

## 𝕏 / TWITTER

**Thibault Sottiaux** announced a 28-day cadence for **Codex** and ChatGPT work users: each day OpenAI will either ship one clear improvement or a full reset. The framing signals a shift from big-bang launches to relentless iteration on the coding harness.

https://x.com/thsottiaux/status/2106845241357824205

**Peter Yang** argued that ChatGPT has become a mess and needs simplification, calling out three areas: **Work** vs. **Codex**, **Spaces** vs. **Pages** vs. **Sites**, and the model and effort picker. His hot take is that the whole Work launch was a mistake, comparing it to Claude folding Cowork back into Chat. He also shared an interview with Sam, co-founder of **Granola**, who admitted a "pang of sadness" as a UI designer watching users skip the app and hit the MCP directly, but has made peace with it: for many workflows the best way to use Granola is to capture context, then use it through an internal agent. Sam's advice to builders: don't just ship version one, hold yourself accountable to whether the person actually gets daily value out of it.

https://x.com/petergyang/status/2106926956554195018
https://x.com/petergyang/status/2106897211766530299
https://x.com/petergyang/status/2106825485624004691

**Guillermo Rauch** noted that as models speed up, as with **Astra ultrafast**, harness overhead matters more and more, and teased better session storage and retrieval plus a big unlock for cloud durability in **libfx**. He weighed in on the Rust debate, saying DHH is fundamentally right: Vercel has been undergoing a Rust-ification, starting with migrating **Turborepo** from Go to Rust, but the ROI was controversial internally because the human migration costs were substantial. His conclusion: what's best for humans is no longer necessarily best for business, and Rust itself was designed before the supersonic tsunami of agents hit. He also shared a rule of thumb for a new project: the README is fully written by hand because it's for human consumption, while documentation internals are AI English because they're for agents.

https://x.com/rauchg/status/2106885457212825983
https://x.com/rauchg/status/2106863842450133114
https://x.com/rauchg/status/2106848085267902815

**Aaron Levie** sketched the new jobs AI is creating: AI engineers building applied products, forward deployed engineers deploying agents into companies, and new services firms. He noted that published stats undercount existing roles being repositioned for AI work across banks, life sciences, manufacturers, and law firms. On a separate thread, he argued that a consumer AI metric may say more about the business model than the state of AI, since consumer AI will almost inevitably be subsidized and monetized via commerce, ads, or device purchases, and may level off lower than expected.

https://x.com/levie/status/2106893015063421357
https://x.com/levie/status/2106802940879192260

**Ryo Lu** shared a design update: full bleed desktop plus a side dock, describing it as a little computer in your pocket.

https://x.com/ryolu_/status/2106777615801713054

**Garry Tan** observed that when everyone is building the same primitives, it speaks to needs that will only intensify, and predicted we will eventually converge on the correct OS.

https://x.com/garrytan/status/2106901111106097210

**Matt Turck** flagged one of the most poorly understood aspects of AI outside AI circles: models are grown, not built, and we don't really know how they work, hence the urgent need for better interpretability, citing Eric Ho of **Goodfire AI**.

https://x.com/mattturck/status/2106821381765956044

**Zara Zhang** marveled at how **Opus 5.5** silently goes off to make something for 20+ minutes and comes back with a complete masterpiece. She also noted that X profiles are replacing resumes.

https://x.com/zarazhangrui/status/2106876921082712250
https://x.com/zarazhangrui/status/2106782239493427588

**Nikunj Kothari** pushed back on making investments over a Zoom call or by just meeting the CEO, arguing there is alpha in meeting founders at their own office: seeing the office energy, how coworkers react and work together, how cofounders complement each other, and what beta product releases look like. He always asks to meet at offices for final meetings, and founders often tell him he's the only one who has ever asked.

https://x.com/nikunj/status/2106957269212742135

**Dan Shipper** said **dot** has become his primary interface to AI over the last few weeks, with his dot named boo. He predicts that in a year he'll still be interacting with ChatGPT as an always-on persistent agent, but boo will have disappeared, comparing it to early OpenClaw days when users loved the personality quirks of their Claws but dropped them as soon as something functionally more powerful arrived.

https://x.com/danshipper/status/2106892868564431255

## 🎙 PODCASTS

**Takeaway**: The biggest AI opportunity may not be building new software but buying old companies and refounding them around engineering, because ownership solves the incentive problem that services and software vendors can't.

On No Priors, Michael Lee, co-founder and CEO of Sequence Holdings, explained why he raised a permanent holding company to buy and refound incumbents for the AI era. Sequence just announced the largest AI take-private to date with the Dell family office of Baldwin for $7,700,000,000. Lee's core argument is that every company has a celebrated persona, and in a world where alpha comes from engineering and AI, you need a culture where the celebrated persona is the engineer. He laid out three options for a Fortune 500 CEO trying to refound: do it yourself, which fails on recruiting and retaining talent; hire a services firm like Accenture, McKinsey, or Palantir, which optimizes for getting into your wallet, staying there, and growing share of wallet; or buy software, which is beta and always sold around the workflow as it exists today, never around a new human assembly line that doesn't exist yet. Ownership, he argues, aligns incentives and duration of capital with the sustained investment required.

The conversation dug into why banking was the perfect first pilot. Lee admitted the cold start problem: without money you can't do a deal, without a deal you can't hire engineers, and without engineers nobody gives you money. They took on a bank as a customer first, then became a permanent partner. The regulated nature of banking turned out to be a feature, not a bug: how it operates is well defined, data hygiene is excellent, and the centralized nature of underwriting means anything built at headquarters gets amortized over all the branches. He contrasted this with roll-ups, which require integrating different systems, sending engineers to many places, and standardizing cultures. On insurance brokerage, he noted it's a $2,000,000,000,000 plus premiums market where the customer doesn't pay the broker, the carrier does, gross retention rates are 90%, and brokers don't compete on price, making it very hard for startups.

Lee also described Atlas, Sequence's shared platform, built at the bank and expected to generalize. It has four layers: a data ontology that makes the business legible in code, an agent builder grounded in ground truth, Lattice for orchestration, and artifacts as the application builder on top. His observation from engineers at Scale and Palantir: 80% of a business is largely homogenous and 20% is vertically specific. The hardest part, he said, is the human engineering problem, which is much more difficult than the engineering problem, and much of the work is making employees feel that AI elevates what they do rather than threatens it.

quote: In a world where you believe that alpha comes from engineering and AI, you need to create a culture whereby the celebrated persona is the engineer, and that's what's required.
quoteBy: Michael Lee · Co-Founder and CEO, Sequence Holdings

## 🧭 Daily Insights

**Core insight**: The conversation today centers on how AI reshapes both products and entire companies. Builders are debating whether consumer AI interfaces are overcomplicated and whether agent-native tools should replace traditional UIs, while investors and operators argue that the biggest AI opportunity may be re-founding existing incumbents rather than building from scratch. The trend forming is a shift from "AI as a feature" to "AI as the operating system" for both software and legacy businesses.

## 𝕏 / TWITTER

Thibault Sottiaux, working on Codex and ChatGPT at OpenAI, announced a 28-day shipping cadence: each day the team will either ship one clear improvement relevant to most Codex and work users, or ship a full reset. The message signals a push to accelerate iteration and let improvements compound.

Peter Yang, who creates practical AI tutorials and interviews, argued that ChatGPT has become a mess and praised OpenAI for focusing on simplification. He listed three areas to streamline: Work versus Codex, Spaces versus Pages versus Sites, and the model and effort picker. His hot take: the whole Work launch was a mistake, and just as Claude folded Cowork back into Chat, Work does not need its own brand. He also shared a clip from his dots review.

Guillermo Rauch, CEO of Vercel, noted that as models speed up, harness overhead matters more and more, and teased that the next release will feature better performance for session storage and retrieval plus a big unlock for cloud durability in libfx. In a separate thread, he argued that DHH is fundamentally right about Rust, describing Vercel's ongoing Rust-ification and the controversial migration of Turborepo from Go to Rust. He said the calculus has changed: what is best for humans is no longer necessarily best for business, and he doubts Rust is the end-all-be-all toolchain because it was designed before the supersonic tsunami of agents. He also shared a rule of thumb: READMEs and blogs should be written by hand for human consumption, while documentation internals can be AI English for agents.

Aaron Levie, CEO of Box, said we are already seeing what kinds of new jobs AI is creating: AI engineers building applied products, forward deployed engineers deploying agents into companies, and new services firms. He noted that published stats undercount existing jobs transitioning to AI work, and that every bank, life sciences company, manufacturer, and law firm is bringing on more technical talent or repositioning roles for agent deployment. In a separate post, he argued that a certain consumer AI metric may tell us more about the business model of consumer AI than the state of AI, since consumer AI will almost inevitably be subsidized and monetized via commerce, ads, or device purchases.

Matt Turck, VC at FirstMark Capital and host of the MAD Podcast, highlighted that models are grown, not built, and we do not really know how they work, which is why better interpretability is urgently needed. He referenced Eric Ho of Goodfire AI.

Zara Zhang, a builder, observed that Opus 5.5 can silently go off to make something for 20+ minutes and come back with a complete masterpiece. She also noted that X profiles are replacing resumes.

Nikunj Kothari, partner at FPV Ventures, made the case for meeting founders at their own offices rather than over Zoom. He said there is alpha in seeing the energy of the office, how coworkers react and work together, how cofounders complement each other, and what beta product releases look like. He always asks to meet at offices for final meetings, and founders often tell him he is the only one who has ever asked.

Dan Shipper, CEO of Every, said dot has become his primary interface to AI over the last few weeks. His dot is named boo. He bets that in a year he will still be interacting with ChatGPT as an always-on persistent agent, but boo will have disappeared, comparing it to early OpenClaw days when people loved the personality quirks of their Claws but dropped them as soon as something functionally more powerful was available.

## 🎙 PODCASTS

**Takeaway**: The biggest AI opportunity may not be building new startups but re-founding existing incumbents, because incumbents hold brand, scale, network effects, and regulatory advantages that startups cannot easily replicate.

In this episode of No Priors, host Sarah Guo speaks with Michael Lee, co-founder and CEO of Sequence Holdings, about the firm's model of buying and re-founding businesses to be market leaders with AI. Sequence just announced the largest AI take-private to date with the Dell family office of Baldwin for $7.7 billion. Michael explains that Sequence started 20 months ago with the idea of partnering with world-class businesses and management teams, working closely with a frontier engineering team. He argues that AI will have an uneven impact on the economy: some industries like restaurants and golf courses will be barely touched, while others like coding will be dominated by startups. But in industries where incumbents have all the advantages, the right move is to acquire the incumbent, inherit those advantages, and forge the market leader.

Michael lays out three options for a Fortune 500 CEO trying to refound their business. Doing it yourself is structurally hard because it is impossible to recruit and retain the talent required. Every company has a celebrated persona, and in a world where alpha comes from engineering and AI, you need to create a culture where the celebrated persona is the engineer. Using a services provider like Accenture, McKinsey, or Palantir runs into an incentives problem: services companies optimize for getting in your wallet, staying in your wallet, and growing share of wallet, which leads to incrementalism. Buying software is also flawed because if it is available to everybody, it is available to everybody, and software is always sold to a workflow as it is designed today, not around a new human assembly line that does not yet exist. Ownership, by contrast, aligns incentives, enables a long-term horizon, and lets Sequence bring frontier engineering to bear.

The conversation covers the BankSouth investment, which started as a services engagement and became Sequence's first permanent partnership. Michael says the regulated nature of the bank was a feature, not a bug: data hygiene is excellent, rules are well defined, and operations are centralized, which works extremely well for agents. He explains Atlas, Sequence's platform, which has four layers: a data ontology that makes the business legible to models, an agent builder grounded in ground truth, Lattice for orchestration, and artifacts for application building. He estimates that 80% of any business is largely homogenous and 20% is vertically specific, so the core infrastructure is reusable across companies.

On insurance brokerage, Michael says it fits Sequence's criteria: a $2 trillion plus market, incumbents with all the advantages, and a business where the customer does not pay the broker, the carrier does, leading to 90% gross retention rates. He also reflects on the human engineering problem, which he says is much harder than the engineering problem. After the bank investment, Sequence learned how much more attuned it needs to be to how employees feel, making people feel that AI elevates what they do rather than replaces them.

Memorable quote: "In a world where you believe that alpha comes from engineering and AI, you need to create a culture whereby the celebrated persona is the engineer, and that's what's required."

headline: The Engineer Becomes the Celebrated Persona
deck: As builders debate ChatGPT's tangled surfaces and Rust's human cost, one investor is buying whole companies to rebuild them around AI, betting ownership beats software and services.
quote: In a world where you believe that alpha comes from engineering and AI, you need to create a culture whereby the celebrated persona is the engineer, and that's what's required.
quoteBy: Michael Lee · Co-Founder and CEO, Sequence Holdings

## 🧭 Daily Insights

**Core insight**: Builders are converging on the same conclusion from opposite directions: the interface and the org chart both need to be rebuilt around agents, not bolted onto legacy surfaces. OpenAI is promising 28 days of Codex improvements or full resets, while investors argue the real AI transformation happens by owning incumbents and making the engineer the celebrated persona, not by selling them software.

## 𝕏 / TWITTER

**Thibault Sottiaux** of OpenAI announced a 28-day cadence for Codex: each day the team will either ship one clear improvement relevant to most Codex and work users, or ship a full reset. The framing suggests OpenAI is treating the coding harness as a product on a public, iterative clock rather than a periodic release.

**Peter Yang** argued that ChatGPT has become a mess and needs simplifying, naming three targets: Work versus Codex, Spaces versus Pages versus Sites, and the model and effort picker. His hot take is that the whole Work launch was a mistake, comparing it to Claude folding Cowork back into Chat, and he does not think Work needs its own brand. He also shared an interview with Sam, co-founder of Granola, who admitted a pang of sadness as a UI designer when people skip the interface and use the MCP directly, but said Granola made peace with the fact that for many workflows the best use is capturing context and running it through an internal agent. Sam added that the easier it gets to build, the more it matters to sweat the details, and that builders should hold themselves accountable not just to shipping but to whether the person gets daily value.

**Guillermo Rauch** of Vercel said it is hard to fathom how much faster things got, noting that as models speed up, harness overhead matters more and more, with the next release bringing better session storage and retrieval plus a big unlock for cloud durability in libfx. He weighed in on the Rust debate, saying DHH is fundamentally right, and described Vercel's own Rust-ification, including migrating Turborepo from Go to Rust, where the return on investment was controversial internally because the human migration costs were substantive even though Rust was the better technical choice. He argued the calculus has changed: what is best for humans is no longer necessarily best for business, and Rust itself was designed before the supersonic tsunami of agents. He also described a new project where the README is fully hand-written for human consumption while the documentation internals are AI English for agents, a rule of thumb he thinks can make the world better.

**Aaron Levie** of Box said we are already seeing what kinds of new jobs AI creates: AI engineers building applied products, forward deployed engineers deploying agents into companies, and new services firms. He noted published stats undercount existing roles being repositioned toward AI work, with every bank, life sciences company, manufacturer, and law firm bringing on more technical talent for agent deployment. In a separate post he argued a certain consumer AI metric may tell us more about the business model than the state of AI, since consumer AI will almost inevitably be subsidized and monetized via commerce, ads, or device purchases.

**Zara Zhang** observed that Opus 5.5 will silently go off to make something for 20+ minutes and come back with a complete masterpiece, and separately noted that X profiles are replacing resumes.

**Nikunj Kothari** of FPV Ventures said he cannot believe how people make investments over a Zoom call or by just meeting the CEO, arguing there is alpha in meeting founders at their own office: seeing the office energy, how coworkers interact, how cofounders complement each other, and what beta product releases look like. He said he always asks to meet at offices for final meetings and founders often tell him he is the only one who has ever asked.

**Dan Shipper** of Every said dot has become his primary interface to AI over the last few weeks, with his dot named boo. He bets that in a year he will still be interacting with ChatGPT as an always-on persistent agent, but boo will have disappeared, comparing it to early OpenClaw days when people loved the personality quirks of their Claws but dropped them as soon as something functionally more powerful arrived.

**Matt Turck** of FirstMark Capital highlighted that models are grown, not built, and we do not really know how they work, hence the urgent need for better interpretability, referencing Eric Ho of Goodfire AI.

**Garry Tan** of Y Combinator noted that when everyone is building the same primitives it speaks to needs that will only intensify, and that we will eventually converge on the correct OS.

## 🎙 PODCASTS

**Takeaway**: The biggest AI opportunity may not be selling software to incumbents but buying them and refounding the whole organization around engineers.

On No Priors, Michael Lee, co-founder and CEO of Sequence Holdings, described a permanent holding company that partners with management teams to buy and refound businesses as AI-era market leaders. Sequence just announced the largest AI take-private to date with the Dell family office of Baldwin for $7,700,000,000, an insurance brokerage he called truly N of one among the dozens of brokers they met. Lee traced the idea back to joining Lone Pine in 2017, when he was asked to cover AI around the time AlphaGo and the first transformer paper landed, and to the moment ChatGPT arrived at the end of 2022, when it became obvious the world had forever changed because here was an architecture that could scale with compute.

His core argument is that most enterprises are handing small machines to every human on the assembly line to speed up work, which is better than nothing but misses the point. When machines can work 24/7 and scale with electricity, the right answer is to reorganize what an organization should be. He laid out three options for a Fortune 500 CEO trying to refound: do it yourself, which fails because you cannot recruit and retain the talent; hire services firms like Accenture, McKinsey, or Palantir, which have an incentives problem because they optimize for getting in your wallet, staying in your wallet, and growing share of wallet; or buy software, which is beta by definition and always sells to the workflow as designed today. Ownership, he argues, solves alignment, and a holding company aligns the duration of capital with the sustained investment required.

The most striking line came on culture: "In a world where you believe that alpha comes from engineering and AI, you need to create a culture whereby the celebrated persona is the engineer, and that's what's required." He contrasted that with Blackstone, where the celebrated persona is the investor, and called Palantir foundationally an organization that aggregates world class engineers and celebrates them.

On BankSouth, their first investment, Lee said the regulated nature of a bank was a feature, not a bug: operations are well defined, data hygiene is excellent, and the rules make it work extremely well for agents. He also values organizational physics, preferring dense, centralized operations where anything built at headquarters amortizes across all branches, unlike roll-ups that require integrating systems and standardizing cultures. Their shared platform, Atlas, has four layers: a data ontology that makes the business legible to models, an agent builder grounded in ground truth, an orchestration engine called Lattice, and an application builder called artifacts. He estimated 80% of any business is largely homogenous and 20% is vertically specific, which is why the core infrastructure built at the bank is reusable at Baldwin. On the human side, he admitted the human engineering problem is much harder than the engineering problem, and that post-investment they learned to be hyper-attuned to employee anxiety, framing their job as elevating what people do and removing rote work.

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TCpRwJBQvW0

headline: The Engineer Becomes the Celebrated Persona
deck: As builders debate ChatGPT's tangled interface and Rust's human cost, one investor is buying whole companies to rebuild them around frontier engineering. The bet: ownership beats software.
quote: The easier it gets to build stuff, the more it matters to really sweat the details and go the extra mile.
quoteBy: Sam · co-founder of Granola

## 🧭 Daily Insights

**Core insight**: Builders are converging on the same conclusion from opposite directions: the hard part is no longer shipping, it is reorganizing around what agents can actually do. On X the talk is interface simplification, harness overhead, and whether AI creates or replaces jobs; in the podcast world the talk is ownership, culture, and rebuilding incumbents from the inside. The trend forming is that "AI transformation" is shifting from buying tools to changing who an organization celebrates, hires, and rewards.

## 𝕏 / TWITTER

**Thibault Sottiaux** announced a 28-day cadence for **Codex** and ChatGPT work users: each day the team will either ship one clear improvement or ship a full reset. It is a public commitment to visible, compounding iteration rather than a single big launch.

**Peter Yang** argued that **ChatGPT** has become a mess and welcomed OpenAI's focus on simplification, listing three things to collapse: **Work** versus **Codex**, **Spaces** versus **Pages** versus **Sites**, and the model and effort picker. His hot take is that the whole **Work** launch was a mistake, comparing it to Claude folding **Cowork** back into Chat, and he is glad his primary harness is getting better. He also shared Sam, co-founder of **Granola**, on people skipping the UI for the **MCP**: there is "a pang of sadness" for a UI designer, but as enterprises grow internal tooling, not playing nice with it is a non-starter, so the team is at peace with capturing context and using it through an internal agent. Sam's advice on building: the easier it gets to build, the more it matters to sweat the details, and the real accountability question is whether the person gets daily value.

**Guillermo Rauch** said it is hard to fathom **Vercel** getting faster, but it now is, noting that as models speed up, as with **Astra 𝚞𝚕𝚝𝚛𝚊𝚏𝚊𝚜𝚝**, harness overhead matters more and more, with the next release improving session storage and retrieval plus cloud durability in **libfx**. On Rust, he called DHH fundamentally right and described Vercel's long-running Rust-ification, including migrating **Turborepo** from Go to Rust, where the ROI was internally controversial because the human migration costs were substantive even though Rust was the better technical choice. He added that what is best for humans is no longer necessarily best for business, and that Rust itself predates the "supersonic tsunami" of agents. He also described a new project whose README is fully hand-written for human consumption while the documentation internals are AI English for agents, arguing human communication is about the storytelling moment, not about em dashes.

**Aaron Levie** sketched the jobs AI is creating: AI engineers building applied products for enterprises, FDEs deploying agents into companies, and new services firms, with published stats undercounting existing data, research, and software roles being repositioned for AI work. He noted every bank, life sciences company, manufacturer, and law firm is bringing on more technical talent, and that it is easier to picture what AI replaces than what it creates until it starts happening. He also cautioned that a consumer AI metric may say more about the business model than the state of AI, since consumer AI will almost inevitably be subsidized and monetized via commerce, ads, or device and service purchases, and may level off lower than expected.

**Ryo Lu** shared a small design update: full bleed desktop plus side dock, a little computer in your pocket.

**Garry Tan** observed that when everyone is building the same primitives, it speaks to needs that will only intensify, and that the field will eventually converge on the correct OS.

**Matt Turck** flagged one of the most poorly understood aspects of AI outside AI circles: models are grown, not built, and we do not really know how they work, hence the urgent need for better interpretability, citing Eric Ho of **Goodfire AI**.

**Zara Zhang** noted that **Opus 5.5** silently goes off to make something for 20+ minutes and comes back with a complete masterpiece, and separately that X profiles are replacing resumes.

**Nikunj Kothari** argued there is alpha in meeting founders at their own office rather than over a Zoom call or a single CEO meeting: you see the office energy, how coworkers react and work together, how cofounders complement each other, and what beta product releases look like. He always asks for final meetings at offices and founders often tell him he is the only one who has ever asked.

**Peter Steinberger** posted a brief update: bug fixes and performance improvements.

**Dan Shipper** said **dot** has become his primary interface to AI over the last few weeks, and his dot is named boo. He bets that in a year he will still interact this way with ChatGPT as an always-on persistent agent, but boo will have disappeared, much like early **OpenClaw** days when people loved the personality quirks of their Claws and dropped them as soon as something functionally more powerful arrived.

## 🎙 PODCASTS

**Takeaway**: The biggest AI opportunity may not be building new software but buying incumbent businesses and refounding them around engineering, because ownership solves the incentive problem that services and software cannot.

On **No Priors**, Michael Lee, co-founder and CEO of **Sequence Holdings**, joined to discuss the largest AI take-private to date, a $7,700,000,000 deal with the Dell family office for **Baldwin**, and the permanent holding company model behind it. Sequence started twenty months ago with the premise that AI will have an uneven impact on the economy: some sectors, like restaurants and golf courses, will barely move; some, like coding, will be won by startups; and others, where brand, scale, network effects, or regulation favor the incumbent, can be acquired and forged into market leaders. Lee traces the idea to his time at Lone Pine in 2017, when he covered AI around AlphaGo and the first transformer paper, and to the moment ChatGPT arrived, when it became obvious the world had changed because there was finally an architecture that could scale with compute.

The core argument is structural. A Fortune 500 CEO trying to refound has three options: do it yourself, which fails on recruiting and retaining talent; hire a services firm, which optimizes for getting in your wallet, staying in your wallet, and growing share of wallet, a path toward incrementalism; or buy software, which is beta by definition and must sell to workflows as they are designed today, around the human assembly line that exists now. Ownership, in his framing, aligns duration of capital with sustained operational commitment and lets you build a culture where the celebrated persona is the engineer, not the investor. He points to Palantir as an organization that aggregated world class engineers and wrapped that capability to sell to others.

The first proof point was a bank. With a cold start problem, no deal meant no engineers and no engineers meant no money, so Sequence took on a customer: a friend's family-owned bank in Georgia, starting August 4, which he remembers because he skipped his anniversary. Operating in a services motion from August to late November, then becoming a permanent partner with a March close after Fed and OCC approval, showed a night and day difference. As an owner, the engineering depth is different because you will be there for a long time, employees are excited that the support is permanent, and you can take a three, five, ten year view. The regulated nature of the bank was a feature, not a bug: well-defined operations, excellent data hygiene, and clear rules work extremely well for agents. So does centralized density, since underwriting happens centrally and anything built at headquarters amortizes across all branches, unlike roll-ups that require integrating systems and standardizing cultures.

That work produced **Atlas**, the shared platform Sequence expects to generalize across industries. It has four layers: a data ontology that makes the business legible in code, an agent builder grounded in ground truth, **Lattice** as the orchestration engine that instruments workflows, and artifacts as the application builder on top. Lee estimates that if you break a business into atomic units, 80% is largely homogenous and 20% is vertically specific. Insurance brokerage fits the same thesis: over $2,000,000,000,000 in premiums per year, carriers that make money through investing and therefore chase asset gathering, customers who do not pay the broker directly, 90% gross retention, and a relationship-centric business that does not compete on price. On the human side, he is candid that the human engineering problem is much harder than the engineering problem, and that the key is making people feel the technology elevates what they do and removes rote work. As he put it: "Every company on the planet has a celebrated persona. In a world where you believe that alpha comes from engineering and AI, you need to create a culture whereby the celebrated persona is the engineer, and that's what's required."

headline: The AI Takeover of Old Economy Incumbents
deck: A $7.7B take-private bets on refounding insurance brokers, while builders debate what AI actually creates, how models are grown not built, and why Rust's calculus just changed.
quote: In a world where you believe that alpha comes from engineering and AI, you need to create a culture whereby the celebrated persona is the engineer, and that's what's required.
quoteBy: Michael Lee · Co-Founder and CEO of Sequence Holdings

## 🧭 Daily Insights
**Core insight**: Builders are split between shipping faster and rethinking the org chart. On one side, OpenAI's Codex team promises 28 days of relentless improvements and Vercel keeps squeezing harness overhead as models speed up. On the other, the loudest thread is that AI's real impact is uneven: it creates new deployment jobs, forces incumbents to refound around engineering, and leaves us still unsure how the models actually work.

## 𝕏 / TWITTER
Thibault Sottiaux, Codex & ChatGPT at OpenAI, announced a 28-day shipping cadence: each day the team will either ship one clear improvement relevant to most Codex and work users, or a full reset. He framed it simply: let the improvements begin.

Peter Yang, who runs practical AI tutorials and interviews, argued OpenAI is right to simplify ChatGPT because it has become a mess. He listed what he would cut: Work vs. Codex, Spaces vs. Pages vs. Sites, and the model and effort picker. His hot take is that the whole Work launch was a mistake, comparing it to Claude folding Cowork back into Chat. He also shared Sam, co-founder of Granola, on people skipping the UI to use the MCP: there is a pang of sadness as a UI designer, but as soon as you become a big enough enterprise, internal tooling is inevitable, and the best way to use Granola is to capture context then use it through your internal agent. Sam added that the easier it gets to build, the more it matters to sweat the details and answer whether the person actually gets daily value.

Guillermo Rauch, CEO of Vercel, noted that as models speed up, as with Astra ultrafast, harness overhead matters more and more, and the next release will bring better session storage and retrieval plus a big unlock for cloud durability in libfx. He weighed in on DHH being fundamentally right about Rust, describing Vercel's ongoing Rust-ification and the controversial Turborepo migration from Go to Rust, where human migration costs were substantive. The calculus has changed: what is best for humans is no longer necessarily best for business, and Rust itself was designed before the supersonic tsunami of agents. He also shared a rule of thumb for a new project: the README is fully written by hand for human consumption, while documentation internals are AI English for agents.

Aaron Levie, CEO of Box, said we are starting to see what kind of new jobs AI creates: AI engineers building applied products, FDEs deploying agents, new services firms, and existing data, research, and software roles repositioned for AI work. Every bank, life sciences company, manufacturer, and law firm is bringing on more technical talent. He also argued a certain consumer AI metric may tell us more about the business model than the state of AI, since consumer AI will almost inevitably be subsidized and monetized via commerce, ads, or devices.

Ryo Lu, who designed Cursor, Notion, and Stripe, shared a bit more work later: full bleed desktop plus side dock, a lil computer in your pocket.

Garry Tan, President and CEO of Y Combinator, observed that when everyone is building the same primitives it speaks to needs that will only intensify, and we will eventually converge on the correct OS.

Matt Turck, VC at FirstMark Capital and host of the MAD Podcast, flagged the most poorly understood aspect of AI outside AI circles: models are grown, not built, and we do not really know how they work, hence the urgent need for better interpretability, citing Eric Ho of Goodfire AI.

Zara Zhang, a builder, marveled that Opus 5.5 silently goes off to make something for 20+ minutes and comes back with a complete masterpiece. She also noted X profiles are replacing resumes.

Nikunj Kothari, partner at FPV Ventures, cannot believe people make investments over a Zoom call or by just meeting the CEO. There is so much alpha in meeting founders at their own office: the energy, how coworkers react, how cofounders complement each other, what beta releases look like. He always asks to meet at offices for final meetings, and founders often tell him he is the only one who has ever asked.

Dan Shipper, CEO of Every, said dot has become his primary interface to AI over the last few weeks, and his dot is named boo. In a year he bets he will still be interacting this way with ChatGPT as an always-on persistent agent, but boo will have disappeared, much like early OpenClaw days when people loved the personality quirks of their Claws but dropped them as soon as something functionally more powerful arrived.

## 🎙 PODCASTS
**Takeaway**: The biggest AI opportunity may not be building new startups but buying old incumbents and refounding them around engineering.

On No Priors, Michael Lee, co-founder and CEO of Sequence Holdings, explained why his firm just announced the largest AI take-private to date with the Dell family office of Baldwin for $7,700,000,000. Sequence is a permanent holding company that partners with management teams to buy and refound businesses as market leaders with AI, doing roughly one deal per year.

Lee traced the idea back to his time at Lone Pine in 2017, when he first covered AI around AlphaGo and the first transformer paper. When ChatGPT arrived at the end of 2022, it became obvious the world had forever changed because there was finally an architecture that could scale with compute. He felt strongly that AI would have an uneven impact on the economy: some industries, like restaurants and golf courses, would barely be touched, while others, like coding, would be won by startups. But in industries where incumbents hold brand, scale, network effects, or regulatory advantages, the winning move is to acquire the right incumbent and inherit those advantages.

The core argument is about culture and incentives. Every company has a celebrated persona, he said, and in a world where alpha comes from engineering and AI, the celebrated persona must become the engineer. He contrasted three options for a Fortune 500 CEO trying to refound: doing it yourself fails on recruiting and retaining talent, hiring services firms like Accenture, McKinsey, or Palantir runs into an incentives problem because they optimize for getting in your wallet and staying there, and buying software means you are buying beta that is available to everybody and selling to a workflow as it is designed today. Ownership, he argued, aligns duration of capital with the sustained investment required.

On the bank investment, Lee admitted there was a cold start problem: without money you cannot do a deal, without a deal you cannot hire engineers. They took on a bank in Georgia as their first customer in August, then became a permanent partner, closing in March after Fed and OCC approval. The regulated nature of banking was a feature, not a bug: operations are well defined, data hygiene is excellent, and underwriting happens centrally, so anything built at headquarters gets amortized across all branches. That density, which he calls organizational physics, is exactly what they look for.

He also described Atlas, their shared platform with four layers: a data ontology that makes the business legible to models, an agent builder grounded in ground truth, an orchestration engine called Lattice, and an application builder called artifacts. Roughly 80% of a business is homogenous and 20% is vertically specific, so the core infrastructure is reusable at Baldwin and beyond. The hardest part, he said, is the human engineering problem, which is much more difficult than the engineering problem: making employees feel that AI elevates what they do, removes rote work, and makes their organization win.

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TCpRwJBQvW0

**Garry Tan** observed that when everyone is building the same primitives, it speaks to needs that will only intensify, and predicted eventual convergence on the correct OS.

**Peter Steinberger** posted a brief update on bug fixes and performance improvements.

**Dan Shipper** said **dot** has become his primary interface to AI, with his dot named boo. ## 🎙 PODCASTS

**Takeaway**: The biggest AI opportunity may not be building new startups but buying old incumbents and refounding them around frontier engineering.

On **No Priors**, Michael Lee, co-founder and CEO of **Sequence Holdings**, joined to discuss the largest AI take-private to date: a $7,700,000,000 deal with the Dell family office for **Baldwin**. Lee explained that Sequence is a permanent holding company that partners with management teams to buy and refound businesses as market leaders with AI, doing roughly one deal per year.

Lee traced the thesis back to 2017 at Lone Pine, when he first covered AI around the time of AlphaGo and the first transformer paper. When ChatGPT arrived at the end of 2022, he concluded the world had changed because there was finally an architecture that could scale with compute. He felt AI would have an uneven impact: some industries like restaurants and golf courses would be untouched, some like coding would be won by startups, but others where incumbents hold brand, scale, network effects, or regulatory advantages could be transformed by acquiring the right incumbent.

He laid out why the three obvious alternatives fail. Doing it yourself makes it nearly impossible to recruit and retain the talent, because every company celebrates a persona, and in an AI world the celebrated persona must be the engineer. Using services firms like Accenture, McKinsey, or Palantir runs into an incentives problem, since they optimize for getting in your wallet, staying there, and growing share of wallet, which leads to incrementalism. Buying software means buying beta available to everyone, and software is always sold around the workflow as designed today, never around a new human assembly line that does not yet exist. Ownership, a culture that celebrates engineers, and a long-term horizon solve all three.

On **BankSouth**, Lee said the regulated nature of banking was a feature, not a bug: data hygiene is excellent and rules are well defined, which works well for agents. He also values centralized operations, since underwriting happens centrally and anything built at headquarters amortizes across all branches. He described **Atlas**, Sequence's shared platform, with four layers: a data ontology that makes the business legible, an agent builder grounded in ground truth, **Lattice** for orchestration, and artifacts as the application builder on top. He estimated 80% of any business is largely homogenous and 20% is vertically specific.

His most memorable line captured the cultural shift required: "In a world where you believe that alpha comes from engineering and AI, you need to create a culture whereby the celebrated persona is the engineer, and that's what's required." headline: The AI Take-Private Era Begins
deck: Sequence Holdings bets $7.7B that incumbents win the AI race, while builders debate whether agents need human interfaces at all and OpenAI races to simplify ChatGPT.
quote: In a world where you believe that alpha comes from engineering and AI, you need to create a culture whereby the celebrated persona is the engineer, and that's what's required.
quoteBy: Michael Lee · Co-Founder and CEO, Sequence Holdings

## 🧭 Daily Insights

**Core insight**: The AI conversation today centers on two converging threads: how established companies transform themselves for the AI era (not just adopt tools, but reorganize around agents), and how the interfaces we use to interact with AI are being fundamentally rethought. Builders are questioning whether traditional UIs even matter when agents can access capabilities directly, while investors are betting billions that incumbents with the right engineering culture will dominate.

## 𝕏 / TWITTER

**Thibault Sottiaux** announced an aggressive shipping cadence for **Codex** and ChatGPT: over the next 28 days, the team will either ship one clear improvement relevant to most codex/work users daily, or ship a full reset. The commitment signals OpenAI's push to rapidly iterate on developer tooling.

**Peter Yang** shared his critique of ChatGPT's complexity, arguing the product has "become a mess" with confusing distinctions between **Work** vs. **Codex**, **Spaces** vs. **Pages** vs. **Sites**, and the model/effort picker. His hot take: the entire Work launch was a mistake, similar to how Anthropic folded **Cowork** back into Chat. He also interviewed Sam, co-founder of **Granola**, who discussed accepting that users may skip the UI entirely and access the product through **MCP** for internal agent workflows. Sam noted: "As soon as you become a big enough enterprise, it's inevitable you have all of this internal tooling. If Granola doesn't play nice with that internal tooling, then it's a non-starter." On building: "The easier it gets to build stuff, the more it matters to really sweat the details and go the extra mile."

**Guillermo Rauch** highlighted performance improvements to **Vercel**, noting that as models speed up (like **Astra ultrafast**), harness overhead matters more. He also weighed in on the Rust vs. Go debate, revealing Vercel migrated **Turborepo** from Go to Rust but found the ROI "quite controversial internally" due to human migration costs. His key insight: "What's 'best for humans' is no longer necessarily 'best for business'" now that agents write code. He also shared a design principle: READMEs should be hand-written for humans, while documentation internals can be "AI English" for agents.

**Aaron Levie** outlined the new jobs AI is creating: AI engineers building applied products, **FDEs** deploying agents into companies, and services firms for AI deployment. He noted that published stats undercount existing jobs transitioning to AI work, with banks, life sciences companies, manufacturers, and law firms all bringing on more technical talent for agent deployment. He also cautioned that a consumer AI metric may reflect business model dynamics more than AI progress, predicting consumer AI will be "subsidized and monetized via commerce, ads, or purchases of devices."

**Ryo Lu** teased a new design project featuring "full bleed desktop + side dock" and a "lil computer in your pocket."

**Garry Tan** observed that when everyone builds the same primitives, it signals intensifying needs, and predicted eventual convergence on "the correct OS."

**Matt Turck** emphasized that "models are grown, not built" and we don't really know how they work, underscoring the urgent need for better interpretability, referencing Eric Ho of **GoodfireAI**.

**Zara Zhang** praised **Opus 5.5** for silently working for 20+ minutes and returning with "a complete masterpiece." She also noted that X profiles are replacing resumes.

**Nikunj Kothari** made the case for meeting founders at their offices rather than over Zoom, arguing there's "so much alpha" in seeing office energy, how cofounders interact, and beta product releases.

**Dan Shipper** shared that **dot** has become his primary AI interface, with his dot named "boo." He predicts that in a year he'll still interact with ChatGPT as an always-on persistent agent, but "boo will have disappeared," comparing it to early **OpenClaw** days when users loved personality quirks but dropped them for more powerful alternatives.

## 🎙 PODCASTS

**No Priors: Re-Founding Incumbents for the AI Era with Sequence Holdings Co-Founder and CEO Michael Lee**

**Takeaway**: The biggest AI opportunity isn't building new startups but acquiring and transforming incumbents who have brand, scale, and regulatory advantages that startups cannot replicate.

Michael Lee, co-founder and CEO of **Sequence Holdings**, discussed his company's $7.7 billion take-private of **Baldwin** with the Dell family office, the largest AI take-private to date. Sequence operates as a permanent holding company that acquires established businesses and "refounds" them around AI, bringing frontier engineering talent to industries where incumbents hold structural advantages.

Lee explained his investment thesis: AI will have an uneven impact on the economy. Some sectors like restaurants and golf courses won't be affected; others like coding will be won by startups. But in industries with brand, scale, network effects, or regulatory moats, incumbents have all the advantages. The key is acquiring the right incumbent and forging a market leader.

The core challenge for incumbents trying to transform: they can't recruit the engineering talent needed, and services firms have misaligned incentives. As Lee put it: "Services companies optimize for kind of three things: getting in your wallet, staying in your wallet, growing the share of your wallet. It is a path towards incrementalism." Buying software also fails because products are built for workflows as they exist today, not for reorganized human assembly lines.

Sequence's approach centers on ownership alignment, a culture that celebrates engineers, and long-term capital. Their platform, **Atlas**, has four layers: a data ontology that makes the business legible to models, an agent builder, an orchestration engine called **Lattice**, and an application builder called **Artifacts**. The insight: 80% of any business is largely homogenous, 20% is vertically specific.

On why banking was the perfect first investment: regulated institutions have well-defined operations and excellent data hygiene, making them ideal for agents. Banks are also centralized, so anything built at headquarters amortizes across all branches. Lee noted the "human engineering problem is much more difficult than the engineering problem," emphasizing the need to make employees feel elevated rather than threatened.

## 🎙 PODCASTS

**Takeaway**: The biggest AI opportunity may not be selling software to incumbents but buying them outright and refounding them around engineering.

On No Priors, Michael Lee, co-founder and CEO of Sequence Holdings, explained the firm's permanent holding company model and its just-announced $7.7 billion take-private of Baldwin with the Dell family office, the largest AI take-private to date. Sequence started twenty months ago to partner with world class businesses and management teams, bringing frontier engineering to forge market leaders.

Lee's framework is a direct challenge to the vendor model. Most software companies push small machines to every human in the assembly line to speed up work, which he calls better than nothing. But when machines can work 24/7 and scale with electricity, the right answer is reorganizing what an organization should be. He laid out why incumbents are the better bet in certain industries: brand, scale, network effects, and regulatory advantages. Coding is a startup win, but buying an outsourced coding services business would be a terrible idea.

He was blunt about the three options for a Fortune 500 CEO trying to refound: do it yourself, which fails on recruiting and retaining talent; hire services firms like Accenture, McKinsey, or Palantir, which have an incentives problem because they optimize for getting in, staying in, and growing share of your wallet; or buy software, which is beta and sold to workflows as designed today. Ownership solves alignment, and a holding company aligns the duration of capital with sustained transformation.

The most striking line came on culture: "In a world where you believe that alpha comes from engineering and AI, you need to create a culture whereby the celebrated persona is the engineer, and that's what's required." He contrasted this with Blackstone, where the celebrated persona is the investor.

On why banking was the perfect first pilot, Lee said the regulated nature was a feature, not a bug: well-defined operations, excellent data hygiene, and centralized underwriting mean anything built at headquarters amortizes across all branches. He described Atlas, Sequence's shared platform, with four layers: a data ontology to make the business legible, an agent builder grounded in ground truth, Lattice for orchestration, and artifacts as the application builder. Roughly 80% of a business is homogenous and 20% vertically specific.

He also admitted the human engineering problem is much harder than the engineering problem, and that post-investment they learned to be hyper-attuned to employee anxiety, framing AI as elevating what people do and removing rote work. On insurance brokerage, he noted $2 trillion plus in annual premiums, 90% gross retention, and the fact that the carrier, not the customer, pays the broker, making it a hard market for startups to crack.

**Aaron Levie** said we are already seeing what kind of new jobs AI is creating, including AI engineers building applied products, forward deployed engineers deploying agents into companies, and new services firms. He noted that published stats undercount existing jobs transitioning to AI work, and that every bank, life sciences company, manufacturer, and law firm is bringing on more technical talent or repositioning roles for agent deployment. He also commented that a certain metric may tell us more about the business model of consumer AI than the state of AI, since consumer AI will almost inevitably be subsidized and monetized via commerce, ads, or device purchases.

**Nikunj Kothari** expressed disbelief at how people make investments over a Zoom call or by just meeting the CEO, arguing there is alpha in meeting founders at their own office to see office energy, how coworkers interact, how cofounders complement each other, and what beta product releases look like. He always asks to meet at offices for final meetings and founders often tell him he is the only one who has ever asked.
