He predicted that in a year he will still be interacting with ChatGPT as an always-on persistent agent, but boo will have disappeared, comparing it to early OpenClaw days when people loved personality quirks but dropped them as soon as something functionally more powerful was available.
https://x.com/danshipper/status/2106892868564431255

## 🎙 PODCASTS

**Takeaway**: The biggest AI opportunity may not be building new software but buying established companies and reorganizing them around AI from the ground up.

In this episode of No Priors, Michael Lee, co-founder and CEO of Sequence Holdings, explains why he started a permanent holding company to acquire and refound incumbent businesses for the AI era. Sequence just announced the largest AI take-private to date with the Dell family office of Baldwin for $7.7 billion.

Lee walks through his thesis: AI will have an uneven impact on the economy. Some industries like restaurants and golf courses will barely be touched. Others like coding will be won by startups. But there is a category where incumbents have all the advantages, whether brand, scale, network effects, or regulatory moats, and those are the targets. The idea is to acquire the right incumbent, inherit those advantages, and forge the market leader by reorganizing the entire operation around what AI makes possible.

He is blunt about why the standard playbook fails. Companies try to refound themselves but cannot recruit the talent. They hire services firms, but those firms optimize for getting in your wallet and staying there, a path toward incrementalism. They buy software, but software is beta and sold to workflows as they are designed today, not around a new human assembly line that does not exist yet. Ownership solves the alignment problem.

The conversation covers the BankSouth investment, where Sequence first operated as a service provider before becoming a permanent partner. Lee describes the night and day difference: as an owner, engineers take on more complexity because they will be there for the long term, employees feel supported, and the company can take a three, five, ten year orientation. He notes that the regulated nature of banking was a feature, not a bug, because data hygiene is excellent and rules are well defined, which works extremely well for agents.

On the platform side, Lee describes Atlas, their shared infrastructure with four layers: a data ontology that makes the business legible to models, an agent builder grounded in ground truth, an orchestration engine called Lattice, and an application builder called Artifacts. The observation from engineers with Scale AI and Palantir backgrounds is that 80% of any business is largely homogenous and 20% is vertically specific, so the core infrastructure is reusable across companies.

The most striking moment comes when Lee explains the cultural requirement for this kind of transformation:

> "In a world where you believe that alpha comes from engineering and AI, you need to create a culture whereby the celebrated persona is the engineer."

He contrasts this with Blackstone, where the celebrated persona is the investor, which is why they aggregate the greatest investors. Sequence is trying to do the same for engineers, and that is what attracts talent from places like Scale AI and Palantir. The human engineering problem, as Lee calls it, is much harder than the technical one, and the playbook is still being refined.

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TCpRwJBQvW0

keywords: AI agents | incumbent AI | refounding
headline: The AI Takeover of Old Economy Incumbents
deck: Sequence Holdings bets $7.7B on refounding an insurance broker, while builders debate whether AI creates jobs or just reshapes them, and whether models are grown rather than built.
quote: In a world where you believe that alpha comes from engineering and AI, you need to create a culture whereby the celebrated persona is the engineer.
quoteBy: Michael Lee · Co-Founder and CEO of Sequence Holdings

## 🧭 Daily Insights
**Core insight**: Builders are converging on the idea that AI's biggest opportunity is not greenfield startups but refounding existing enterprises, with Sequence Holdings' $7.7B take-private of Baldwin as the flagship example. At the same time, the conversation is shifting from raw model capability to the messy human and organizational work of deploying agents inside real companies, and to the interpretability problem that we still do not really understand how models work.

## 𝕏 / TWITTER
Thibault Sottiaux, working on Codex and ChatGPT at OpenAI, announced a 28-day shipping cadence: each day the team will either ship one clear improvement relevant to most Codex and work users, or ship a full reset.

Peter Yang, who makes practical AI tutorials and interviews, argued that ChatGPT has become a mess and needs simplifying, pointing to Work vs. Codex, Spaces vs. Pages vs. Sites, and the model and effort picker. He called the whole Work launch a mistake, comparing it to Claude folding Cowork back into Chat. He also shared Sam, co-founder of Granola, on people skipping the UI to use the MCP: "There's definitely a pang of sadness to that as a UI designer... At this point we're at peace with the fact that for a bunch of workflows, the best way to use Granola is to capture the context, then use it through your internal agent." Sam added that the easier it gets to build, the more it matters to sweat the details and ask whether the person actually gets daily value.

Guillermo Rauch, CEO of Vercel, said it is hard to fathom Vercel getting faster but it now is much faster, noting that as models speed up, harness overhead matters more, with the next release improving session storage and retrieval plus cloud durability in libfx. He also weighed in on Rust, saying DHH is fundamentally right and that Vercel has been undergoing a Rust-ification, with the Turborepo migration from Go to Rust having controversial ROI because of human migration costs. He argued the calculus has changed: what is best for humans is no longer necessarily best for business, and Rust itself predates the supersonic tsunami of agents. He also described a new project where the README is fully written by hand for human consumption while the documentation internals are AI English for agents.

Aaron Levie, CEO of Box, said we are already seeing what kinds of new jobs AI creates: AI engineers building applied products, FDEs deploying agents, and new services firms, plus existing data, research, and software roles being repositioned for AI work across banks, life sciences, manufacturers, and law firms. He also argued a certain consumer AI metric may tell us more about the business model than the state of AI, since consumer AI will almost inevitably be subsidized and monetized via commerce, ads, or device purchases.

Ryo Lu, who designed Cursor, Notion, and Stripe, shared progress on a full-bleed desktop with a side dock, describing it as a little computer in your pocket.

Garry Tan, President and CEO of Y Combinator, noted that when everyone is building the same primitives it speaks to needs that will only intensify, and that we will eventually converge on the correct OS.

Matt Turck, a VC at FirstMark Capital and host of the MAD Podcast, highlighted that models are grown, not built, and we do not really know how they work, hence the urgent need for better interpretability, citing Eric Ho of Goodfire AI.

Zara Zhang, a builder, observed that Opus 5.5 silently goes off to make something for 20+ minutes and comes back with a complete masterpiece, and that X profiles are replacing resumes.

Nikunj Kothari, a partner at FPV Ventures, made the case for meeting founders at their own office rather than over Zoom, saying there is alpha in seeing the office energy, how coworkers interact, how cofounders complement each other, and what beta product releases look like.

Peter Steinberger, who works on OpenClaw and OpenAI, posted about bug fixes and performance improvements.

Dan Shipper, CEO of Every, said dot has become his primary interface to AI over the last few weeks, with his dot named boo. He bets that in a year he will still interact this way with ChatGPT as an always-on persistent agent, but boo will have disappeared, comparing it to early OpenClaw days when people loved the personality quirks of their Claws but dropped them as soon as something functionally more powerful arrived.

## 🎙 PODCASTS
**Takeaway**: The biggest AI opportunity may not be building new startups but buying and refounding incumbents, because ownership solves the incentive problem that services firms and software vendors cannot.

On No Priors, Michael Lee, co-founder and CEO of Sequence Holdings, joined to discuss the largest AI take-private to date: a $7,700,000,000 deal with the Dell family office for Baldwin, an insurance broker. Sequence is a permanent holding company that works with management teams to buy and refound businesses to be market leaders with AI, doing roughly one deal per year.

Lee traced the idea back to his time at Lone Pine in 2017, when he first covered AI around AlphaGo and the first transformer paper, and to the moment ChatGPT arrived at the end of 2022, when it became obvious the world had forever changed because here was an architecture that could scale infinitely with compute. He felt AI would have an uneven impact on the economy: some industries like restaurants and golf courses would barely be touched, some like coding would be won by startups, but others where incumbents hold brand, scale, network effects, or regulatory advantages could be transformed by acquiring the right incumbent and inheriting those advantages.

He laid out why the three obvious paths for a Fortune 500 CEO trying to refound fail. Doing it yourself makes it impossible to recruit and retain the talent, because every company has a celebrated persona, and in a world where alpha comes from engineering, the celebrated persona must become the engineer. Partnering with services firms like Accenture, McKinsey, or Palantir runs into an incentives problem, since services companies optimize for getting in your wallet, staying in your wallet, and growing share of wallet, which leads to incrementalism. Buying software is available to everybody and is always sold around the workflow as it is designed today, never around a new human assembly line that does not exist yet.

The BankSouth investment came about as a cold-start solution: Sequence took on a customer, a bank owned by the family of a friend, operated in a services motion from August to late November, and then became a permanent partner, closing in March after Fed and OCC approval. Lee said the regulated nature of a bank was a feature, not a bug, because operations are well defined, data hygiene is excellent, and the business is centralized, so anything built at headquarters gets amortized across all branches. He contrasted this with roll-ups, which require integrating different systems, sending engineers to many places, and standardizing procedures and cultures.

He described Atlas, Sequence's shared platform, with four layers: a data ontology that makes the business legible to models, an agent builder grounded in ground truth, Lattice as an orchestration engine for instrumenting workflows, and artifacts as an application builder on top. He estimated that 80% of a business is largely homogenous and 20% is vertically specific, which is why the core infrastructure built at the bank is reusable at Baldwin and beyond. He also noted that the human engineering problem is much more difficult than the engineering problem, and that making employees feel elevated rather than anxious is central to the playbook.

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TCpRwJBQvW0

Doing it yourself makes it nearly impossible to recruit and retain the talent, because every company has a celebrated persona, and if alpha comes from engineering, the celebrated persona must become the engineer. Lee added that Sequence has two problems, an engineering problem and a human engineering problem, and the human one is much more difficult, because transformation brings anxiety and the job is to make people feel their work is elevated rather than replaced.

Dan Shipper, CEO of Every, said his dot named boo has become his primary interface to AI, predicting he will still interact this way with ChatGPT as an always-on persistent agent in a year, but boo will have disappeared, much like early OpenClaw personalities were dropped once something more powerful arrived.

## 🎙 PODCASTS
**Takeaway**: The biggest AI opportunity may be buying and re-founding incumbents, not building startups, because ownership aligns incentives in a way services and software cannot.

On No Priors, Michael Lee, co-founder and CEO of Sequence Holdings, discussed the firm's $7.7 billion take-private of Baldwin with the Dell family office, the largest AI take-private to date. Sequence is a permanent holding company that partners with management teams to buy and re-found businesses as market leaders with AI. Lee explained that when ChatGPT arrived, he saw an architecture that could scale infinitely, and concluded AI would have an uneven impact: some industries startups would win, like coding, but others favor incumbents with brand, scale, network effects, or regulation. He laid out why a Fortune 500 CEO cannot simply refound alone: it is nearly impossible to recruit and retain the talent, because every company has a celebrated persona, and in a world where alpha comes from engineering, the celebrated persona must become the engineer. Vendors optimize for getting in your wallet and staying there, and software is always sold around the workflow as designed today, so it cannot reorganize the human assembly line. Ownership solves this. He described the BankSouth partnership as the perfect pilot: a regulated institution has well-defined operations and excellent data hygiene, which works extremely well for agents, and its centralized underwriting means anything built at headquarters amortizes across all branches. He contrasted this with roll-ups, which require integrating systems and standardizing cultures. On insurance brokerage, he noted $2 trillion plus in annual premiums, 90% gross retention, and the fact that the carrier, not the customer, pays the broker, making it hard for startups to enter. Sequence's shared platform, **Atlas**, has four layers: a data ontology, an agent builder, an orchestration engine called **Lattice**, and an application builder called **artifacts**. He estimated 80% of any business is largely homogenous and 20% vertically specific. On the human side, he said the human engineering problem is much harder than the engineering problem, and the key is making employees feel their jobs are elevated and their organization is winning. As he put it: "In a world where you believe that alpha comes from engineering and AI, you need to create a culture whereby the celebrated persona is the engineer, and that's what's required."

keywords: Codex reset | agent deployment | AI jobs
headline: Codex Ships Daily, Agents Reshape the Enterprise
deck: OpenAI promises 28 days of Codex improvements as builders debate bloated interfaces, while a $7.7B take-private shows AI eating the old economy from the inside.
quote: Every company on the planet has a celebrated persona. In a world where you believe that alpha comes from engineering and AI, you need to create a culture whereby the celebrated persona is the engineer, and that's what's required.
quoteBy: Michael Lee · Co-Founder and CEO, Sequence Holdings

## 🧭 Daily Insights

**Core insight**: Builders are converging on the same conclusion: the harness around the model now matters as much as the model itself. OpenAI is promising 28 straight days of Codex improvements or full resets, Vercel is racing to cut agent overhead, and investors are debating whether AI creates more jobs than it replaces. Meanwhile, the biggest thread is that AI transformation is moving from demos into the messy work of reorganizing real companies.

## 𝕏 / TWITTER

**Thibault Sottiaux** announced a public 28-day cadence for **Codex** and ChatGPT: each day OpenAI will either ship one clear improvement relevant to most Codex and work users, or ship a full reset. The framing is unusually aggressive, treating the product as something to be rebuilt in public rather than polished behind closed doors.

**Peter Yang** argued that ChatGPT has become a mess and that OpenAI is right to simplify it. His list: collapse **Work** versus **Codex**, untangle **Spaces** versus **Pages** versus **Sites**, and rethink the model and effort picker. His hot take is that the whole **Work** launch was a mistake, comparing it to Claude folding **Cowork** back into Chat, since he does not think Work needs its own brand. He also shared an interview with Sam, co-founder of **Granola**, who admitted there is a pang of sadness when people skip the UI and just use the **MCP**. Granola fought that for a while, but as an enterprise grows, internal tooling makes it inevitable: if Granola does not play nice with that tooling, it is a non-starter. Sam's advice on building: the easier it gets to build, the more it matters to sweat the details, and the real question is whether the person gets daily value out of it.

**Guillermo Rauch** said it is hard to fathom **vLLM** getting faster, but it now is much faster, and as models speed up, harness overhead matters more and more. The next release will improve session storage and retrieval plus cloud durability in **libfx**. He also weighed in on Rust, saying DHH is fundamentally right and that Vercel has been undergoing a Rust-ification, starting with migrating **Turborepo** from Go to Rust. The ROI was controversial internally because the human migration costs were substantive, but the calculus has changed: what is best for humans is no longer necessarily best for business, and Rust itself was designed before the supersonic tsunami of agents. On a new project, he is writing the **README** fully by hand because it is for human consumption, while the documentation internals are AI English because they are for agents.

**Aaron Levie** said we are starting to see what kinds of new jobs AI creates. AI needs significant technical work and surrounding services to deploy into the economy, which means jobs for AI engineers building applied products, **FDEs** deploying agents into companies, and new services firms. Published stats undercount existing roles being repositioned toward AI work, and every bank, life sciences company, manufacturer, and law firm is bringing on more technical talent for agent deployment. He also cautioned that a consumer AI metric may say more about the business model than the state of AI, since consumer AI will almost inevitably be subsidized and monetized via commerce, ads, or device purchases.

**Ryo Lu** shared a small design update: full bleed desktop plus a side dock, describing it as a little computer in your pocket.

**Garry Tan** observed that when everyone is building the same primitives, it speaks to needs that will only intensify, and predicted we will eventually converge on the correct OS.

**Matt Turck** highlighted one of the most poorly understood aspects of AI outside AI circles: models are grown, not built, and we do not really know how they work, hence the urgent need for better interpretability, citing Eric Ho of **Goodfire**.

**Zara Zhang** noted that **Opus 5.5** will silently go off to make something for 20+ minutes and come back with a complete masterpiece. She also observed that X profiles are replacing resumes.

**Nikunj Kothari** said he cannot believe how people make investments over a Zoom call, sometimes by just meeting the CEO. There is alpha in meeting founders at their own office: you see the energy, how coworkers react, how cofounders complement each other, and what beta releases look like. He always asks to meet at offices for final meetings, and founders often tell him he is the only one who has ever asked.

**Dan Shipper** said **dot** has become his primary interface to AI over the last few weeks, and his dot is named boo. He bets that in a year he will still interact with ChatGPT as an always-on persistent agent, but boo will have disappeared, much like early **OpenClaw** days when people loved the personality quirks of their Claws but dropped them as soon as something functionally more powerful arrived.

## 🎙 PODCASTS

**Takeaway**: The biggest AI opportunity may not be building new startups but buying old incumbents and refounding them around frontier engineering.

On **No Priors**, Michael Lee, co-founder and CEO of **Sequence Holdings**, joined to discuss the largest AI take-private to date: a $7,700,000,000 deal with the Dell family office for **Baldwin**. Sequence is a permanent holding company that works with management teams to buy and refound businesses to be market leaders with AI, doing roughly one deal per year.

Lee's core argument is that most enterprises are getting AI wrong. They are handing small machines to every human on the assembly line to speed up existing work, which he calls better than nothing but not the point. When machines can work 24/7, scale with electricity, and accomplish what no group of humans can, the right answer is to reorganize what the organization should be. He laid out why incumbents win in certain industries through brand, scale, network effects, and regulation, and why a startup would never buy an outsourced coding business when you would just fund Cognition or Anthropic instead.

He walked through the three options a Fortune 500 CEO has for refounding: do it yourself, which fails because you cannot recruit and retain the talent; hire a services firm like Accenture, McKinsey, or Palantir, which has an incentives problem since they optimize for getting in your wallet, staying there, and growing their share of it; or buy software, which is beta and always sold around the workflow as it is designed today. Sequence's answer is ownership plus a platform called **Atlas**, built at their first investment, a Georgia bank. Atlas has four layers: a data ontology that makes the business legible to models, an agent builder grounded in ground truth, an orchestration engine called **Lattice**, and an application builder called **artifacts**. Lee estimates 80% of any business is largely homogenous and 20% is vertically specific, which is why the core infrastructure is reusable across Baldwin and future companies.

His most memorable line was about culture: "Every company on the planet has a celebrated persona. In a world where you believe that alpha comes from engineering and AI, you need to create a culture whereby the celebrated persona is the engineer, and that's what's required." He also noted that the regulated nature of a bank was a feature, not a bug, because data hygiene is excellent and rules are well defined, which works extremely well for agents. On the human side, he admitted the human engineering problem is much harder than the engineering problem, and that Sequence has learned to be hyper attuned to employee anxiety, framing the work as elevating what people do rather than replacing them.

headline: AI's Next Act: Rebuilding the Incumbents
deck: OpenAI promises 28 days of Codex shipping while a $7.7B take-private bets that AI's real prize is refounding existing companies, not just building new ones.
quote: The easier it gets to build stuff, the more it matters to really sweat the details and go the extra mile.
quoteBy: Sam · co-founder of Granola

## 🧭 Daily Insights
**Core insight**: Builders are converging on a single question: now that models can do the work, what should the product around them actually look like? OpenAI is promising 28 straight days of Codex improvements, while investors argue the bigger prize is refounding existing enterprises rather than launching new startups. The consensus forming is that harness, interface, and organizational design now matter more than raw model capability.

## 𝕏 / TWITTER
Thibault Sottiaux, who works on Codex and ChatGPT at OpenAI, announced a 28-day shipping cadence: each day the team will either ship one clear improvement relevant to most **Codex** and work users, or ship a full reset. He framed it simply as letting the improvements begin.

Peter Yang, who writes practical AI tutorials and interviews, argued that OpenAI is right to simplify **ChatGPT** because it has become a mess. He listed what he would cut: the split between **Work** and **Codex**, the tangle of **Spaces** versus **Pages** versus **Sites**, and the model and effort picker. His hot take is that the whole Work launch was a mistake, comparing it to Claude folding **Cowork** back into Chat, and he is glad his primary harness will get better. He also shared a clip from his interview with Sam, co-founder of **Granola**, who admitted there is a pang of sadness when people skip the UI and just use the **MCP**, but that at enterprise scale it is inevitable: the best way to use Granola for many workflows is to capture context and then use it through an internal agent. Sam added that the easier it gets to build, the more it matters to sweat the details, and that builders should hold themselves accountable not just to shipping but to whether the person gets daily value.

Guillermo Rauch, CEO of Vercel, noted that a tool has gotten much faster as models speed up, and that harness overhead matters more and more as models like **Astra ultrafast** arrive, with the next release bringing better session storage and retrieval plus a cloud durability unlock in **libfx**. He also weighed in on the Rust debate, saying DHH is fundamentally right and that Vercel has been undergoing a Rust-ification, with **Turborepo** migrated from Go to Rust, though the ROI was internally controversial because of human migration costs. He argued the calculus has changed now that what is best for humans is no longer necessarily best for business, and that Rust itself predates the supersonic tsunami of agents. Separately, he described a new project where the **README** is fully hand-written for human consumption while the documentation internals are AI English for agents, a rule of thumb he thinks can make the world better.

Aaron Levie, CEO of Box, said we are starting to see what kinds of new jobs AI creates: AI engineers building applied products, forward deployed engineers deploying **agents** into companies, and new services firms. He noted published stats undercount existing roles being repositioned toward AI work, with every bank, life sciences company, manufacturer, and law firm bringing on more technical talent. He also argued a widely cited consumer AI metric may say more about the business model of consumer AI than the state of AI, since consumer AI will almost inevitably be subsidized and monetized via commerce, ads, or device purchases, and may level off lower than people think.

Ryo Lu, who designed at Cursor, Notion, and Stripe, shared a small update on a project: full bleed desktop plus side dock, describing it as a little computer in your pocket.

Garry Tan, President and CEO of Y Combinator, observed that when everyone is building the same primitives it speaks to needs that will only intensify, and that the field will eventually converge on the correct OS.

Matt Turck, a VC at FirstMark Capital and host of the MAD Podcast, flagged what he considers the most poorly understood aspect of AI outside AI circles: that models are grown, not built, and we do not really know how they work, which is why better interpretability matters, citing Eric Ho of Goodfire AI.

Zara Zhang, a builder, marveled that **Opus 5.5** silently goes off to make something for 20+ minutes and comes back with a complete masterpiece. She also noted that X profiles are replacing resumes.

Nikunj Kothari, a partner at FPV Ventures, made the case for meeting founders at their own office rather than over Zoom, arguing there is alpha in seeing office energy, how coworkers interact, how cofounders complement each other, and what beta product releases look like. He said he always asks to meet at offices for final meetings and founders often tell him he is the only one who has ever asked.

Peter Steinberger, who works on OpenClaw and with OpenAI, posted a brief note about bug fixes and performance improvements.

Dan Shipper, CEO of Every, said **dot** has become his primary interface to AI over the last few weeks, with his dot named boo. He bets that in a year he will still be interacting this way with ChatGPT as an always-on persistent agent, but boo will have disappeared, comparing it to early OpenClaw days when people loved the personality quirks of their Claws but dropped them as soon as something functionally more powerful arrived.

## 🎙 PODCASTS
**Takeaway**: The biggest AI opportunity may not be building new startups but buying established companies and refounding them around frontier engineering.

On No Priors, Michael Lee, co-founder and CEO of Sequence Holdings, joined to discuss the largest AI take-private to date: a $7,700,000,000 deal with the Dell family office for Baldwin, an insurance brokerage. Sequence is a permanent holding company that partners with management teams to buy and refound businesses as market leaders with AI, doing roughly one deal per year.

Lee traced the thesis back to his time at Lone Pine starting in 2017, when he covered AI around the AlphaGo era and the first transformer paper. When ChatGPT arrived at the end of 2022, he concluded the world had permanently changed because here was an architecture that could scale with compute. He felt AI would have an uneven impact on the economy: some sectors like restaurants and golf courses would barely be touched, while others like coding would be won by startups. But in industries where incumbents hold advantages of brand, scale, network effects, or regulation, he believed the winning move was to acquire the right incumbent and forge the market leader.

He laid out why the holding company structure was the only natural fit: it aligns the duration of capital with sustained transformation, builds a culture oriented around forging leaders rather than deploying capital, and lets retained earnings fund both existing companies and new investments. He argued a Fortune 500 CEO trying to refound has three bad options: do it yourself, which fails on recruiting and retaining talent; hire services firms like Accenture, McKinsey, or Palantir, which optimize for getting in, staying in, and growing share of your wallet; or buy software, which is available to everyone and is always sold around the workflow as it exists today, never around a human assembly line that does not yet exist.

The most memorable line came on culture: "Every company on the planet has a celebrated persona. In a world where you believe that alpha comes from engineering and AI, you need to create a culture whereby the celebrated persona is the engineer, and that's what's required."

On BankSouth, Sequence's first investment, Lee explained it began as a services engagement with a friend's family-owned bank in Georgia, starting August 4 of last year, before becoming a permanent partnership closed in March after Fed and OCC approval. He said the regulated nature of banking was a feature, not a bug: operations are well defined, data hygiene is excellent, and rules are clear, which works extremely well for agents. He also values centralized operations, since underwriting happens centrally and anything built at headquarters amortizes across all branches. On Baldwin, he cited a $2,000,000,000,000 plus premiums market, 90% gross retention, and the fact that the carrier, not the customer, pays the broker, making it hard for startups to compete.

On the platform side, Lee described Atlas, built at the bank and expected to generalize: a data ontology layer to make the business legible, an agent builder grounded in ground truth, an orchestration engine called Lattice, and an application builder called Artifacts. He estimated 80% of any business is largely homogenous and 20% vertically specific. He closed by noting the human engineering problem is much harder than the engineering problem, and that Sequence must make employees feel the work elevates what they do rather than threatens it.

## 🎙 PODCASTS

**Takeaway**: The biggest AI opportunity isn't building new startups, it's buying incumbent businesses and refounding them around frontier engineering, with a permanent holding company structure that aligns long-term capital with deep operational transformation.

On No Priors, Michael Lee, co-founder and CEO of Sequence Holdings, discussed the company's $7.7 billion take-private of Baldwin with the Dell family office, the largest AI take-private to date. ## 🧭 Daily Insights

**Core insight**: Builders are converging on the idea that the hard part of AI is no longer the model but the harness, the organization, and the human details around it. Vercel is optimizing agent overhead as models get faster, OpenAI is promising 28 days of Codex improvements, and Sequence Holdings is buying whole incumbents to rebuild them around agents. The trend forming: agents are becoming infrastructure, and the winners are whoever reorganizes work, not just ships features.

## 𝕏 / TWITTER

Thibault Sottiaux, who works on Codex and ChatGPT at OpenAI, announced a 28-day cadence: each day OpenAI will either ship one clear improvement relevant to most Codex and work users, or ship a full reset. He framed it simply as "let the improvements begin."

Peter Yang, who makes practical AI tutorials and interviews, argued that OpenAI is right to simplify ChatGPT because it has become a mess. He listed what he would cut: Work versus Codex, Spaces versus Pages versus Sites, and the model and effort picker. His hot take is that the whole Work launch was a mistake, comparing it to Claude folding Cowork back into Chat, and he is excited to see his primary harness improve. He also shared an interview with Sam, co-founder of Granola, who admitted "there's definitely a pang of sadness" when people skip the Granola UI and use the MCP instead, but said the team made peace with it: for many workflows the best way to use Granola is to capture context and run it through an internal agent. Sam added that the easier it gets to build, the more it matters to sweat the details, and that builders should hold themselves accountable not just to shipping but to whether the person actually gets daily value out of it.

Guillermo Rauch, CEO of Vercel, said it is hard to fathom the platform getting even faster, but it now is much faster, noting that as models speed up, as with Astra ultrafast, harness overhead matters more and more. The next release will feature better session storage and retrieval plus a big unlock for cloud durability in libfx. He also weighed in on Rust, saying DHH is fundamentally right and that Vercel has been undergoing a Rust-ification, with Turborepo migrated from Go to Rust, though the ROI was controversial internally because of human migration costs. His key point: what is best for humans is no longer necessarily best for business, and Rust itself was designed before the supersonic tsunami of agents. Separately, he described a new project where the README is fully written by hand because it is for human consumption, while the documentation internals are AI English because they are for agents.

Aaron Levie, CEO of Box, said we are already seeing what kinds of new jobs AI creates: AI engineers building applied products, forward deployed engineers deploying agents into companies, and new services firms. He noted published stats undercount existing roles being repositioned for AI work, and that every bank, life sciences company, manufacturer, and law firm is bringing on more technical talent for agent deployment. In a second post he argued a certain metric may say more about the business model of consumer AI than the state of AI, since consumer AI will almost inevitably be subsidized and monetized via commerce, ads, or device purchases, and may level off lower than people think.

Ryo Lu, who designed Cursor, Notion, and Stripe, shared a bit more work on a full bleed desktop with a side dock, describing it as a little computer in your pocket.

Garry Tan, President and CEO of Y Combinator, observed that when everyone is building the same primitives it speaks to needs that will only intensify, and that we will eventually converge on the correct OS.

Matt Turck, a VC at FirstMark Capital and host of the MAD Podcast, flagged one aspect of AI that is poorly understood outside AI circles: models are grown, not built, and we do not really know how they work, hence the urgent need for better interpretability, citing Eric Ho of Goodfire AI.

Zara Zhang, a builder, marveled that Opus 5.5 silently goes off to make something for 20+ minutes and comes back with a complete masterpiece. She also noted that X profiles are replacing resumes.

Nikunj Kothari, a partner at FPV Ventures, said he cannot believe how people make investments over a Zoom call or by just meeting the CEO, arguing there is alpha in meeting founders at their own office to see office energy, how coworkers interact, how cofounders complement each other, and what beta product releases look like. He always asks to meet at offices for final meetings and founders often tell him he is the only one who has ever asked.

Peter Steinberger, who works on OpenClaw and with OpenAI, posted briefly about bug fixes and performance improvements.

Dan Shipper, CEO of Every, said dot has become his primary interface to AI over the last few weeks, and his dot is named boo. He bets that in a year he will still be interacting this way with ChatGPT as an always-on persistent agent, but boo will have disappeared, comparing it to early OpenClaw days when people loved the personality quirks of their Claws but dropped them as soon as something functionally more powerful arrived.

## 🎙 PODCASTS

**Takeaway**: The biggest AI opportunity may not be building new startups but buying incumbents and refounding them around agents, because ownership aligns incentives in a way that services contracts and software licenses never can.

On No Priors, Michael Lee, co-founder and CEO of Sequence Holdings, joined to discuss the largest AI take-private to date: a $7,700,000,000 deal with the Dell family office for Baldwin, an insurance brokerage. Sequence is a permanent holding company that partners with management teams to buy and refound businesses as market leaders with AI, doing roughly one deal per year.

Lee traced the thesis back to his time at Lone Pine starting in 2017, when he was asked to cover AI around the AlphaGo and first transformer era. When ChatGPT arrived at the end of 2022, he concluded the world had forever changed because we finally had an architecture that could scale with compute. He expected AI's impact on the economy to be uneven: restaurants and golf courses would barely change, while coding would be won by startups. But in industries where the incumbent holds brand, scale, network effects, or regulatory advantages, he saw the opposite play: acquire the right incumbent, inherit its advantages, and forge the market leader.

His critique of the alternatives is sharp. Doing it yourself fails because you cannot recruit and retain the talent, and the reason is cultural: every company has a celebrated persona, and at Blackstone it is the investor, which is why they aggregate the greatest investors. In a world where alpha comes from engineering, the celebrated persona has to be the engineer. Services firms like Accenture, McKinsey, and Palantir do celebrate the engineer, but they optimize for getting into your wallet, staying there, and growing share of wallet, which is a path to incrementalism and cannot change how people are organized or incentivized. Buying software has two problems: it is beta, available to everybody, and it is always sold around the workflow as designed today, because you cannot sell a product around a human assembly line that does not exist yet.

The BankSouth investment started as a services engagement in August, with Lee skipping his anniversary to kick it off, and became a permanent partnership closed in March after Fed and OCC approval. He said the difference between operating as a vendor and as an owner was night and day: as an owner you take on far more complexity and depth, employees get excited that you are staying, and you can lay a technological foundation over a three, five, ten year horizon. He called the regulated nature of a bank a feature, not a bug, because operations are well defined and data hygiene is excellent, which suits agents, and because banking is centralized: underwriting happens at headquarters, so anything built there amortizes across every branch. That is what Sequence calls organizational physics, dense organizations with centralized operations.

On the platform side, Sequence built Atlas at the bank and expects it to generalize. Lee's observation, drawn from engineers with Scale and Palantir backgrounds, is that 80% of a business is largely homogenous and 20% is vertically specific. Atlas has four layers: a data ontology that makes the business legible in code, an agent builder for high performance agents grounded in ground truth, an orchestration engine called Lattice, and an application builder called artifacts. The core infrastructure is reusable at Baldwin and beyond.

Asked why insurance brokerage, Lee pointed to a $2,000,000,000,000 plus market in annual premiums, an industry where incumbents hold the advantages, and a business where the customer does not even pay the broker, the carrier does, with gross retention rates around 90%. He also described the human side as the harder problem, joking that Sequence has an engineering problem and a human engineering problem, and the human one is much more difficult. The playbook there is making employees feel that AI elevates what they do, removes rote work, and makes their organization win.

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TCpRwJBQvW0

Builders are debating whether value accrues to greenfield startups or to incumbents that can be re-founded around engineering, and whether consumer AI is a real business or a subsidized one waiting on commerce and ads. Meanwhile, the tooling layer keeps consolidating: harnesses, interfaces, and agent platforms are being simplified and hardened as models get faster.

## 𝕏 / TWITTER

Thibault Sottiaux, working on Codex and ChatGPT at OpenAI, announced a 28-day cadence: each day the team will either ship one clear improvement relevant to most Codex and work users, or ship a full reset. It reads as a public accountability mechanism for a product surface that has been growing fast.

Peter Yang, who makes practical AI tutorials and interviews, argued that ChatGPT has become a mess and needs simplifying, naming three concrete targets: Work versus Codex, Spaces versus Pages versus Sites, and the model and effort picker. His hot take is that the whole Work launch was a mistake, comparing it to Claude folding Cowork back into Chat. He also shared a clip of Sam, co-founder of Granola, admitting a "pang of sadness" as a UI designer watching people skip the interface and use the MCP directly, and concluding that for many workflows the best way to use Granola is to capture context and then use it through an internal agent. Sam's other point: the easier it gets to build, the more it matters to sweat the details, and shipping version one is not the same as delivering daily value.
https://x.com/petergyang/status/2106926956554195018
https://x.com/petergyang/status/2106897211766530299
https://x.com/petergyang/status/2106825485624004691

Guillermo Rauch, CEO of Vercel, said it is hard to fathom the platform getting faster, but it now is much faster, noting that as models speed up, harness overhead matters more and more. He flagged that the next release will improve session storage and retrieval plus a big unlock for cloud durability in libfx. On Rust, he argued DHH is fundamentally right, describing Vercel's ongoing Rust-ification and the controversial migration of Turborepo from Go to Rust, where human migration costs were substantive even though Rust was better for low-level OS access. His conclusion: what is best for humans is no longer necessarily best for business, and Rust itself was designed before the "supersonic tsunami" of agents. He also described a new project where the README is fully hand-written for humans while internal documentation is AI English for agents.
https://x.com/rauchg/status/2106885457212825983
https://x.com/rauchg/status/2106863842450133114
https://x.com/rauchg/status/2106848085267902815

Aaron Levie, CEO of Box, laid out the new jobs AI is creating: AI engineers building applied products for enterprises, forward deployed engineers deploying agents into companies, and new services firms. He noted published stats undercount existing roles being repositioned toward AI work across banks, life sciences, manufacturers, and law firms. On a separate metric about consumer AI, he cautioned it may say more about the business model than the state of AI, since consumer AI will almost inevitably be subsidized and monetized via commerce, ads, or device purchases, and may level off lower than expected.
https://x.com/levie/status/2106893015063421357
https://x.com/levie/status/2106802940879192260

Matt Turck, VC at FirstMark Capital and host of the MAD Podcast, pointed to the most poorly understood aspect of AI outside AI circles: models are grown, not built, and we do not really know how they work, which is why better interpretability is urgent. He credited Eric Ho of Goodfire AI.
https://x.com/mattturck/status/2106821381765956044

Dan Shipper, CEO of Every, said dot has become his primary interface to AI over the last few weeks, with his dot named boo. He predicts that in a year he will still interact this way with ChatGPT as an always-on persistent agent, but boo will have disappeared, comparing it to early OpenClaw days when people loved the personality quirks of their Claws and dropped them as soon as something functionally more powerful arrived.
https://x.com/danshipper/status/2106892868564431255

Nikunj Kothari, partner at FPV Ventures, made the case for meeting founders at their own office rather than over Zoom, arguing there is alpha in seeing office energy, how coworkers interact, how cofounders complement each other, and what beta product releases look like. He said he always asks for offices for final meetings and founders often tell him he is the only one who has ever asked.
https://x.com/nikunj/status/2106957269212742135

Zara Zhang, a builder, observed that Opus 5.5 silently goes off to make something for 20+ minutes and comes back with a complete masterpiece, and separately noted that X profiles are replacing resumes.
https://x.com/zarazhangrui/status/2106876921082712250
https://x.com/zarazhangrui/status/2106782239493427588

Garry Tan, President and CEO of Y Combinator, noted that when everyone is building the same primitives it speaks to needs that will only intensify, and that the field will eventually converge on the correct OS.
https://x.com/garrytan/status/2106901111106097210

## 🎙 PODCASTS

**Takeaway**: The biggest AI opportunity may not be building new startups but buying incumbents and re-founding them around engineering, because ownership solves the incentive problem that services firms and software vendors cannot.

On No Priors, Michael Lee, co-founder and CEO of Sequence Holdings, explained the firm's model: a permanent holding company that partners with management teams to buy and re-found businesses as AI-era market leaders. Sequence just announced the largest AI take private to date with the Dell family office of Baldwin for $7,700,000,000, following its earlier investment in BankSouth.

Lee's core argument is that most enterprises are doing the equivalent of handing small machines to every human on the assembly line, which is better than nothing but misses the point. When machines can work 24/7 and scale with electricity, the right answer is to reorganize what an organization should be. He laid out why the three obvious paths fail: doing it yourself makes it nearly impossible to recruit and retain the talent, because every company has a celebrated persona and most celebrate the investor or operator rather than the engineer; services firms optimize for getting into your wallet, staying there, and growing share of wallet, which is a path to incrementalism; and buying software means buying beta available to everyone, built around the workflow as it exists today rather than a new human assembly line that does not exist yet. Ownership, he argued, aligns incentives, duration, and the ability to bring frontier engineering to bear.

On why banking was the perfect first target, Lee said the regulated nature of a bank was a feature, not a bug: operations are well defined, data hygiene is excellent, and the rules make it a good fit for agents. He also emphasized organizational physics, preferring dense organizations with centralized operations so anything built at headquarters amortizes across all branches, contrasting that with roll-ups that require integrating systems and standardizing cultures. The platform they built at the bank, Atlas, has four layers: a data ontology that makes the business legible to models, an agent builder grounded in ground truth, Lattice for orchestration, and artifacts as an application builder on top. He estimated that 80% of a business is largely homogenous and 20% is vertically specific, which is why he expects Atlas to generalize across industries.

The most memorable line came when Lee described the cultural precondition for this kind of transformation: "In a world where you believe that alpha comes from engineering and AI, you need to create a culture whereby the celebrated persona is the engineer, and that's what's required." He also admitted the human side is harder than the technical side, joking that Sequence has an engineering problem and a human engineering problem, and the human one is much more difficult, especially managing employee anxiety about what AI means for their roles.

His hot take: the whole Work launch was a mistake, much like Claude folded Cowork back into Chat, and he does not think Work needs its own brand. Sam's other point: "The easier it gets to build stuff, the more it matters to really sweat the details and go the extra mile," and builders should hold themselves accountable not just to shipping but to whether the person gets daily value.

He also weighed in on Rust, saying DHH is fundamentally right and that Vercel has been undergoing a Rust-ification, with Turborepo migrated from Go to Rust, though the ROI was controversial internally because of human migration costs. His conclusion: what is best for humans is no longer necessarily best for business, and Rust itself was designed before the supersonic tsunami of agents. Separately, he described a new project where the README is fully written by hand for human consumption while the documentation internals are AI English for agents, arguing blogs, tweets, and READMEs are the storytelling moment for connecting with other humans.

Aaron Levie, CEO of Box, said we are starting to see what kinds of new jobs AI creates: AI engineers building applied products, FDEs deploying agents into companies, and new services firms. He noted published stats undercount existing jobs transitioning into AI work, with banks, life sciences companies, manufacturers, and law firms bringing on more technical talent or repositioning roles for agent deployment. He also argued a certain metric may tell us more about the business model of consumer AI than the state of AI, since consumer AI will almost inevitably be subsidized and monetized via commerce, ads, or device purchases, and may level off lower than expected.

Ryo Lu, who designed Cursor, Notion, and Stripe, shared a bit more work: a full bleed desktop with a side dock, describing it as a little computer in your pocket.

Garry Tan, President and CEO of Y Combinator, observed that when everyone is building the same primitives, it speaks to needs that will only intensify, and that we will eventually converge on the correct OS.

Matt Turck, a VC at FirstMark Capital and host of the MAD Podcast, flagged one of the most poorly understood aspects of AI outside AI circles: models are grown, not built, and we do not really know how they work, hence the urgent need for better interpretability, citing Eric Ho of Goodfire AI.

Nikunj Kothari, a partner at FPV Ventures, said he cannot believe how people make investments over a Zoom call or by just meeting the CEO, arguing there is alpha in meeting founders at their own office to see office energy, how coworkers interact, how cofounders complement each other, and what beta releases look like. He always asks to meet at offices for final meetings, and founders often tell him he is the only one who has ever asked.

Peter Steinberger, who works on OpenClaw and OpenAI, posted simply about bug fixes and performance improvements.

Dan Shipper, CEO of Every, said dot has become his primary interface to AI over the last few weeks, and his dot is named boo. He bets that in a year he will still be interacting with ChatGPT as an always-on persistent agent, but boo will have disappeared, comparing it to early OpenClaw days when people loved the personality quirks of their Claws but dropped them as soon as something functionally more powerful arrived.

## 🎙 PODCASTS

**Takeaway**: The biggest AI opportunity may not be building new startups but buying incumbent companies and refounding them around frontier engineering.

On No Priors, Michael Lee, co-founder and CEO of Sequence Holdings, joined to discuss the firm's model and its largest AI take-private to date, a $7,700,000,000 deal with the Dell family office for Baldwin. Sequence is a permanent holding company that works with management teams to buy and refound businesses to be market leaders with AI, and Lee explained why ownership, not vendorship, is the only structure that aligns incentives for a multi-year transformation.

Lee traced the idea back to his time at Lone Pine in 2017, when he was asked to cover AI around the time of AlphaGo and the first transformer paper. When ChatGPT arrived at the end of 2022, he felt the world had forever changed because there was finally an architecture that could scale with compute. He reasoned that AI would have an uneven impact: some industries like restaurants and golf courses would barely change, some like coding would be won by startups, but others where incumbents hold brand, scale, network effects, or regulatory advantages could be transformed if you could acquire the right one.

The core argument is about culture and talent. "In a world where you believe that alpha comes from engineering and AI, you need to create a culture whereby the celebrated persona is the engineer," Lee said, using Blackstone as an example of a firm whose celebrated persona is the investor. He argued that a Fortune 500 CEO trying to refound has three options: do it yourself, which makes recruiting and retaining talent nearly impossible; hire services firms like Accenture, McKinsey, or Palantir, which optimize for getting into, staying in, and growing their share of your wallet; or buy software, which is available to everyone and always sells to a workflow as it is designed today. Sequence's answer is ownership plus a frontier engineering team plus a long-term horizon.

Lee described the BankSouth partnership as the perfect pilot. It began as a services engagement in August, became a permanent investment in March after Fed and OCC approval, and showed a night and day difference between operating as a vendor and as an owner. He called the regulated nature of a bank a feature, not a bug, because operations are well defined, data hygiene is excellent, and rules are clear, all of which works well for agents. He also emphasized organizational physics: Sequence likes dense, centralized organizations where anything built at headquarters gets amortized across all branches, unlike roll-ups that require integrating different systems and standardizing cultures.

On the platform side, Lee described Atlas, built at the bank and expected to generalize across industries. It has four layers: a data ontology that makes the business legible in code, an agent builder grounded in ground truth, an orchestration engine called Lattice, and an application builder called artifacts. He estimated that 80% of a business is largely homogenous and 20% is vertically specific. On the human side, he admitted the human engineering problem is much harder than the engineering problem, and that Sequence has learned to be hyper-attuned to employee anxiety, framing the goal as elevating what people do and removing rote work. On insurance brokerage, he noted it fits their criteria: a $2,000,000,000,000 plus premiums market, incumbents with advantages, 90% gross retention, and customers who do not even pay the broker, since the carrier does.

headline: The Great Refounding: AI Eats the Enterprise
deck: Incumbents get rebuilt from the inside while ChatGPT gets a hard reset. Meanwhile, builders debate what AI actually creates, and one firm bets $7.7B that ownership beats software.
quote: In a world where you believe that alpha comes from engineering and AI, you need to create a culture whereby the celebrated persona is the engineer.
quoteBy: Michael Lee · Co-Founder and CEO of Sequence Holdings

## 🧭 Daily Insights

**Core insight**: The conversation has split into two camps: those rebuilding existing institutions from the inside with AI, and those rebuilding their own products to survive the agent era. Michael Lee's $7.7B take-private of Baldwin shows the thesis that incumbents with centralized operations and regulatory moats are the best AI targets, while Thibault Sottiaux's 28-day shipping sprint at OpenAI signals that even the model makers feel the pressure to simplify and ship faster. The through-line: AI is no longer a feature layer, it is a forcing function for organizational and product redesign.

## 𝕏 / TWITTER

**Thibault Sottiaux** announced a 28-day sprint at OpenAI where each day the team will either ship one clear improvement relevant to most Codex and work users, or ship a full reset. The framing suggests internal recognition that the product has accumulated complexity and needs either incremental wins or a hard pivot. The "let the improvements begin" tone is confident but the reset option signals real stakes.

**Peter Yang** argued that ChatGPT has become a mess and praised OpenAI for focusing on simplification. His specific targets: the Work vs. Codex split, Spaces vs. Pages vs. Sites confusion, and the model and effort picker. His hot take is that the entire Work launch was a mistake, comparing it to Claude folding Cowork back into Chat. He also shared an interview with Sam, co-founder of Granola, who admitted a "pang of sadness" as a UI designer when users skip the interface entirely and just use the MCP. Sam's conclusion: "As soon as you become a big enough enterprise, it's inevitable you have all of this internal tooling. If Granola doesn't play nice with that internal tooling, then it's a non-starter." The second clip from Sam: "The easier it gets to build stuff, the more it matters to really sweat the details and go the extra mile."

**Guillermo Rauch** noted that Vercel's platform is now much faster, and as models speed up with Astra ultrafast, harness overhead matters more and more. The next release will feature better session storage and retrieval plus a big unlock for cloud durability in libfx. He also weighed in on the Rust debate, revealing Vercel has been undergoing a "Rust-ification" for a while, starting with Turborepo's migration from Go to Rust. The migration completed but the ROI was "quite controversial internally" because the human migration costs were substantial. His key insight: "The calculus has now changed. What's 'best for humans' is no longer necessarily 'best for business'." He also shared a rule of thumb for a new project: READMEs written by hand for human consumption, documentation internals in "AI English" for agents.

**Aaron Levie** outlined the new jobs AI is creating: AI engineers building applied products, forward deployed engineers deploying agents into companies, and new services firms. He emphasized that published stats undercount existing jobs transitioning to AI work, with banks, life sciences companies, manufacturers, and law firms all bringing on more technical talent or repositioning roles. He also argued that a consumer AI metric may tell us more about the business model than the state of AI, predicting consumer AI will be subsidized and monetized via commerce, ads, or device purchases.

**Matt Turck** highlighted that "models are grown, not built" and we don't really know how they work, citing Eric Ho of Goodfire AI on the urgent need for better interpretability.

**Zara Zhang** observed that Opus 5.5 "just silently goes off to make something for 20+ minutes and comes back with a complete masterpiece." She also noted that X profiles are replacing resumes.

**Nikunj Kothari** made the case for meeting founders at their own offices rather than over Zoom, arguing there is alpha in seeing office energy, how coworkers interact, how cofounders complement each other, and what beta product releases look like. He noted founders often tell him he is the only one who has ever asked.

**Dan Shipper** shared that dot has become his primary interface to AI, with his dot named "boo." He predicts that in a year he will still be interacting with ChatGPT as an always-on persistent agent, but boo will have disappeared, comparing it to early OpenClaw days when users loved personality quirks but dropped them as soon as something functionally more powerful arrived.

**Garry Tan** observed that when everyone is building the same primitives, it speaks to needs that will only intensify, and predicted eventual convergence on the correct OS.

**Ryo Lu** shared progress on a full-bleed desktop with side dock, describing it as a "lil computer in your pocket."

## 🎙 PODCASTS

**No Priors: Re-Founding Incumbents for the AI Era with Michael Lee**

**Takeaway**: The biggest AI opportunity is not building new startups but buying and rebuilding existing institutions with centralized operations and regulatory moats.

Michael Lee, co-founder and CEO of Sequence Holdings, joined No Priors to discuss the firm's $7.7 billion take-private of Baldwin with the Dell family office, the largest AI take-private to date. Sequence is a permanent holding company that works with management teams to buy and "refound" businesses to be market leaders with AI. The core thesis: AI will have an uneven impact on the economy, and certain industries where incumbents have advantages like brand, scale, network effects, or regulatory moats are better targets for transformation than startups.

Lee explained why the holding company structure was the only natural fit: "How do we align the duration of capital with the sustained investment and operational commitments that are going to be required to drive the transformation end to end?" He contrasted this with the three options a Fortune 500 CEO has for refounding: do it yourself (impossible to recruit and retain the talent), use services firms (incentives are misaligned, they optimize for getting in your wallet and staying there), or buy software (it is beta, available to everyone, and sold to workflows as they exist today, not as they could be).

The BankSouth investment served as the pilot. Lee noted that the regulated nature of banking was "a feature, not a bug" because operations are well defined, data hygiene is excellent, and the centralized nature means anything built at headquarters gets amortized over all branches. He described Sequence's platform, Atlas, with four layers: a data ontology that makes the business legible to models, an agent builder grounded in ground truth, Lattice for orchestration, and artifacts for application building. About 80% of the platform is homogenous across industries, with 20% vertically specific.

On the human side, Lee was candid: "We have an engineering problem and a human engineering problem, and the human engineering problem is much more difficult than the engineering problem." The key is making employees feel that AI elevates what they do rather than replaces them. On why insurance brokerage is the next target: it is a $2 trillion plus market, gross retention rates are 90%, the customer does not pay the broker (the carrier does), and it has been very hard for startups to compete. Sequence does about one deal per year.

keywords: AI agents | enterprise AI | AI transformation
headline: The AI Era Rewrites the Playbook for Incumbents and Builders
deck: A record take-private bets on refounding old companies with AI, while builders debate what agents mean for products, jobs, and the craft of software itself.
quote: In a world where you believe that alpha comes from engineering and AI, you need to create a culture whereby the celebrated persona is the engineer, and that's what's required.
quoteBy: Michael Lee · Co-Founder and CEO of Sequence Holdings

## 🧭 Daily Insights
**Core insight**: Builders are converging on the idea that AI's real value comes from reorganizing how work and companies are structured, not just speeding up existing workflows. At the same time, the tooling layer is consolidating fast, with agents becoming persistent interfaces and incumbents racing to refound themselves around frontier engineering.

## 𝕏 / TWITTER
Thibault Sottiaux, who works on Codex and ChatGPT at OpenAI, announced a 28-day cadence where each day the team will either ship one clear improvement relevant to most Codex and work users or ship a full reset, framing it as the start of a run of improvements.

Peter Yang, who makes practical AI tutorials and interviews, argued that OpenAI is right to simplify ChatGPT because it has become a mess. He listed what he would simplify: Work versus Codex, Spaces versus Pages versus Sites, and the model and effort picker. His hot take is that the whole Work launch was a mistake, comparing it to Claude folding Cowork back into Chat, and he does not think Work needs its own brand. He also shared an interview with Sam, co-founder of Granola, who said there is a pang of sadness as a UI designer when people skip the UI and just use the MCP, but that as soon as you become a big enough enterprise, internal tooling is inevitable, and if Granola does not play nice with it, it is a non-starter. Sam added that the easier it gets to build stuff, the more it matters to sweat the details, and that builders should hold themselves accountable not just to shipping but to whether the person actually gets daily value out of it.

Guillermo Rauch, CEO of Vercel, noted that a product is now much faster, and that as models speed up, harness overhead matters more and more, with the next release featuring better performance for session storage and retrieval and a big unlock for cloud durability in libfx. He also weighed in on Rust, saying DHH is fundamentally right, and that Vercel has been undergoing a Rust-ification, with Turborepo migrated from Go to Rust, though the ROI was controversial internally because the human migration costs were substantive. He argued the calculus has changed: what is best for humans is no longer necessarily best for business, and that Rust is unlikely to be the end-all toolchain since it was designed before the supersonic tsunami of agents. Separately, he described a new project where the README is fully written by hand for human consumption while the documentation internals are AI English for agents, suggesting blogs, tweets, and READMEs should stay human communication.

Aaron Levie, CEO of Box, said we are already seeing what kinds of new jobs AI is creating, including AI engineers building applied products, forward deployed engineers deploying agents into companies, and new services firms for deploying AI. He noted that published stats undercount existing jobs transitioning to AI work, and that every bank, life sciences company, manufacturer, and law firm is bringing on more technical talent or repositioning roles for agent deployment. In a second post, he argued a certain metric may tell us more about the business model of consumer AI than the state of AI, since consumer AI will almost inevitably be subsidized and monetized via commerce, ads, or device and service purchases, and the metric may level off lower than expected.

Ryo Lu, who designed Cursor, Notion, and Stripe, shared a bit more work on a full bleed desktop with a side dock, describing it as a little computer in your pocket.

Garry Tan, President and CEO of Y Combinator, observed that when everyone is building the same primitives it speaks to needs that will only intensify, and that we will eventually converge on the correct OS.

Matt Turck, a VC at FirstMark Capital and host of the MAD Podcast, highlighted that one aspect of AI is still poorly understood outside AI circles: models are grown, not built, and we do not really know how they work, hence the urgent need for better interpretability, citing Eric Ho of Goodfire AI.

Zara Zhang, a builder, marveled that Opus 5.5 just silently goes off to make something for 20+ minutes and comes back with a complete masterpiece. She also said X profiles are replacing resumes.

Nikunj Kothari, a partner at FPV Ventures, said he cannot believe how people make investments over a Zoom call and sometimes by just meeting the CEO, arguing there is so much alpha in meeting founders at their own office, where you can see the energy, how coworkers react and work together, how cofounders complement each other, and what beta product releases look like. He always asks to meet at offices for final meetings, and founders often tell him he is the only one who has ever asked.

Peter Steinberger, who describes himself as Polyagentmorous ClawFather and works on OpenClaw and with OpenAI, posted about bug fixes and performance improvements.

Dan Shipper, CEO of Every, said dot has become his primary interface to AI over the last few weeks, and his dot is named boo. He bets that in a year he will still be interacting with ChatGPT as an always-on persistent agent, but boo will have disappeared, comparing it to early OpenClaw days when people loved the personality quirks of their Claws but dropped them as soon as something functionally more powerful was available.

## 🎙 PODCASTS
**Takeaway**: The biggest AI opportunity may not be building new startups but buying and refounding incumbents, because the hardest part is not the engineering but the human engineering.

On No Priors, Michael Lee, co-founder and CEO of Sequence Holdings, joined to discuss the largest AI take-private to date, a $7,700,000,000 deal with the Dell family office for Baldwin, and how AI transformation will actually permeate the economy. Lee explained that Sequence is a permanent holding company that works with management teams to buy and refound businesses to be market leaders with AI, and that the firm aims to do one deal per year. He traced the idea back to his time at Lone Pine in 2017, when he first covered AI around AlphaGo and the first transformer paper, and to the moment ChatGPT arrived at the end of 2022, when it became obvious the world had forever changed because we finally had an architecture that could scale with compute. He argued AI will have an uneven impact on the economy: some parts, like restaurants and golf courses, will barely be touched, while others, like coding, will be won by startups, leaving a set of industries where incumbents hold all the advantages through brand, scale, network effects, or regulation. That is where Sequence wants to acquire the right incumbent and inherit those advantages.

Lee laid out why a holding company structure is the natural fit: it aligns the duration of capital with sustained investment, creates a culture oriented around forging market leaders rather than deploying capital, and lets retained earnings support both existing companies and new investments. He described the three options a Fortune 500 CEO has for refounding: doing it yourself, which founders struggle with because it is nearly impossible to recruit and retain the talent; hiring a services provider, which has an incentives problem since services firms optimize for getting in your wallet, staying there, and growing share of wallet; or buying software, which is beta and always sold around the workflow as it is designed today. Ownership, he said, solves the alignment problem.

On BankSouth, Lee said the regulated nature of a bank was a feature, not a bug, because operations are well defined, data hygiene is excellent, and the centralized nature of underwriting means anything built at headquarters gets amortized over all the branches. He contrasted this with roll-ups, which require integrating different systems and standardizing cultures. On Baldwin, he said the brokerage space fits because it is a $2,000,000,000,000 plus premiums market where incumbents have the advantages, gross retention rates are 90%, and the customer does not actually pay the broker, the carrier does. He also described Atlas, Sequence's shared platform, with four layers: a data ontology that makes the business legible to models, an agent builder grounded in ground truth, an orchestration engine called Lattice, and an application builder called artifacts. He noted that 80% of a business is largely homogenous and 20% is vertically specific, so the core infrastructure is reusable across companies.

One memorable quote from Lee: "In a world where you believe that alpha comes from engineering and AI, you need to create a culture whereby the celebrated persona is the engineer, and that's what's required." He added that Sequence has two problems, an engineering problem and a human engineering problem, and the human engineering problem is much more difficult than the engineering problem.

## 🎙 PODCASTS
**Takeaway**: The biggest AI opportunity may not be building new startups but buying great incumbents and re-founding them around frontier engineering.

On No Priors, Michael Lee, co-founder and CEO of Sequence Holdings, joined to discuss the largest AI take-private to date: a $7,700,000,000 deal with the Dell family office for Baldwin, an insurance brokerage. Sequence is a permanent holding company that partners with management teams to buy and re-found businesses as AI-era market leaders, and it aims to do roughly one deal per year.

Lee's thesis starts from an uneven impact of AI on the economy. Restaurants and golf courses will barely change, and in some industries a startup clearly wins, as with coding. But in industries where incumbents hold the advantages, whether brand, scale, network effects, or regulation, the better move is to acquire the right incumbent and inherit those advantages. He described the current moment as the equivalent of the next industrial revolution, and criticized the common pattern of giving small machines to every human in the human assembly line to speed up work. When machines can work 24/7 and scale with electricity, the right answer is to reorganize what an organization should be.

The structure matters. A holding company aligns the duration of capital with sustained investment, builds a platform shared across portfolio companies, and orients the culture around forging market leaders rather than deploying capital. Lee laid out why the alternatives fail: doing it yourself makes it nearly impossible to recruit and retain the talent, since every company has a celebrated persona, and in a world where alpha comes from engineering, the celebrated persona has to be the engineer. Services firms optimize for getting into your wallet, staying there, and growing their share of it, a path toward incrementalism, and they cannot change how people are organized or incentivized. Buying software means buying beta available to everyone, and vendors must sell to workflows as they are designed today, around a human assembly line that may not exist tomorrow.

BankSouth was the accidental perfect pilot. Sequence started in a services motion with a bank owned by the family of a friend, then became a permanent partner, closing in March after Fed and OCC approval. Lee said the difference between services and ownership was night and day: engineers take on more complexity when they know they will stay, employees feel supported for the long term, and the team can plan three, five, ten years out. The regulated nature of banking was a feature, not a bug, because operations are well defined and data hygiene is excellent, which works well for agents. Centralization mattered too: underwriting happens centrally, so anything built at headquarters amortizes across all branches, unlike roll-ups that require integrating systems and standardizing cultures.

On the platform side, Sequence built Atlas, which it expects to generalize across industries. Atlas has four layers: a data ontology that makes the business legible in code, an agent builder grounded in ground truth, Lattice as the orchestration engine that instruments workflows, and artifacts as the application builder on top. Lee estimated that 80% of a business is largely homogenous and 20% is vertically specific. He also admitted the human engineering problem is much harder than the engineering problem, and that post-investment the team learned to be far more attuned to employee anxiety, framing the work as elevating what people do and removing rote tasks.

The most memorable line came early: "In a world where you believe that alpha comes from engineering and AI, you need to create a culture whereby the celebrated persona is the engineer, and that's what's required."
