Peter Yang, who makes practical AI tutorials and interviews, called ChatGPT "a mess" and listed what he would simplify: Work versus Codex, Spaces versus Pages versus Sites, and the model and effort picker. His hot take is that the whole Work launch was a mistake, comparing it to Claude folding Cowork back into Chat. He also shared a clip of Sam, co-founder of Granola, on users skipping the UI entirely to use the MCP: "There's definitely a pang of sadness to that as a UI designer," Sam said, adding that for many workflows the best way to use Granola is to capture context and run it through an internal agent. In a separate clip, Sam argued that the easier it gets to build, the more the details matter: hold yourself accountable not just to shipping, but to whether the person gets daily value out of it.

Guillermo Rauch, CEO of Vercel, noted that as models speed up, harness overhead matters more and more, and teased better session storage and retrieval plus a cloud durability unlock in libfx. He weighed in on the Rust debate, saying DHH is fundamentally right and that Vercel has been undergoing a Rust-ification, starting with Turborepo's migration from Go. The migration completed, but the ROI was controversial internally because the human migration costs were substantive, and Go is fast and easy to iterate on. Now, he says, what's best for humans is no longer necessarily best for business, and Rust itself was designed before the supersonic tsunami of agents. He also described a new project where the README is fully written by hand for human consumption while the documentation internals are AI English for agents.

Aaron Levie, CEO of Box, mapped the jobs AI is creating: AI engineers building applied products for enterprises, forward deployed engineers deploying agents into companies, and new services firms. He noted that published stats undercount existing data, research, and software roles being repositioned for AI work, with every bank, life sciences company, manufacturer, and law firm bringing on more technical talent. In a second post, he argued that a consumer AI metric may say more about the business model than the state of AI, since consumer AI will almost inevitably be subsidized and monetized via commerce, ads, or device purchases, and may level off lower than expected.

Ryo Lu, who designed Cursor, Notion, and Stripe, shared a work-in-progress: full bleed desktop plus a side dock, a little computer in your pocket.

Garry Tan, President and CEO of Y Combinator, observed that when everyone is building the same primitives, it speaks to needs that will only intensify, and predicted eventual convergence on the correct OS.

Matt Turck, a VC at FirstMark Capital and host of the MAD Podcast, flagged what he considers the most poorly understood aspect of AI outside AI circles: models are grown, not built, and we don't really know how they work, hence the urgent need for better interpretability, citing Eric Ho of Goodfire AI.

Zara Zhang, a builder, marveled that Opus 5.5 silently goes off to make something for 20+ minutes and comes back with a complete masterpiece. She also noted that X profiles are replacing resumes.

Nikunj Kothari, a partner at FPV Ventures, pushed back on making investments over Zoom calls or after meeting only the CEO, arguing there is alpha in meeting founders at their own office: seeing office energy, how coworkers interact, how cofounders complement each other, and what beta releases look like. He said founders often tell him he is the only one who has ever asked to meet at their offices.

Dan Shipper, CEO of Every, said dot has become his primary interface to AI, with his dot named boo. He predicts that in a year he will still interact this way with ChatGPT as an always-on persistent agent, but boo will have disappeared, comparing it to early OpenClaw days when users loved the personality quirks but dropped them as soon as something functionally more powerful arrived.

## 🎙 PODCASTS

**Takeaway**: The biggest AI transformation may not come from startups disrupting incumbents, but from buying the incumbents and refounding them around engineering.

On No Priors, Michael Lee, co-founder and CEO of Sequence Holdings, explained why his firm just announced the largest AI take private to date with the Dell family office of Baldwin for $7,700,000,000. Sequence is a permanent holding company that works with management teams to buy and refound businesses to be market leaders with AI, and Lee says the firm does one deal per year: "What we do is scarce. We're trying to do one deal per year. That's it. Our job is to do one."

Lee traced the idea back to his time at Lone Pine in 2017, when he was asked to cover AI around the time AlphaGo and the first transformer paper came out. When ChatGPT arrived at the end of 2022, he realized the world had changed because there was finally an architecture that could scale with compute. He felt AI would have an uneven impact: restaurants and golf courses would be untouched, coding would be won by startups, but in industries where incumbents hold brand, scale, network effects, or regulatory advantages, the right move was to acquire the incumbent and inherit those advantages.

The core argument is about talent and incentives. Lee said every company has a celebrated persona, and at Blackstone it is the investor, which is why they aggregate the greatest investors. "In a world where you believe that alpha comes from engineering and AI, you need to create a culture whereby the celebrated persona is the engineer, and that's what's required." He described three options for a Fortune 500 CEO trying to refound: do it yourself, which fails on recruiting and retaining talent; hire services firms like Accenture, McKinsey, or Palantir, which optimize for getting in your wallet, staying in your wallet, and growing share of wallet; or buy software, which is beta by definition and always sells to the workflow as designed today, around the human assembly line as it exists now. Ownership, he argued, is what aligns incentives and duration of capital with sustained transformation.

On BankSouth, Sequence's first investment, Lee said the regulated nature of a bank was a feature, not a bug: operations are well defined, data hygiene is excellent, and rules are explicit, which works extremely well for agents. He also values centralized operations, or what he calls organizational physics: a bank may have many branches, but underwriting happens centrally, so anything built at headquarters amortizes across all branches. He contrasted this with roll-ups, which require integrating different systems, sending engineers to many places, and standardizing procedures and cultures.

Lee described Atlas, Sequence's shared platform, built at the bank and expected to generalize across industries. It has four layers: a data ontology that makes the business legible in code, an agent builder grounded in ground truth, an orchestration engine called Lattice that instruments workflows using those agents, and an application builder called artifacts on top. He said roughly 80% of a business is largely homogenous and 20% is vertically specific, which is why the core infrastructure is reusable at Baldwin and beyond.

The hardest part, he admitted, is human. "We have an engineering problem and a human engineering problem, and the human engineering problem is much more difficult than the engineering problem." Post-investment at the bank, he learned how much more attuned Sequence needs to be to how employees feel, since the work draws anxiety about what it means for them. The playbook is to elevate what people do, remove rote repetitive work, and make them feel their organization is winning.

keywords: evals | agents | proofs
headline: Evals Are the Product Spec
deck: Builders push agents from demo to deployment, arguing that evaluation harnesses and compile-time proofs now matter more than model choice, while a new generation of local agent environments quietly takes shape.
quote: The most common mistake teams make is to treat evals as an additional QA step once the agent is built. AI products are fundamentally different. Your evals are your product spec.
quoteBy: Madhu Guru · Sr Director, AI at Meta; Prev: Google - Led Gemini, Veo, Nano Banana.

## 🧭 Daily Insights

**Core insight**: The conversation has shifted from what models can do to how teams prove they work. Evals are being reframed as the product spec itself, and safety constraints are moving into the type system so agents cannot ship catastrophic bugs. Meanwhile builders are experimenting with local agent environments and token-efficient planning, treating the harness, not the model, as the real differentiator.

## 𝕏 / TWITTER

**Madhu Guru** argues that the most common mistake teams make is treating evals as an additional QA step once the agent is built. AI products are fundamentally different, and your evals are your product spec.

**Guillermo Rauch** introduced **gdp-ts**, Ghosts of Departed Proofs for TypeScript, a library, linter and AI skill for safer API design. Under this contract, sensitive functions require proofs that the caller performed an authorization check, and the typechecker verifies these proofs at compile time, preventing teams and agents from shipping catastrophic security bugs. He notes these patterns were niche in ecosystems like Haskell because of human code review and cognitive overhead, but the situation is now inverted: agents write more code than we can review and thrive in tight loops with hard constraints. The README models a real Vercel API product constraint where changing a Project password requires a proof of a certain role plus entitlement.
https://x.com/rauchg/status/2107119811444748555

**Aaron Levie** says a decent amount of agent adoption is bottlenecked by the ability to test, tune, and optimize agents on real work environments: the files agents need to access, CRM environments, email, and more. It is impossible to know how agents perform without understanding how well they execute on your evals and how they will perform after a model change or workflow upgrade. Every enterprise has to do this one by one right now, which is slow and tedious, and every enterprise will eventually have someone managing evals, infrastructure for building and running evals, and simulated environments. Huge space.
https://x.com/levie/status/2107283615247999257

**Thariq** highlights that planning this way is far more token efficient compared to raw HTML, since the model does not need to remake components or logic for common things like state machines, diagrams, and code snippets. His favorite name for the pattern is **local hands**: Claude runs in the cloud but can access your files locally, and it is also coming to cowork.
https://x.com/trq212/status/2107294499282293017
https://x.com/trq212/status/2107229483015258493

**Aditya Agarwal** says it would be interesting to run the **Muse/Dot** computer locally, since it feels like a better agent environment than increasingly locked down MacOS.
https://x.com/adityaag/status/2107133989941387282

**Garry Tan** argues that harnesses from labs have an incentive to burn tokens, which means harnesses from startups have real utility, like how **Grep** can automatically swap token burn into deterministic tested code that is repeatable just by observing agent use. He also points to **Halmos** building Muse/Instinct for coming AGI Science Loops.
https://x.com/garrytan/status/2107129959550685660
https://x.com/garrytan/status/2107173670699622830

**Amjad Masad** notes that the US is catching up on open-weights models, and says he is proud of how many family-run businesses are powered by **Replit**.
https://x.com/amasad/status/2107222388429766970
https://x.com/amasad/status/2107222889946898893

**Peter Yang** built an AI language learning app that teaches Japanese via live voice calls, with a tutorial covering using his spec skill to create key designs, setting up **Gemini Live** APIs for voice, and creating diorama art with **Nano Banana**. You can follow along to build your own app to learn 100 phrases for any language before a trip.
https://x.com/petergyang/status/2107108755699900459

**Ryo Lu** made a tool for language learners: watch Netflix with subtitles in any two languages, plus pronunciation guides for Japanese, Chinese, and Korean, with customizable styles and hand-picked defaults.
https://x.com/ryolu_/status/2107146629338042853

**Thibault Sottiaux** calls this possibly his best day so far at OpenAI, with ridiculous amounts of fun and intensity, and highlights Sergio cooking up magic with collaborative space right in ChatGPT, improving leaps and bounds every day.
https://x.com/thsottiaux/status/2107311729768353844
https://x.com/thsottiaux/status/2107200530477101461

Thariq, working on Claude Code at Anthropic, shared three threads. He pointed to game design resources for people getting into the field, explained that planning this way is far more token efficient than raw HTML because the model does not need to remake components or logic for state machines, diagrams, and code snippets, and named his favorite pattern "**local hands**": Claude runs in the cloud but can access your files locally, with the feature also coming to cowork.

Amjad Masad, CEO of Replit, showed a prompt-style use case, "Promote my app on tiktok," expressed pride in how many family-run businesses are powered by Replit, and observed that the US is catching up on **open-weights models**.

Guillermo Rauch, CEO of Vercel, introduced **gdp-ts**, Ghosts of Departed Proofs for TypeScript, a library, linter, and AI skill for safer API design. Under the contract, sensitive functions require proofs that the caller performed an authorization check, verified by the typechecker at compile time. He notes that while such patterns existed in ecosystems like Haskell, human code review plus cognitive and syntactic overhead kept them niche, and the situation is now inverted because agents write more code than we can review and thrive under hard constraints. The README models a real Vercel API constraint: changing a Project password requires proof of a certain role plus entitlement.

Aaron Levie, CEO of Box, said a decent amount of agent adoption is bottlenecked by the ability to test, tune, and optimize agents on real work environments: the files, CRM environments, email, and more. Without understanding how well agents execute on your evals, you cannot know how they will perform after a model change or workflow upgrade, and every enterprise is doing this one by one right now, which is slow and tedious. He predicts every enterprise will have someone managing evals, infrastructure for building and running them, and simulated environments.

Ryo Lu, who designed Cursor, Notion, and Stripe, wrote a long reflection on Steve Jobs, from growing up with beige boxes to seeing the iMac G4 in Canada and learning interface design by making his PC look like a Mac. He argues that since Jobs died we have been stuck in a loop of constant refinement, better supply chains, and more ways to keep people scrolling, with too little room for something truly great and heartfelt, and that we spend so much energy trying to beat humans instead of learning from people's lives and making them better. He also shipped **ryOS Subtitles** for Chrome, which lets you watch Netflix with subtitles in any two languages plus pronunciation guides for Japanese, Chinese, and Korean.

Garry Tan, President and CEO of Y Combinator, said AGI science loops are coming and there will be Muse/Instinct for those loops, which Halmos is building. He argued that harnesses from labs have an incentive to burn tokens, which gives startup harnesses real utility, like how Grep can automatically swap token burn into deterministic tested code that is repeatable just by observing agent use.

Aditya Agarwal, General Partner at SPC and co-founder of Bevel Health, said it would be interesting to run the Muse/Dot "computer" locally, calling it a better agent environment than increasingly locked down MacOS. He also noted that Sergey Levine, Berkeley EECS faculty since 2016 and cofounder of Physical Intelligence, is coming to SPC to talk about algorithms that let robots learn from experience.

## 🎙 PODCASTS

No podcasts in today's feed.

keywords: evals | agents | open-weights
headline: Evals Are the Product Spec Now
deck: Builders argue that testing agents on real work environments is the new bottleneck, while open-weights momentum shifts and Codex ships collaborative magic inside ChatGPT.
quote: The most common mistake teams make is to treat evals as an additional QA step once the agent is built. AI products are fundamentally different. Your evals are your product spec.
quoteBy: Madhu Guru · Sr Director, AI at Meta; Prev: Google - Led Gemini, Veo, Nano Banana.

## 🧭 Daily Insights

**Core insight**: The conversation has shifted from building agents to proving they work. Builders are converging on the idea that evals and simulated real-world environments are not a QA afterthought but the actual product spec, and that whoever owns the infrastructure for testing agents on real work will own the enterprise market. Meanwhile, the open-weights gap is narrowing and tooling for safer, more token-efficient agent workflows keeps maturing.

## 𝕏 / TWITTER

Madhu Guru, Sr Director of AI at Meta, argues that the most common mistake teams make is treating evals as an additional QA step once the agent is built. AI products are fundamentally different, and your evals are your product spec.

Aaron Levie, CEO of Box, says a decent amount of agent adoption is bottlenecked by the ability to test, tune, and optimize agents on real work environments, including the files, CRM environments, and email agents need to access. It is impossible to know how agents are performing without understanding how well they execute on your evals and how they will perform after a model change or workflow upgrade. Every enterprise has to do this one by one right now, which is slow and tedious, and every enterprise will eventually have someone managing evals and simulated environments. Huge space.

Guillermo Rauch, CEO of Vercel, introduced **gdp-ts**, Ghosts of Departed Proofs for TypeScript, a library, linter, and AI skill for safer API design. Under this contract, sensitive functions require proofs that the caller performed an authorization check, and the typechecker verifies these proofs at compile time, preventing teams and agents from shipping catastrophic security bugs. He notes that while these patterns have existed in ecosystems like **Haskell**, human code review plus cognitive and syntactic overhead made them niche, but the situation is now inverted since agents write more code than we can review and thrive in tight loops with hard constraints.

Thariq, on Claude Code at Anthropic, highlights that planning this way is far more token efficient compared to raw HTML, since the model does not need to remake components or logic for common things like state machines, diagrams, and code snippets. He calls his favorite name for the pattern **local hands**, where Claude runs in the cloud but can access your files locally, and notes it is also coming to **cowork**.

Amjad Masad, CEO of Replit, says he is really proud of how many family-run businesses are powered by Replit, and observes that the US is catching up on **open-weights** models.

Peter Yang, who writes practical AI tutorials, built an AI language learning app that teaches him Japanese via live voice calls. His tutorial covers using a spec skill to create key designs, setting up **Gemini Live** APIs for voice, and creating diorama art with **Nano Banana**, so you can build your own app to learn 100 phrases for any language before a trip.

Aditya Agarwal, General Partner at SPC, says it would be interesting to be able to run the **Muse/Dot** computer locally, since it feels like a better agent environment than increasingly locked down MacOS.

Garry Tan, President and CEO of Y Combinator, argues that harnesses from labs have an incentive to burn tokens, which means harnesses from startups have real utility, like how **Grep** can automatically swap token burn into deterministic tested code that is repeatable just by observing agent use. He also says AGI Science Loops are coming and there will be Muse/Instinct for those loops, which **Halmos** is building.

Ryo Lu, who designed Cursor, Notion, and Stripe, shipped **ryOS Subtitles** for Chrome, a tool for language learners to watch Netflix with subtitles in any two languages plus pronunciation guides for Japanese, Chinese, and Korean, with customizable styles and hand-picked defaults.

## 𝕏 / TWITTER
Thibault Sottiaux, Codex & ChatGPT at OpenAI, called it possibly his best day so far at the company, citing "ridiculous amounts of fun and intensity," and highlighted Sergio cooking up magic with collaborative space right inside **ChatGPT**, improving leaps and bounds daily.

Peter Yang, who makes practical AI tutorials and interviews, published a new tutorial on building an AI language learning app that teaches Japanese via live voice calls. It covers using a spec skill for key designs, setting up **Gemini Live** APIs for voice, and creating diorama art with **Nano Banana**, so you can build your own app to learn 100 phrases for any language before a trip.

Madhu Guru, Sr Director, AI at Meta, warned that the most common mistake teams make is treating **evals** as an additional QA step once the agent is built. AI products are fundamentally different: your evals are your product spec.

Thariq, of Claude Code at Anthropic, shared that planning this way is far more token efficient than raw HTML, since the model does not need to remake components or logic for common things like state machines, diagrams, and code snippets. His favorite name for the pattern is "local hands": **Claude** runs in the cloud but can access your files locally, and it is also coming to cowork.

Amjad Masad, CEO of Replit, celebrated how many family-run businesses are powered by **Replit**, and observed that the US is catching up on **open-weights models**.

Guillermo Rauch, CEO of Vercel, introduced **gdp-ts**: Ghosts of Departed Proofs for TypeScript, a library, linter, and AI skill for safer API design. Under this contract, sensitive functions require proofs that the caller performed an authorization check, and the typechecker verifies these at compile time. While such patterns existed in ecosystems like Haskell, human code review plus cognitive and syntactic overhead kept them niche. The situation is now inverted: agents write more code than we can review and thrive in tight loops with hard constraints, as seen with the rise of **Rust** and the borrow checker.

Aaron Levie, CEO of Box, argued that agent adoption is bottlenecked by the ability to test, tune, and optimize agents on real work environments: the files, CRM environments, email, and more. It is impossible to know how agents perform without understanding execution on your **evals** and how they will hold up after a model change or workflow upgrade. Every enterprise is doing this one by one right now, which is slow and tedious, and every enterprise will soon have someone managing evals, eval infrastructure, and simulated environments. Huge space.

Ryo Lu, who designed at Cursor, Notion, and Stripe, wrote a remembrance of Steve Jobs, tracing how seeing the iMac G4 pulled him into interface design and how he burned DVDs of keynotes to study them. He lamented that since Jobs died we have gotten stuck in a loop of constant refinement, better supply chains, and more ways to keep people scrolling, with so much talent spent on tiny improvements and so little room for something truly great and heartfelt. He also shipped **ryOS Subtitles** for Chrome, letting language learners watch Netflix with subtitles in any two languages plus pronunciation guides for Japanese, Chinese, and Korean.

Garry Tan, President and CEO of Y Combinator, said AGI Science Loops are coming and there will be Muse/Instinct for those loops, with **Halmos** building that. He noted harnesses from labs have an incentive to burn tokens, which gives startup harnesses real utility, like how **Grep** can automatically swap token burn into deterministic tested code that is repeatable just by observing agent use.

Aditya Agarwal, General Partner at SPC and Co-Founder of Bevel Health, said it would be interesting to run the Muse/Dot "computer" locally, since that feels like a better agent environment than increasingly locked down **MacOS**.
